Paraguay in brief You’ve been learning Spanish and practicing tú eres, tú tienes, and tú quieres. Then someone in Paraguay asks you ¿Vos sos de Estados Unidos? (Are you from the United States?), or you hear ¿Querés algo más? (Would you like anything else?) at a restaurant. Wait, wasn’t that different in Spanish class?
I know that feeling all too well. Even now, after a few years here in Paraguay, I sometimes need a moment to think when someone asks me a question using vos or tenés. My brain first searches for the form I’m used to. 😄
But that’s perfectly normal in Paraguayan Spanish. The informal form of address is often vos instead of tú. Linguists call this voseo.
Why Do People Use “Vos” in Paraguay? # Vos wasn’t invented in Paraguay, and it didn’t come from Guaraní. It dates back to older Spanish and was once even used as a polite form of address.
Over time, tú became the familiar form of address in Spain, while vos remained in use in several parts of Latin America. Besides Paraguay, these include Argentina and Uruguay.
Today, vos is completely normal in Paraguay as an informal, familiar form of address. You’ll hear it between friends, in families, and among acquaintances, but also in casual everyday encounters, such as when shopping or having a quick chat while you’re out. For more formal situations, people still use usted, for example with certain professional contacts or when speaking to older people. But this isn’t a strict rule. Which form is appropriate also depends on how well you know each other.
From “Tú Tienes” to “Vos Tenés” # With voseo, it’s not just the pronoun that changes. Some verb forms sound different, too:
In Spanish class with tú In Paraguay with vos Tú eres Vos sos Tú tienes Vos tenés Tú quieres Vos querés Tú puedes Vos podés Tú hablas Vos hablás But don’t worry, you don’t have to relearn all of Spanish grammar. Words like te and tu stay the same, for example in ¿Cómo te llamás? (What’s your name?) or tu casa (your house).
And then there’s Jopará in Paraguay, too. This refers to mixing or switching between Spanish and Guaraní in everyday conversation. Voseo, on the other hand, is part of Spanish itself.
Do I Have to Use “Vos” Too? # No, of course not. If you’ve learned to use tú, you can keep using it. People in Paraguay will understand you that way, too.
But as you become more familiar with typical vos forms, you’ll feel a bit more confident and at home in conversations. And when you hear ¿Querés algo más?, maybe one day you’ll only have to think about whether you’ve got room for dessert. 😉
Would you like to learn more about this topic? ➔ Yes, please Do you still have a question about this topic? Feel free to write to me. Send your question
summary: You learn tú in Spanish class, but in Paraguay you hear vos. Find out why, which forms are common, and whether you need to use them yourself.
title: Why Do People in Paraguay Say “Vos” Instead of “Tú”?

On October 1, Jopara is served. A full pot is meant to keep the feared Karai Octubre and the threat of scarcity at bay. You might notice a red bracelet around a baby’s wrist. On Palm Sunday, carefully woven palm arrangements are brought to be blessed.
You’ll come across customs in Paraguay throughout the year, at festivals and in everyday life. They bring families together, give religious celebrations their familiar character, or express hopes for good luck and protection. Some are widely known; others you may only discover through personal encounters.
Which customs people follow and what they mean to them vary from one family, region, or community to another. Here you’ll find an overview of typical examples and the beliefs behind them.
Quick Facts at a Glance Throughout the year: Well-known examples include Kurusu Ára on May 3, San Juan around June 24, Carrulim on August 1, and Jopara on October 1. Family and everyday life: Godparenthood, Tupanói (asking for a blessing), protective bracelets for babies, and sharing Tereré are also among the customs and everyday habits described here. Folk beliefs: Some customs and objects are associated with protection, good luck, or bad luck. People who follow these traditions do not necessarily take the beliefs behind them literally. Regional diversity: Arete Guasu in the Chaco and San Baltazar in Kamba Kua are examples of customs closely connected to particular communities. Not automatically a public holiday: Even if a custom has a fixed date, that does not mean the day is an official day off work. Customs, Folk Beliefs, and Stories: What’s the Difference? # Tradition is the broadest of these terms. It includes actions and rituals, as well as knowledge, habits, and stories passed down through generations. A custom is one part of this.
Customs: repeated practices # A custom is something people do repeatedly on a particular occasion or in a particular situation. It is passed down within a family or community and often has a special meaning.
Eating Jopara on October 1, decorating a cross on Kurusu Ára, or asking older relatives for their blessing are all examples. The occasion might be a particular date, a religious celebration, or a family gathering. Everyday life has its customs, too.
Customs do not stay the same forever. As the people who practice them change, customs can also change or become less important over time.
Folk beliefs: traditional ideas # Folk beliefs are ideas passed down over time about good luck, protection, bad luck, or supernatural influences. A custom can grow out of such a belief, but not every belief is connected to a particular action.
One example is a baby’s red bracelet: according to this belief, it is meant to protect against ojeo, the evil eye. Eating Jopara is connected to the belief in Karai Octubre and the threat of scarcity.
Myths and legends: stories about beings and events # Myths, legends, and other traditional stories tell of extraordinary beings, events, or places. In Paraguay, these include figures such as Pombero, Jasy Jatere, and Luisón, as well as stories about ghosts, treasure, and landscapes.
These stories are part of Paraguay’s cultural heritage. Just because someone knows or retells them does not mean they personally believe in them.
The boundaries often overlap: Jopara on October 1 brings together a custom, folk beliefs, and the story of Karai Octubre.
Customs Throughout the Year # Many customs have a fixed place on the calendar. But that does not mean they are celebrated on exactly the same date everywhere. Some local festivities take place on another day or over the weekend.
When? Custom What happens? Palm Sunday and Holy Week Pindó karai and Chipa apo Having palm arrangements blessed and baking Chipa together May 3 Kurusu Ára Decorating crosses, praying, and sharing Chipa June, especially around the 24th San Juan Community celebrations with games, food, and performances August 1 Carrulim Drinking a mixture of Caña, Ruda, and Limón October 1 Jopara and Karai Octubre Cooking and eating Jopara to symbolically keep scarcity away November 1 and 2 Todos los Santos and Día de los Fieles Difuntos Visiting graves, bringing flowers, and remembering loved ones who have died December Caacupé and the Christmas season Going on pilgrimages, fulfilling vows, and setting up nativity scenes Semana Santa: palm arrangements and baking Chipa together # On Palm Sunday, woven palm arrangements and small palm objects are brought to be blessed. Some people then keep them at home or take them along when they go out. These objects are also associated with beliefs about protection.
During Holy Week, baking Chipa together, known as chipa apo, is a particularly visible family tradition. Preparing and baking it together also passes on each family’s way of making Chipa. This helps keep knowledge and customs alive across generations.
You can learn more about the Easter period in our detailed article on Semana Santa in Paraguay.
May 3: Kurusu Ára and decorated crosses # Kurusu Ára, the Day of the Cross, is observed on May 3. Crosses or niches containing crosses are decorated with plants, ornaments, and Chipa. After the prayers, the Chipa may be taken down in a custom known as chipa po’o and then shared.
If you come across the different names, here’s what they mean: Kurusu Ára refers to the occasion, Kurusu Jegua to the decorated cross, and chipa po’o to taking down the Chipa.
June: San Juan, games, food, and community # San Juan celebrations are among the most visible community festivals during Paraguay’s winter. The religious observance falls on June 24, but schools, communities, chapels, and clubs also hold celebrations on other days in June.
Traditional games include kambuchi jejoka, where a pot is broken, and carrera vosa, the familiar sack race. One of the fire-related customs is pelota tata, in which a burning cloth ball is kicked around the festival grounds.
Love also has its place around San Juan. The traditional pruebas de San Juan are small fortune-telling rituals about love and the future. For example, candle wax dripped into water is said to reveal the first letter of a future love’s name. People also look for that letter in the rust marks on a knife that has been stuck into a banana plant.
And, of course, sharing food is part of the celebration. Our collection of traditional San Juan dishes is a good place to start exploring the food.
August 1: Carrulim for good luck and protection # For some people, August begins with a small glass of Carrulim. Its name comes from the ingredients Caña, Ruda, and Limón.
The mixture is associated with traditional beliefs about good luck, protection, and cleansing. How Carrulim is prepared and drunk varies depending on the tradition. The number of sips can vary, too.
October 1: Jopara and Karai Octubre # On October 1, people traditionally eat Jopara, a hearty dish made with white corn (Locro) and beans. It is linked to Karai Octubre, a figure associated with scarcity and a time when food supplies run low.
A full pot is a symbolic way of saying: There is enough food in the house. In this way, people seek to keep the threat of scarcity at bay.
You can learn more about the custom and the idea of October as a time of scarcity in our article on Jopara and Karai Octubre.
November 1 and 2: visiting graves and remembering # Around All Saints’ Day on November 1 and All Souls’ Day (Día de los Fieles Difuntos) on November 2, relatives visit cemeteries and bring flowers to graves. Families remember their loved ones who have died and observe these days in their own way.
December: pilgrimages, vows, and nativity scenes # December 8 is closely connected to the Virgen de los Milagros de Caacupé. Many pilgrims set out for Caacupé in the days leading up to it. Prayers and personal promesas, or vows, are part of this religious tradition.
During the Christmas season, you’ll come across the pesebre, the nativity scene. Families decorate their nativity scenes with different materials and decorations. One typically Paraguayan feature is the Flor de coco, whose scent is part of Christmas for many people.
Each family decides when to set up its nativity scene. There is no single date everyone follows.
Customs in Family and Everyday Life # Not all customs are tied to a particular day. Many are part of family life or everyday habits. Here are a few examples.
Babies and the red bracelet # According to folk beliefs, a red bracelet around a newborn’s wrist is meant to protect against negative influences or ojeo, the so-called evil eye. Whether a baby wears one depends on the family.
This belief has been documented in Paraguay, including in a study at the Niños de Acosta Ñu children’s hospital in San Lorenzo.
Godparenthood: more than a role at baptism # The role of godparents begins with baptism and can extend well beyond the ceremony. It also creates a social bond between parents and godparents, known as compadrazgo. Parents call the godparents compadres or comadres. They can become important people in the family’s wider circle.
You can see how this connection continues in everyday life through small things. People proudly share in status updates that they are now a comadre or compadre. At birthdays and other family celebrations, you may see messages thanking godparents who organized a party for their godchild or gave them a special gift.
How close the compadrazgo relationship becomes depends on the family. Each family decides for itself whether and how godparents contribute to celebrations, gifts, or financial support.
Tupanói: blessings and respect # Another custom connected to godparenthood and respect for older family members is Tupanói, asking for a blessing.
Children or younger relatives may greet parents, grandparents, or godparents with their hands clasped and ask for their blessing. This religious gesture also expresses respect for older family members or those with whom they share a particularly close bond. Giving the blessing is called jehovasa.
We’ve seen this greeting several times out here in the countryside, too. For example, when the son of one of our workers came by to bring food, he first greeted his father with his hands clasped. In that brief moment, a greeting, respect for his father, and a request for a blessing came together.
Death and mourning: praying and remembering together # After a death, relatives and neighbors come together to pray. Traditional customs include novenas lasting nine days and their special conclusion, the novena pahá. Depending on the family, sharing food may also be part of the gathering.
Prayer, remembrance, and being together can help relatives feel connected during this time. How each day is observed varies, but gathering gives people space to share their grief.
Reliques: protective objects for the home, car, or wallet # The woven palm objects from Palm Sunday can remain part of everyday life even after they have been blessed.
These reliques, small protective objects or amulets, and similar palm items may be kept alongside religious objects such as a Bible, in a wallet, or in a car. They are believed to protect against misfortune or negative influences. Larger blessed palm arrangements may also be kept behind doors or elsewhere in the home.
Small folk beliefs around the home # Sometimes folk beliefs are reflected in very simple actions. One traditional belief says that turning a glass upside down in a corner can help you find something you’ve lost. Sweeping at night, on the other hand, is associated with bad luck.
You’ll often see snake plants (lengua de suegra or espada de San Jorge) near home entrances, outside shops, or around properties. They are associated with protection against negative influences, good luck, and prosperity.
We’ve also been told here that the plant is supposed to protect the house and property and even attract money. So naturally, we planted a few.
Such beliefs are often passed on casually. People may know them from their family or have heard about them at some point. Some are still followed, while others are retold with a smile.
Promesas: a personal vow # Promesas are especially visible around Caacupé, but they are not limited to that occasion. A promesa often links a request or an expression of thanks to a personal promise.
For example, someone might promise to make a pilgrimage to a shrine or carry out a particular action. What someone promises is a personal choice. The connection between asking, giving thanks, and keeping that promise is an important part of the custom.
Sharing Tereré as an everyday tradition # Some traditions do not need a festival or religious occasion. Sharing Tereré is one of them: people sit together, drink, and talk.
The gathering also passes on habits around preparation and knowledge of the traditional medicinal herbs (pohã ñana) used in the drink. Spending time together is just as much a part of Tereré’s cultural significance as the drink itself.
You can learn more about this social side and the national day dedicated to Tereré in our article on Día Nacional del Tereré.
Regional and Community Traditions # Some festivals and customs are closely connected to particular regions or communities. They show how varied cultural traditions can be across Paraguay.
Arete Guasu is celebrated by communities of the Guaraní Occidental people in the Paraguayan Chaco. Masks, dancing, flutes, and drums are part of the celebration, along with the corn harvest and remembrance of ancestors.
During Guaykurú Ñemondé in Compañía Minas near Emboscada, promeseros wear striking feather costumes and masks during celebrations for San Francisco Solano. Vows and religious devotion are central to this local tradition, which is passed down within families.
Around January 6, San Baltazar in Kamba Kua, in Fernando de la Mora, takes center stage. The Afro-Paraguayan community honors its patron saint with drums and dancing, passing on its own forms of cultural expression.
These celebrations are part of the history and community life of the people who observe them. They bring together customs, religious beliefs, remembrance of ancestors, and the passing on of traditions.
How Might You Encounter These Traditions Today? # Some customs are easy to notice. Others may only catch your attention when someone explains why a palm arrangement hangs in a car or why a family member asks for a blessing with their hands clasped.
In everyday life, people do not always call something a custom. Often, they simply say: That’s just how we do things here. Talking to them can help you understand what the action means to their family and whether religion or folk beliefs play a role.
If something catches your attention, a simple question is a good place to start: How do you do this in your family or where you live? The answer can give you a better understanding of how people themselves see and practice their customs.

Well-known examples include Carrulim on August 1, Jopara on October 1, San Juan celebrations in June, Kurusu Ára on May 3, and customs around Semana Santa. There are also family traditions such as godparenthood and asking for blessings, communal prayers, and everyday customs such as sharing Tereré. Are Jopara, Carrulim, or San Juan official public holidays? No. These days and customs have cultural or religious significance, but they are not regular public holidays in Paraguay. A well-known custom or commemorative day does not automatically mean that government offices, banks, or shops are closed. How are traditions, customs, and folk beliefs different? Tradition is the broadest term and includes actions, knowledge, habits, and stories passed down over time. A custom is a repeated practice, such as eating Jopara on October 1 or decorating a cross on Kurusu Ára. Folk beliefs are traditional ideas, for example about protection, good luck, or bad luck. These beliefs may be connected to a custom. What does Tupanói mean? Tupanói means asking for a blessing, for example from parents, grandparents, or godparents. This greeting is also a traditional way of showing respect to older family members or people with whom someone shares a particularly close bond. Giving the blessing is called jehovasa. What does a red bracelet on a baby mean? The red bracelet is believed to protect against negative influences or ojeo, the so-called evil eye. This belief is documented in Paraguay, but not every family follows this custom in the same way. Conclusion # Customs show what connects people and what matters to them: family, faith, remembering those who have died, or the hope for good luck and protection. Sometimes this takes the form of a big celebration, sometimes a small gesture that barely stands out in everyday life.
That is also why traditions remain part of life in Paraguay today. They are passed on, change, or become less important over time. Knowing their background helps you understand why a plate of Jopara, a palm arrangement, or a request for a blessing can mean more than you might first think.
If you want to know when public holidays and special days take place in Paraguay and what they mean for everyday life, you can find dates and background information in our overview of public holidays in Paraguay.

content:
October 12, 2026, falls on a Monday – and since it is an official commemorative day, it is natural to wonder whether it is also a public holiday. In fact, the “Day of the Republic” in Paraguay is not a regular day off work.
Still, this date marks an important historical step: on October 12, 1813, Paraguay adopted a new system of government and was explicitly described as a republic. Let’s take a closer look at why this step has its own significance alongside independence in 1811, and what the day means in everyday life today.
Quick Facts at a Glance Date: Monday, October 12, 2026 Official name: Día de la Proclamación del Paraguay como República Status: statutory commemorative day; as of October 4, 2026, not a nationwide public holiday or general day off Occasion: commemoration of the government regulation adopted on October 12, 1813 Significance: Congress reorganized the government and named Yegros and Francia as consuls of the Republic of Paraguay. Everyday life in 2026: No nationwide day off. Local or institutional asuetos may apply independently. What Is October 12 in Paraguay? # October 12 is an official commemorative day in Paraguay.
It commemorates October 12, 1813, when Congress adopted the Reglamento de Gobierno, the government regulation for the new political order, and Paraguay was proclaimed a republic.
The official name is Día de la Proclamación del Paraguay como República, which roughly translates as “Day of the Proclamation of Paraguay as a Republic.” A shorter name for the day is Día de la República (Day of the Republic).
Since 2020, Ley 6576 has officially designated October 12 as an annual commemorative day. Paraguay now formally commemorates a political step taken more than two centuries ago.
Is October 12, 2026, a Public Holiday in Paraguay? # No. As things currently stand, Monday, October 12, 2026, is not a nationwide public holiday or general day off in Paraguay.
The law establishing the Día de la Proclamación del Paraguay como República declares October 12 a commemorative day, but does not make it a general day off work. The date is also not included in the current list of national public holidays.
For everyday planning, that distinction matters. If you normally work on Mondays, go to school, or have an appointment at a government office, you should not automatically expect a day off or public holiday schedules because of the commemorative day. Shops, transport services, and private businesses also do not automatically switch to public holiday schedules on October 12.
Independently of this, local or institutional asuetos may apply. They then only affect the explicitly specified area or institution and do not turn October 12 into a nationwide public holiday.
The day is mainly historical and institutional in character and is less associated with parades or other established traditions. Daily life remains fairly quiet. The commemoration is most visible in historical or official posts and reports around the anniversary.
Why Are Both 1811 and 1813 Important for Paraguay? # The two years represent different steps in the early development of the Paraguayan state.
On May 14 and 15, 1811, the independence movement succeeded in Asunción. Paraguay then established its own government. These events remain the central reference point for Independence Day in Paraguay.
Yegros, Francia, and Pedro Juan Caballero were among the leading figures of the independence period. In 1813, Yegros and Francia became consuls of the Republic.
Artwork: Guillermo Da Re, 1890 · Public Domain · Source: Wikimedia Commons In 1813, a different question took center stage: How should Paraguay now be governed and politically organized? Congress adopted a new system of government and explicitly used the name República del Paraguay.
Year What Does the Date Represent? What Changed? 1811 The independence movement and the beginning of independent rule Paraguay established its own political leadership. 1813 A republican form of government Congress adopted a new government regulation and placed two consuls at the head of the republic. Independence and a republic therefore do not mean the same thing. Independence mainly concerns political self-rule free from outside control. A republic, by contrast, describes how the state is organized and governed.
What Did the Congress of 1813 Decide? # The Second National Congress met in Asunción on September 30, 1813. Historical accounts describe more than a thousand representatives from different parts of the country.
Relations with Buenos Aires were an important political issue. Congress rejected the idea of sending Paraguayan representatives to the planned assembly there. This made clear that Paraguay wanted to decide for itself how it would be governed.
On October 12, the Reglamento de Gobierno, consisting of 17 articles, was finally adopted.
Congress met in what was then the Templo or Convento de la Merced. Today, the site lies in the area of the Plaza de la Democracia in Asunción. The former monastery building no longer exists.
What Did the Government Regulation Set Out? # The Reglamento de Gobierno consisted of 17 articles. It set out not only who would govern Paraguay, but also how this joint government would work:
Fulgencio Yegros and José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia were to lead the government jointly as consuls. Important government business generally had to be signed by both. The chairmanship alternated between them every four months. A congress was also to meet every year to discuss the country’s well-being, improvements to the government, and possible abuses. Another interesting point is that this arrangement was not intended to be permanent. It was to remain in place only until a later congress decided otherwise.
Yegros and Francia as Consuls # The regulation refers to Yegros and Francia as consuls of the Republic of Paraguay. They were to lead the government together and initially had equal standing.
This office had nothing to do with a modern consulate or with a diplomat serving abroad.
The consulate lasted only a short time. In 1814, Francia took over sole leadership of the state. His later rule shaped Paraguay for many years. In Paraguayan historical accounts, Francia is still referred to as Karai Guasu, roughly meaning “great lord.” This is a historical nickname, not an official title from 1813.
What Did “Republic” Actually Mean in 1813? # The term “republic” did not mean that Paraguay was already a democracy in the modern sense in 1813. The Reglamento de Gobierno mainly dealt with the leadership of the state and the joint government by the two consuls. Universal voting rights, today’s separation of powers, and modern fundamental rights did not yet exist in this form.
October 12 therefore commemorates an important step in the further development of Paraguay’s political system, not the creation of today’s democratic system of government. The current constitutional system came much later. You can read more about it in the article on Constitution Day in Paraguay.

You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → ❓ Frequently Asked Questions About October 12 in Paraguay # Is October 12, 2026, a public holiday in Paraguay? No. As things currently stand, October 12, 2026, is not a nationwide public holiday or general day off. It is a commemorative day established by law. Limited local or institutional asuetos may apply separately. Can there still be an Asueto on October 12? Yes. A local or institutional asueto may be declared independently of the commemorative day. It then applies only to the explicitly specified area or institution; this does not turn October 12 into a nationwide statutory public holiday. Why is 1811 the year of independence if Paraguay became a republic in 1813? The years represent different steps. 1811 is associated with the independence movement and the beginning of independent Paraguayan rule. 1813 marks the new republican form of government and the regulation naming Yegros and Francia as consuls. Was the government regulation of 1813 Paraguay’s first constitution? Views on this differ. The Reglamento de Gobierno of 1813 addressed central questions about how the state was governed and therefore had constitutional significance. Whether it should be called Paraguay’s first constitution depends on how narrowly the term “constitution” is defined. In any case, it was not a modern democratic constitution in today’s sense. Conclusion # This commemorative day shows that historical significance and visibility in everyday life do not always go hand in hand. For most people in Paraguay, daily routines change very little on this day, but the date still recalls an important step in the country’s political development.
Looking at 1811 and 1813 makes it clear that independence and the further organization of the state did not happen on the same date. This also helps explain why October 12 still has its own place in Paraguay’s historical memory.
If you would like to see how Paraguay developed from those early years onward, you can find the wider context in History of Paraguay: From the Guaraní to Today.

Paraguay in brief Yes, foreigners can generally vote in municipal elections in Paraguay. However, simply living in Paraguay is not enough. The Paraguayan Constitution explicitly refers to foreigners with radicación definitiva (permanent residency). You must also meet the legal requirements and be registered in the Registro Cívico Permanente (RCP) (permanent voter register).
The legal basis is Article 120 of the Paraguayan Constitution ↗.
What do voters elect in municipal elections? # In the Elecciones municipales (municipal elections), eligible voters elect the Intendente Municipal (municipal mayor) and the members of the Junta Municipal (roughly, the municipal council).
The Intendente is responsible for the general administration of the Municipalidad. The Junta Municipal, by contrast, is the municipality’s regulatory, oversight, and deliberative body. Both are part of the municipal government, but they have different responsibilities.
The voting rights of foreign residents apply to these municipal elections – they do not provide a general right to vote in all elections in Paraguay.
What requirements apply to foreigners? # The first important requirement is radicación definitiva. According to the Justicia Electoral, temporary residency alone is not enough.
You must also be at least 18 years old, legally eligible to vote, and registered in the Registro Cívico Permanente. You vote in the electoral district where you are registered.
However, the rule is not as simple as “permanent residency = voting rights.” The Paraguayan Código Electoral (Electoral Code) contains an additional provision concerning foreigners who are eligible to exercise voting rights in another country.
You can find this rule in Article 122 of the Paraguayan Electoral Code ↗. Whether this restriction applies in an individual case should therefore be checked against your own registration status and, if necessary, directly with the Justicia Electoral.
What about the 2026 municipal elections? # The municipal elections will take place on October 4, 2026. For this election, RCP registrations and updates completed by December 30, 2025 are taken into account.
So if you only registered in the RCP during 2026, you can no longer use that registration to participate in the October 2026 municipal elections. These new registrations will apply to later elections.
You can check whether you are registered for the current election and find your polling place through the official RCP lookup provided by the Justicia Electoral ↗ using your Paraguayan Cédula number and date of birth.
Note: This article provides general information and is not a substitute for individual legal advice. Whether you are eligible to vote in a specific election depends on your personal status, your registration in the RCP, and the applicable Paraguayan electoral law. For binding information, contact the Justicia Electoral.

Paraguay in brief In Paraguayan recipes, locro can actually mean two different things: dried white corn used in a variety of dishes, and a traditional dish that is also called locro. Which meaning is intended usually becomes clear from the context.
What does locro mean as an ingredient? # If a Paraguayan recipe lists, for example, “200 g of locro”, it does not mean a ready-made soup. Here, locro refers to dried white corn that is usually soaked before cooking and then simmered for a long time.
You will find it, for example, in Jopara, the traditional corn-and-bean dish associated with October 1. White corn is also used for Mazamorra, known in Guaraní as Kaguyjy.
In Paraguay, you may also come across the term Locrillo. It refers to peeled and more finely crushed or cracked corn. As a result, the cooking time can also be different.
And when is locro a dish? # Locro is also the name of traditional dishes. A classic example is Locro blanco, a thick preparation made with locro corn, onions, and Queso Paraguay. There are also versions with meat or cassava.
This also explains why the term can be confusing at first: in an ingredient list, locro means the corn – while on a menu or in a recipe title, it can refer to the finished dish.
In other South American countries, locro also often refers to a hearty stew. The ingredients and preparation methods vary by country and region.
Locro is part of Paraguay’s culinary heritage # In Paraguay, locro does not refer only to white corn used as an ingredient. The name is also used for traditional dishes made from it. In 2017, the Secretaría Nacional de Cultura recognized the traditional preparation of Locro, together with Sopa Paraguaya, Vori Vori, and Jopara, as part of Paraguay’s intangible cultural heritage.
So the next time you see “locro” in the ingredient list of a Paraguayan recipe, you will know: it most likely means the white corn – not a ready-made stew.

White corn, beans, squash, a few vegetables, and, above all, a little time: These simple ingredients, common in Paraguay, come together as Jopara, a hearty corn and bean stew that is surprisingly filling. From one kitchen to another, the dish can be simple or much richer.
Here, we make Jopara without meat or cheese—a budget-friendly version with just a few ingredients. Along with the step-by-step instructions, you’ll also find well-known variations and ideas for building on the basic stew.
📝 Jopara Recipe: Step by Step # At a Glance Difficulty: easy Soaking time: 8 to 12 hours Prep time: about 20 to 25 minutes Cooking time: about 1½ to 2 hours Servings: about 5 main-dish servings Suitable for: vegan (and therefore vegetarian); gluten-free when made with water or vegetable broth labeled gluten-free Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 🛒 Ingredients for Jopara # Many of these ingredients are everyday staples in Paraguay and are easy to find there.
Main Ingredients # 200 g locro (dried white corn) 200 g dried red or black beans (poroto) 2 onions 2 tomatoes 1 small green bell pepper (locote) 1 carrot 250 to 300 g squash (zapallo) 2 garlic cloves 2 tbsp vegetable oil 1 bay leaf about 2 liters of water or mild vegetable broth a little extra hot water, if needed salt and pepper parsley, green onion, or fresh cilantro (kuratũ) to taste If possible, use just one type of bean. Different varieties may take different amounts of time to soften.
What Can You Substitute? # Ingredient Substitutions Locro/Locrillo: Outside Paraguay, you may find white corn sold as maíz blanco para locro. Locrillo is another option; depending on the product, the grain size and cooking time may vary. Precooked white corn or canned hominy: Both can work as quicker alternatives and should be added later in the cooking process. Hominy is nixtamalized corn, however, so it is not the same as dried locro; the flavor and texture may differ. Beans: You can use dried red or black beans. Canned beans also work and save time. Add them later and use the drained weight when measuring. Squash: Hokkaido or butternut squash can work well as alternatives to Paraguayan zapallo. Equipment # 2 bowls for soaking 1 large cooking pot 1 skillet or small pot for the vegetables strainer knife and cutting board cooking spoon 👩‍🍳 Step-by-Step Instructions # Prepare the Day Before # Put the locro and beans in separate bowls and cover each generously with water. Soak for 8 to 12 hours, preferably overnight. The next day, discard the soaking water and rinse the locro and beans thoroughly. Chop the onions, tomatoes, and locote. Cut the carrot into slices or small cubes. Cut the squash into pieces about 2 cm (about ¾ inch) across. Finely chop the garlic. Cook the Jopara # Cook the locro and beans first: Bring the locro and beans to a boil with the bay leaf and about 2 liters of fresh water. Cook over medium heat for about 50 to 60 minutes, then check them. Continue cooking until the locro and beans are almost tender. Add hot water if needed. The actual cooking time may vary depending on the product and how long it has been stored. Sauté the vegetables: Once the locro and beans are almost tender, heat the oil in a skillet. Sauté the onions and garlic until softened. Add the locote, tomatoes, and carrot, and cook for a few more minutes. Add the vegetables to the stew: Add the sautéed vegetables and squash to the locro and beans. Stir well. Finish cooking: Simmer everything gently for another 20 to 30 minutes, until the locro and beans are fully tender and the carrot and squash are cooked. If the Jopara becomes too thick, add hot water a little at a time. For a thicker stew: Mash a few soft pieces of squash right in the pot.
Season: Add salt and pepper to taste. Stir in parsley, green onion, or finely chopped kuratũ just before serving. The finished Jopara should be thick, but still have enough liquid to remain a stew.
Nutrition Information # For a batch of about 5 servings, the estimated nutrition per serving is:
Nutrient Per Serving Calories about 360 kcal Protein about 14.5 g Carbohydrates about 63 g Fat about 6 g Fiber about 12 g Note: These are calculated averages and may vary somewhat depending on the type of beans, the size of the vegetables, and the serving size. The calculation uses water; vegetable broth may especially affect the sodium content. Side dishes and variations with cheese or meat are not included.
🍽️ What Goes with Jopara? # Jopara is already a filling main dish, but it is often served with a simple side.
Sides Drinks Classic: Boiled mandioca goes well with Jopara. Savory: Tortilla paraguaya is also served with it. For a heartier meal: A small serving of Sopa Paraguaya can also be served alongside it. Simple: Water always works and lets the flavor of the stew stand on its own. Fruity: A fruit juice that isn’t too sweet is an easy alternative. 🔄 Jopara Recipe Variations # Although the basic ingredients are shared, one pot of Jopara can be quite different from another.
Jopara kesu: with Queso Paraguay # For Jopara kesu, add about 150 to 200 g Queso Paraguay near the end. Coarsely crumble the cheese and stir it in during the last few minutes. Depending on the recipe, this version may also include a little milk.
Jopara so’o: with Beef # So’o is Guaraní for “meat.” This variation uses beef, such as beef shank (osobuco) or other cuts. The meat is cut into pieces, browned, and then cooked with the stew. Depending on the cut, it may need more cooking time.
Kure jopara: with Pork # Jopara with pork is another known variation. One particular version is kure pykue jopara, made with pig’s feet. This cut needs considerably more time to cook. For a simpler variation, you can use another pork cut suitable for slow cooking.
From jopara peky to joparaite # Other known versions show just how varied Jopara can be:
Jopara peky: a version documented in southern Paraguay, especially in the Colonias Unidas, made with fresh Poroto Peky. A preparation without locro is also described for this variation. Cecina piru jopara: a version also associated with the Chaco and made with dried meat (cecina piru). Jopara norteño: an especially rich version described as using several types of beans, along with cheese and milk. Joparaite: a rich mixed version described as including beef, pork, and chicken, along with other ingredients such as rice or noodles. This variety helps explain why Jopara is hard to reduce to one definitive recipe.

Go to the Telegram channel → 🇵🇾 Jopara in Paraguay: Everyday Food, Tradition, and Karai Octubre # Jopara isn’t tied to just one date on the calendar. This corn and bean stew is also an easy, filling meal for cooler days, and it can be adapted differently from one household to another.
However, Jopara is especially closely linked to October 1. According to folk belief, a well-filled pot is meant to show that there is enough food in the house and, in turn, keep Karai Octubre and the hardship associated with him at bay. Read more about the custom and why October was traditionally considered a difficult time in our article Jopara and Karai Octubre: Paraguay’s October 1 Tradition.
The dish also has official cultural recognition: In 2017, Paraguay’s Secretaría Nacional de Cultura ↗ recognized Jopara, Sopa Paraguaya, Vori Vori, and Locro—along with the traditional preparations, recipes, and knowledge associated with them—as part of Paraguay’s intangible cultural heritage.
Did you know? Jopara, also spelled Jopará or Yopará, roughly means “mixture.” In Paraguay, the word refers not only to the stew but also to forms that mix Guaraní and Spanish and are often heard in everyday life.
❓ Frequently Asked Questions About the Jopara Recipe # What Kind of Corn Do You Need for Jopara? Use dried white corn called locro.
Cornmeal, cornstarch, and sweet corn are not direct substitutes. Locrillo can also be used; cooking time may vary somewhat depending on the product and grain size.
And if you already have locro at home, try our Mazamorra too—a sweet Paraguayan dish.
Do You Need to Soak Locro and Beans? For dried locro and dried beans, soaking overnight is the most practical approach. Many Paraguayan recipes call for at least eight hours. Discard the soaking water afterward and continue cooking with fresh water. Why Is the Locro Still Hard When the Beans Are Tender? Corn and beans do not always cook at the same rate. Product type, grain size, and storage time all play a role. Keep cooking and add hot water if needed. If this happens often, you can cook the locro and beans separately next time and combine them once both are almost tender. Is Jopara Vegetarian or Vegan? Not necessarily. Some versions contain meat, cheese, milk, or animal fat. The version described here contains no animal ingredients if you use water or vegan vegetable broth. Can I Make Jopara a Day Ahead? Yes. Jopara can be prepared ahead of time, but it becomes much thicker as it cools. When reheating, stir in a little water or broth as needed and heat the stew thoroughly. How Long Does Jopara Keep in the Refrigerator? Cool leftovers promptly, store them in a sealed container in the refrigerator, and eat them within about two to three days. Conclusion # Jopara’s strength lies in its simplicity. A simple base and many ways to build on it make the dish so versatile. Depending on what you have at home or what you feel like eating, you can keep it simple or make it richer with cheese, beef, or pork. That same base can lead to a slightly different stew each time.
That makes Jopara an easy everyday meal, not just a dish for October 1.
Enjoy making it, and buen provecho!
Do you like hearty Paraguayan stews? Try our Vori Vori recipe next, or explore more dishes in our collection of soups and stews from Paraguay.

On October 1, Jopara is traditionally served in Paraguay. This corn-and-bean stew is closely connected with Karai Octubre on that day, a figure from folklore associated with scarcity and empty pantries.
There is more to this simple stew than you might expect: folk belief, the changing seasons, and keeping food in reserve.
A traditional explanation, still passed down today, helps explain why Jopara has this special role on October 1. And there is no single fixed version of the dish either – depending on the recipe, Jopara can look quite different.
Key points at a glance Date: Jopara is especially associated with October 1. Dish: Locro and beans form the base of this hearty Paraguayan corn-and-bean stew. Tradition: According to tradition, eating it is meant to keep Karai Octubre and the scarcity associated with him away. Context: The tradition is well documented. Exactly when and how it began cannot be clearly established. What is Jopara? # In Paraguay, the word Jopara can refer to two different things. The word can be roughly understood as “mixture” – and that meaning shows up in both food and language.
In cooking, Jopara – also written Jopará or Yopará – is a traditional dish made with beans and locro (white corn). What ends up in the pot varies from recipe to recipe. The combination of corn and beans remains at its core.
The word jopara is also used for the mixing of Guaraní and Spanish in everyday speech. This article focuses on the dish and the tradition associated with it on October 1.
Jopara’s cultural importance is also reflected in its national recognition: In 2017, the Secretaría Nacional de Cultura (SNC) recognized the traditional preparation, recipes, knowledge, and practices associated with Jopara – together with Locro, Sopa Paraguaya and Vori Vori – as part of Paraguay’s intangible cultural heritage.
Why is Jopara eaten on October 1? # Because October 1 is traditionally associated with Karai Octubre.
According to tradition, people cook and eat Jopara that day to keep scarcity out of the home. A well-filled pot takes on a symbolic meaning: There is food in the house, and the family has prepared ahead.
That does not mean everyone who eats Jopara on October 1 today literally believes in Karai Octubre. For some, the figure is part of folk belief. For others, the meal is mainly a familiar tradition or simply a reason to share Jopara together.
This is where Karai Octubre comes in.
Who is Karai Octubre? # Karai Octubre – also written Karaí Octubre, roughly meaning “Mr. October” – is a figure from Paraguayan folklore, often associated with Guaraní mythology. He is linked to scarcity and hardship. In the stories, he wanders around at the beginning of October and checks how well stocked the households are.
Artistic depiction of Karai Octubre based on descriptions from Paraguayan folk belief. Where there is enough food, the household has prepared ahead. Plenty of food in reserve stands for abundance and having enough, while empty supplies stand for scarcity and need. The stew is meant to symbolically drive Karai Octubre away and show: There is enough here.
In this story, a very everyday concern takes shape as a figure: Will the food supplies last?
Spring, food supplies, and the traditional explanation # The tradition is often explained in connection with the agricultural cycle and a time when food supplies could be running low. October falls at a particular point in Paraguay’s seasons: Winter is over, and spring has just begun. The weather and nature are changing, plants are putting out new growth, and a new growing season is beginning in the fields.
Food stored from the previous harvest may already be running low, while new harvests are not yet sufficient everywhere.
This context also helps explain why Jopara fits the tradition so well: Corn and beans can be stored. Other ingredients in the dish are also among the staples kept in many Paraguayan households and are used in many ways in Paraguayan cooking. This makes it easier to understand why this particular dish is so closely connected with the idea of preparing ahead and having enough food in reserve.
Exactly how the tradition began remains unclear. There are different explanations and stories about its origins, but no fully documented history that firmly traces today’s tradition to a particular point in time or a single person.
How the tradition is practiced today # Karai Octubre is not only a figure from old stories.
Around October 1, the tradition is still observed in different ways. For some people, the day has little significance. Other families cook Jopara at home, while elsewhere the tradition is visible at markets and public events – especially where people cook, sell food, and celebrate together.
In this context, you may also come across the Guaraní expression karu guasu, roughly meaning a large shared meal. It is less about one specific dish and more about eating together and the idea of having enough – in other words, abundance rather than scarcity.
One well-documented example is Mercado 4 in Asunción. A Festival del Jopará took place there on October 1, 2023. Women who work as cooks at the market served Jopara, folk groups performed, and an actor appeared as Karai Octubre.
The Festival Nacional del Jopara is another public celebration of the tradition. Its ninth edition was held in 2024 at Plaza Uruguaya in Asunción.
Events like these show how several parts of the tradition come together: the dish itself, the story of Karai Octubre, and the shared celebration.
How Jopara is prepared # How Jopara tastes and looks depends on the recipe. Locro and beans form the base. Depending on the version, ingredients such as onions, locote, tomatoes, or squash may be added. Some recipes include Queso Paraguay (Jopara kesu), while others include meat (Jopara so’o).
Depending on the type of locro and beans used, they may first need to be soaked and partially cooked. They then cook with the vegetables until everything is tender and a hearty stew forms. You can add other ingredients to the stew to suit your taste. The amount of liquid needed and the cooking time depend mainly on the type of corn and beans used.
If you would like to make Jopara yourself, our Jopara recipe gives you a meatless base version with step-by-step instructions and well-known variations with cheese or meat.
Locro is not only used in savory dishes in Paraguay. In Mazamorra, the same white corn is used for a sweet dish – with a completely different result.

Its special connection with Karai Octubre and this tradition, however, is tied to October 1. Is October 1 a public holiday in Paraguay? No. October 1 is not an official public holiday in Paraguay. Jopara and Karai Octubre are part of a cultural tradition, so the day is not generally a day off work. Conclusion # On October 1, Jopara in Paraguay is more than a hearty corn-and-bean stew. Karai Octubre is tied to the traditional idea of preparing ahead and keeping scarcity out of the home.
Some people may still take the figure literally, while others mainly serve Jopara out of tradition. Either way, a full pot makes the old story about food supplies easy to understand: There is enough food to keep scarcity away.

Why is September 28 a public holiday in Paraguay in 2026 when the anniversary of the Batalla de Boquerón is September 29? That simple calendar question points back to an event from the Chaco War that still holds special meaning for Paraguay.
The Battle of Boquerón was one of the first major battles of the war. Let’s take a closer look at what happened there in 1932, why the battle became so important to Paraguay, and where its impact can still be seen in everyday life.
Quick facts at a glance Battle: September 9–29, 1932 Countries involved: Paraguay and Bolivia Anniversary: September 29, officially Día de la Batalla de Boquerón Public holiday in 2026: Monday, September 28 Special note: September 29 is also the Día del Soldado Paraguayo, the Day of the Paraguayan Soldier. Significance: Boquerón was an important early Paraguayan success in the Chaco War. Today, Fortín Boquerón is a historic site where the battle is remembered. What was the Battle of Boquerón? # The Battle of Boquerón took place in the Chaco from September 9 to 29, 1932. At the time, Paraguay and Bolivia were fighting for control of the disputed Chaco region. The battle was part of the early phase of the Chaco War, which lasted from 1932 to 1935.
Boquerón was not a large stone fortress. In the Chaco, the Spanish term fortín referred to a military outpost. These outposts were important for controlling territory, routes, and supply lines.
Fortín Boquerón was originally a Paraguayan outpost. Bolivian troops captured it on July 31, 1932. A few weeks later, Paraguay began trying to retake the position.
This also makes it clearer why people often speak of a “recapture” in connection with Boquerón. This was not an attack on some isolated point in the Chaco, but an attempt to retake a military outpost Paraguay had previously lost.
For the broader historical context, take a look at the history of Paraguay. It places the Chaco War within the country’s wider history.
How did the battle begin, and what happened there? # The conflict between Paraguay and Bolivia over the Chaco had already intensified before September 1932. Both countries maintained military outposts in the sparsely populated and hard-to-reach region. After several armed clashes, the conflict escalated into open war.
In early September, Paraguayan troops under the command of José Félix Estigarribia advanced toward Boquerón. Manuel Marzana commanded the Bolivian garrison at the Fortín. The battle for the outpost began on September 9, 1932.
From attack to encirclement # Paraguayan troops could not capture the Fortín right away. The initial attacks turned into an increasingly tight encirclement of the Bolivian position.
Keeping the troops supplied became increasingly important. Water, supplies, and reliable transport and communication links were already major challenges in the Chaco. For the soldiers surrounded at Boquerón, these problems grew more serious with each passing day.
Bolivian attempts to relieve the garrison could not turn the situation around. After about three weeks, the fighting ended on September 29, 1932, when the Bolivian garrison surrendered and Paraguay recaptured the Fortín.
Figures for troop numbers and casualties vary considerably depending on the source and the time period used. What is clear is that the fighting caused heavy losses and immense hardship on both sides.
Three dates for context July 31, 1932: Bolivian troops capture the Paraguayan Fortín Boquerón. September 9, 1932: The Battle of Boquerón begins. September 29, 1932: The fighting ends with Paraguay’s recapture of the Fortín. Why did Boquerón become so important to Paraguay? # Boquerón was an important early success for Paraguay in the Chaco War. To this day, official Paraguayan accounts often call it the Victoria de Boquerón, or Victory of Boquerón.
The term itself shows the national perspective from which the battle is remembered. Over time, September 29 also took on a meaning that extended far beyond the military success of 1932.
José Félix Estigarribia later described the effect of the capture of Boquerón in his memoirs ↗ with these words:
“La toma de Boquerón retempló la fe de nuestros soldados y del Paraguay entero en la victoria …”
In essence, he wrote that the capture of Boquerón had strengthened belief in victory among the soldiers and across the country. Above all, the quote shows the psychological and symbolic importance the success had from Estigarribia’s own perspective.
Another observance on September 29 September 29 is also the Día del Soldado Paraguayo, the Day of the Paraguayan Soldier. The date is therefore dedicated both to remembering Boquerón and to honoring Paraguay’s soldiers.
Historically, however, the battle should not be equated with the outcome of the entire war. The Chaco War continued for several more years after Boquerón. On June 12, 1935, Paraguay and Bolivia signed a peace protocol; the fighting ended two days later. Today, the Paz del Chaco commemorates this step toward peace.
Two perspectives Boquerón is remembered differently in Paraguay and Bolivia. In Paraguay, the battle is closely associated with military success. Bolivian accounts place particular emphasis on the defense of the Fortín and the soldiers who held out there under difficult conditions. Both are part of the history of the same place.
Boquerón public holiday in 2026: Why September 28 is a day off # The historical anniversary remains September 29 in 2026.
The official name of the public holiday is Día de la Batalla de Boquerón. Official commemorative events may also use terms such as aniversario de la Victoria de Boquerón or conmemoración de la Batalla de Boquerón.
This day is one of Paraguay’s movable public holidays, known as feriados móviles, and was moved to Monday, September 28, in 2026.
Specifically:
Monday, September 28, 2026: national public holiday Tuesday, September 29, 2026: historical anniversary of the battle, but not a second nationwide public holiday because of this move For people who already have Saturdays and Sundays off, this creates a three-day weekend.
What does the holiday mean for daily life? # On Monday, expect government offices, banks, schools, and other public institutions to operate on holiday schedules or be closed. If you have a specific appointment, it is worth checking directly with the relevant office or institution.
For medical care, emergency services and dialysis continue on the holiday. Regular doctors’ offices and health centers may be closed or offer limited services. Pharmacy hours depend on the location and duty schedule, so it is best to get any essential medications beforehand.
There are no standard opening hours across the country for supermarkets, smaller stores, shopping centers, or restaurants. Larger stores and restaurants may still open on public holidays, sometimes with adjusted hours. If you need something specific, check ahead or ask.
For travel, the long weekend may also mean more people are traveling or taking day trips. That does not automatically mean traffic jams everywhere or fully booked buses. Still, it makes sense to plan a little earlier for longer bus trips, accommodation, and especially a trip into the Chaco.
Around September 29, official commemorations (acto de conmemoración) and tributes to the fallen (homenaje a los caídos) are also part of how Boquerón is remembered. These may include ceremonies or wreath-laying at the Fortín, as well as other local events.
Fortín Boquerón today: Where the history remains visible # Anyone looking into the Batalla de Boquerón will sooner or later come across today’s Fortín Boquerón.
The historic site is in the Paraguayan Chaco, in the area around Neuland. It is about 50 to 60 kilometers from Filadelfia. A visit can therefore fit well into a stay in the Mennonite-influenced communities of the central Chaco.
The grounds include visible traces of the former positions and trenches, along with the Paraguayan and Bolivian cemeteries. The historical museum displays photographs, maps, weapons, and other objects related to the Chaco War. The Lápida de la Amistad, a friendship plaque, is also on the grounds.
Together, these elements make Fortín Boquerón a place of remembrance today. It stands for the Paraguayan victory, but it also commemorates the people who fought and died on both sides of the war. The focus is therefore not only on military history, but also on remembering both sides.
🗓️ Quick guide: What you need to know for your plans # 🗹 Monday, September 28, 2026, is the public holiday. The historical anniversary remains Tuesday, September 29. 🗹 If you normally have the weekend off, this makes a long weekend. 🗹 Expect holiday schedules or closures at government offices, banks, and schools on Monday; check the opening hours of private businesses individually. 🗹 Plan a little earlier for longer trips, bus connections, or overnight stays that weekend. The historical anniversary of the Batalla de Boquerón is September 29. In 2026, the public holiday was moved to Monday, September 28. Are September 28 and 29 both public holidays in 2026? No. Monday, September 28, 2026, is the rescheduled public holiday. Tuesday, September 29, remains the historical anniversary, but under this arrangement it is not a second nationwide public holiday. When did the Batalla de Boquerón take place? The battle itself lasted from September 9 to 29, 1932. Bolivian troops had already captured Fortín Boquerón, which had previously been a Paraguayan outpost, on July 31, 1932. What is the Día del Soldado Paraguayo? The Día del Soldado Paraguayo, or Day of the Paraguayan Soldier, is observed on September 29 and is closely tied to the remembrance of the Batalla de Boquerón. Did the Battle of Boquerón end the Chaco War? No. Boquerón was an important early Paraguayan success, but the war continued until 1935. The peace protocol was signed on June 12, 1935, and the fighting stopped on June 14. The final peace treaty followed in 1938. Can you visit Fortín Boquerón? Yes. Fortín Boquerón can be visited; the grounds include the museum, trenches, and both sides’ cemeteries. Check the current opening hours before planning a visit. Final thoughts # Boquerón shows particularly clearly how closely history and remembrance are connected in Paraguay today. The battle gave September 29 a meaning that is still visible in the calendar, at official commemorations, and at the Fortín itself.
Understanding what lies behind this date also makes it easier to see why the Chaco War still holds a special place in Paraguay. At the same time, looking at both sides reminds us that the Victoria de Boquerón was not just a military success, but part of a war with severe consequences for Paraguay and Bolivia.

A piece of surubí, some vegetables, and a large pot: that is where Pira Caldo starts. This Paraguayan fish soup is one of the country’s traditional fish dishes, and the recipe can vary. Some versions include milk and Queso Paraguay, while others are made with potatoes or different vegetables.
For our version, we use surubí fillet, milk, and Queso Paraguay. We also show you suitable alternatives and what to keep in mind so the soup turns out well outside Paraguay too.
📝 Pira Caldo Recipe: Step-by-Step Instructions # At a Glance Difficulty: easy to moderate Total time: about 45 minutes, including around 15 to 20 minutes of prep Servings: 4 as a main course Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 🛒 Ingredients for Pira Caldo # The vegetables are straightforward. It is worth taking a closer look at the fish and cheese, since both shape the soup’s flavor and texture.
Main Ingredients # 600 g surubí fillet, cleaned 1 medium onion 1 bell pepper (locote), red or green 1 medium carrot 3 ripe tomatoes 2 garlic cloves 2 tbsp vegetable oil 500 ml hot water 400 ml milk 150 g Queso Paraguay 1 tsp dried oregano 2 tbsp chopped parsley salt and black pepper Optional Ingredients # a little fresh cilantro (kuratũ) instead of or in addition to the parsley a little ají for mild heat 1 bay leaf for the vegetable broth Which Ingredients Can You Substitute? # Ingredient Alternatives Fish in Paraguay:
For our recipe, we use surubí fillet. A traditional alternative is Mandi’i, a native catfish. Fish outside Paraguay:
catfish fillet zander fillet cod fillet Queso Paraguay: If you cannot find it, mild, soft cheeses such as queso fresco or farmer’s cheese work well. Mild mozzarella also works, although it melts more readily. Feta is much saltier, so use it more sparingly.
Without milk: You can leave out the milk and replace the missing liquid with fish stock or a mild broth. This makes the soup less creamy and a little lighter.
Locote: A regular red or green bell pepper is an easy substitute.
Kitchen Equipment You Will Need # large pot cutting board and sharp knife cooking spoon soup ladle small bowl for the prepared fish 👩‍🍳 Step-by-Step Preparation # Prep # Carefully check the fish fillet for any remaining bones with your fingers, then cut it into large bite-sized pieces. Finely chop the onion and garlic. Dice the locote and tomatoes. Finely chop or coarsely grate the carrot. Crumble the Queso Paraguay. Chop the parsley or cilantro. Even with store-bought fillets, it is worth checking for bones. Small bones are much harder to spot later among the vegetables and fish in the soup.
Cooking Process # Heat the oil in a large pot. Sauté the onion, locote, carrot, and garlic over medium heat for a few minutes, until the onion starts to soften.
Add the tomatoes and, if desired, the bay leaf. Cook for another 3 to 5 minutes, until the tomatoes begin to break down.
Pour in the hot water and add the oregano. Let the vegetable base simmer gently for about 8 to 10 minutes.
Carefully add the fish pieces to the soup. Reduce the heat and let the fish cook gently for about 3 to 4 minutes.
Pour in the milk and stir carefully. Heat for another 3 to 4 minutes without letting the soup boil vigorously.
Once the fish is opaque and flakes easily with a fork, add the crumbled Queso Paraguay. Stir gently so the fish pieces stay as whole as possible.
Remove the pot from the heat. Add the parsley or cilantro, then season with salt and black pepper.
Let the Pira Caldo rest for a few minutes, then serve hot.
💡 Practical Tips for Pira Caldo # For Tender Fish and a Flavorful Soup Add the fish near the end: The vegetables take longer to cook than the fillet. This keeps the fish moist and prevents it from falling apart during cooking. Simmer gently: High heat and frequent stirring make the fish pieces fall apart more quickly. Check for bones first: Even with a fillet, do not assume that every bone has been removed. Wait before adding salt: Queso Paraguay and substitute cheeses contain different amounts of salt. It is best to adjust the seasoning at the very end. Adjust the consistency: Pira Caldo should remain a soup. If it is too rich or too thick for you, add a little hot water. Nutrition Information # The values are for one of four main-course servings, without a side dish.
Calories: about 445 kcal Protein: about 41 g Carbohydrates: about 16 g Fat: about 25 g Fiber: about 3 g Note: The nutritional values are calculated estimates and may vary depending on the size of the vegetables and the fish, milk, and Queso Paraguay used.
🍽️ What Goes Well with Pira Caldo? # Pira Caldo is already a complete meal on its own. You do not need much to serve with it.
Paraguayan: Boiled mandioca goes very well with the soup. Simple: A little bread or galleta works well for soaking up the broth. 🔄 Recipe Variations # Pira Caldo is prepared a little differently depending on the fish and other ingredients. Some versions are lighter, while others are much more filling with potatoes or extra vegetables.
Common Variations # With Mandi’i: Pira Caldo is also made with Mandi’i instead of surubí. This preparation with vegetables, milk, Queso Paraguay, and herbs is especially well known in Ayolas.
With potatoes and more vegetables: If you prefer a heartier soup, you can cook potatoes in it. Depending on the recipe, carrots, tomatoes, locote, pumpkin, or celery may also go into the pot. This makes the fish soup a more substantial meal.
Extra creamy: Some versions use cream instead of milk, making the soup noticeably creamier.
With fish stock and white wine: Some recipes use fish stock and a splash of white wine. This gives the broth a stronger flavor.

Go to the Telegram channel → 🇵🇾 Pira Caldo in Paraguay # What Does Pira Caldo Mean? # The name combines Guaraní and Spanish. Pira means “fish” in Guaraní, while caldo is the Spanish word for broth or soup. The name describes very directly what goes into the pot.
Fish Along the Paraná and Río Paraguay # Fish is especially common in local cooking where Paraguay’s major rivers are part of everyday life. Ayolas on the Paraná is a good example. There, fish such as surubí, Mandi’i, boga, dorado, and pacú are served in soups, prepared as milanesa, used in empanadas, made as Chupín de Surubí, or grilled.
Fish is also part of the local cuisine along the Río Paraguay. The Remanso area north of Asunción has long had fish stalls and comedores that serve surubí, pacú, dorado, Mandi’i, and other fish.
When Pira Caldo Is Served # When the cooler days arrive in Paraguay, this fish soup appears on the table more often alongside Vori Vori and Soyo. Hearty, hot, and filling, these dishes are just right for that time of year. Of course, these soups are also prepared outside the winter months.
Fish dishes also have a place during Semana Santa. Meatless dishes play a larger role, especially around Good Friday, and fish is a natural alternative. Pira Caldo fits this time of year just as well as other fish dishes. You can find more examples in our Easter recipe ideas from Paraguay.
Festivals Celebrating Pira Caldo and Fish # Regional food festivals also show how important fish dishes are in some parts of the country.
The Festival Nacional del Pira Caldo is held in San Antonio in the Central Department. At the sixth edition on August 2, 2026, more than 30 vendors offered a variety of fish dishes. Along with Pira Caldo, the festival also featured other dishes made with river fish.
A larger fish festival takes place in San Cosme y Damián in the Itapúa Department. The 28th edition of the Festival Nacional del Pescado will be held there on September 25, 2026. The festival originally grew out of initiatives by fishers and local groups and focuses on the region’s fish cuisine as a whole. This year’s edition was even recognized by Paraguay’s Chamber of Deputies as an event of national cultural, gastronomic, and tourism interest.
❓ Frequently Asked Questions # Which fish works well for Pira Caldo? In Paraguay, Pira Caldo is made with fish such as surubí and Mandi’i. For our version, we use surubí fillet. If surubí is unavailable outside Paraguay, catfish fillet, zander, or cod are practical substitutes. Can I use frozen fish? Yes. Let the fillet thaw completely in the refrigerator first, then pat off any excess liquid. Afterward, check it carefully for bones, just as you would with fresh fish. Do milk and cheese always go into Pira Caldo? No. Some recipes contain milk and Queso Paraguay, while others are made without milk. Without milk, Pira Caldo can be prepared with fish stock or a mild broth, for example. Our version is made with milk and cheese. How can I avoid bones in the fish soup? Carefully run your fingers over the fillet before cutting it. You can remove any bones you see or feel with clean tweezers. Whole small fish require much more preparation. How long does Pira Caldo keep in the refrigerator? Cool leftovers promptly, refrigerate them, and use them within 1 to 2 days. When reheating, heat the soup thoroughly, but do not cook it longer than necessary so the fish does not become dry or fall apart too much. Conclusion # There is no single way to make Pira Caldo. The fish, vegetables, and liquid can vary without the soup losing its Paraguayan character.
If you can find surubí, you can make the soup with one of Paraguay’s typical river fish and stay especially close to Paraguayan fish cooking. With a suitable substitute fish, the dish also turns out well.
Enjoy making it, and buen provecho!

summary: Surubí from Paraguay’s rivers, vegetables, and a rich broth: Pira Caldo brings Paraguayan fish cuisine to the table.

Around September 21, many parts of Paraguay become noticeably livelier. Schoolyards are decorated, music is part of the program, and depending on where you are, streets and public squares may be busier too. Some schools hold small celebrations, while elsewhere there are parades or larger public events. On this day, Paraguay celebrates both youth and spring.
In 2026, the Día de la Primavera y de la Juventud falls on Monday, September 21. It is not a nationwide public holiday, however. Its importance is more visible in celebrations at schools, universities, and local events than in closed businesses or offices.
Quick facts at a glance Date: September 21 every year; a Monday in 2026 Status: commemorative day established by law and widely marked as a cultural occasion; not a nationwide public holiday Where it is most visible: especially at schools, universities, and municipal or public events Meaning: youth and spring symbolize new beginnings, growth, energy, and the future Typical activities: music, dancing, sports, school programs, flowers, parades, decorated floats, and concerts In short: everyday life generally continues as normal. The occasion can still be highly visible at schools, universities, and local events. 🧭 Día de la Juventud y de la Primavera: Status and meaning # Ley Nº 4882 uses the name Día de la Juventud y de la Primavera, meaning Youth and Spring Day. In everyday use, the name also appears in the reversed order Día de la Primavera y de la Juventud or in the shorter form Día de la Primavera y la Juventud.
Celebrations of youth and spring have been documented in Paraguay for decades. Music, flowers, and decorated vehicles were part of the festivities long before the day was recognized by law.
In 2013, the date was formally established by law. Ley Nº 4882 was promulgated on April 5 and published on April 11. Since then, September 21 has been legally designated as the Día de la Juventud y de la Primavera.
That legal recognition does not make the day a public holiday. Under Ley Nº 7544/2025, it is not one of the public holidays in Paraguay. Employees are not automatically entitled to the day off, and government offices and schools do not close solely because of this commemorative day.
September 21 is the fixed date for the cultural observance. The astronomical start of spring, however, is determined by the equinox and may fall on a different date. In 2026, astronomical spring in Paraguay begins on September 22, one day later.
Why does Paraguay celebrate youth and spring together? # The link comes mainly from the symbolism the two share. Spring represents renewal, growth, and new life, while youth represents energy, development, new beginnings, and the future.
The bill’s explanatory statement draws the same parallel. It connects the freshness, energy, colors, and vitality of spring with youth, described there as a stage of development. It also associates the new season with hope and vitality.
The connection is also reflected in how the day is celebrated. Every year, schools, universities, and municipalities organize their own programs, which vary widely by place and institution.
🪅 How is September 21 celebrated in Paraguay? # Depending on the location, celebrations may include music, dancing, sports, theater, art activities, competitions, decorated floats, and larger public festivals. Some programs take place at schools and universities, while others are held on streets, public squares, or at other public venues.
Schools and universities # Families with school-age children often encounter the day first through school activities: Classrooms and schoolyards are decorated, and depending on the school, there may also be music, dancing, sports, performances, or group projects. In Ayolas, for example, students and teachers paraded through the city in colorful clothing with decorated floats in 2024.
Higher-education institutions also mark the occasion, often with broader programs. Alongside cultural and sports activities, they may organize talks, social projects, or health initiatives.
Check the school schedule in advance The commemorative day does not automatically mean a day off from school. Depending on the institution, there may be regular classes, an adjusted schedule, or an internal celebration.
Palmear on Calle Palma # Calle Palma in Asunción has a special place in the history of this celebration.
Archive images from the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s show large spring festivals there. Flowers, balloons, music, and decorated vehicles were already part of the celebrations, along with crowds of young people gathering in the city center.
The local Asunción expression palmear fits that history well: it means strolling along Calle Palma, meeting friends, and seeing and being seen. The word itself offers a small glimpse into the street’s long-standing role as a social meeting place.
Palma Joven 2026 in Asunción The third edition of Palma Joven has been announced for Saturday, September 26, 2026, on Calle Palma. It was originally scheduled for September 19 but was postponed by one week because of the forecast rain. Music, food, and the Feria de Oportunidades are among the activities planned from 11 a.m. to 11 p.m..
Information as of September 18, 2026.
Celebrations differ from place to place # Cities outside the capital hold their own events too. In Villarrica, the Corso de las Flores returns in 2026. Decorated floats, the selection of Miss Primavera, and music are part of the program in the main area around Calle General Díaz and the Plazoleta Municipal. Encarnación and other places in Paraguay may also hold their own events and activities around the day.
Some programs are mainly organized by schools and local groups, while elsewhere concerts, markets, or public festivals take center stage.
A simple greeting A simple ¡Feliz Día de la Primavera y de la Juventud! works well with friends, acquaintances, or at events.
🧩 What does the day mean in everyday life? # If you are new to Paraguay, the day may look like a public holiday at first. But it does not come with a general day off. Supermarkets, shopping malls, small businesses, restaurants, pharmacies, government offices, and banks are not required to close simply because of the occasion.
Schools and universities may operate differently. Many organize their own celebrations or adjust the usual schedule. What matters is what the individual institution announces.
Unlike on major national holidays, there is usually no nationwide travel rush. Areas around concerts, parades, or street festivals may still be busier than usual, and temporary road closures are possible.
