The day is established by Ley Nº 4882, but it is not a nationwide public holiday. It is not included in the country’s list of national public holidays, so businesses, government offices, and banks do not close automatically. Are schools and businesses closed in Paraguay on September 21? No, not as a general rule. Businesses are not required to close on this commemorative day.
Schools may follow a different schedule. Many organize celebrations, sports, cultural activities, or project days. Whether regular classes take place or the schedule is adjusted depends on the individual school and its latest announcements.
Why are youth and spring celebrated together in Paraguay? Both symbolize development, new beginnings, and the future. This connection also appears in the explanatory statement accompanying the bill that later became Ley Nº 4882. However, the spring and youth celebrations themselves are much older than the law. Does spring begin in Paraguay on September 21? Not necessarily. The cultural date is fixed, while the astronomical beginning of spring depends on the equinox. In 2026, it falls on September 22 in Paraguay. Conclusion # The Día de la Primavera y de la Juventud is culturally significant in Paraguay even without a nationwide day off. Depending on the place, it may show up in decorations, music, parades, or a local festival.
Celebrations vary from place to place, but the common thread is the connection between spring, youth, and celebrating together.
To get a better sense of what spring itself is like in Paraguay, take a look at Spring in Paraguay. It covers weather, nature, and everyday life from September through November.

Pumpkin, cornmeal, and cheese may sound like an unusual combination. Together, they make Kivevé, a creamy Paraguayan pumpkin dish with a mild sweetness and a texture somewhere between smooth mashed pumpkin and soft polenta.
Kivevé can lean a little more savory or noticeably sweeter, depending on how it is prepared and served. That range is part of what makes the dish so interesting.
If you are just starting to explore Paraguayan cuisine, this pumpkin classic is a good introduction. The ingredient list is short, the steps are simple, and there are practical substitutes for both Andai squash and Queso Paraguay outside Paraguay.
📝 Kivevé Recipe: Step-by-Step Instructions # At a Glance Difficulty: Easy Total time: about 60 minutes Servings: about 8 as a side dish or small meal Suitable for: vegetarians; gluten-free if made with certified gluten-free cornmeal Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 🛒 Ingredients for Kivevé # The basic recipe uses just a few ingredients, with practical substitutes if you live outside Paraguay.
Main Ingredients # 1 kg pumpkin flesh (Andai) 750 ml water 250 ml whole milk 280 g finely ground cornmeal 200 g Queso Paraguay 3 tbsp neutral-flavored oil 2 tbsp sugar about 1 tsp salt Optional Ingredients # a little more sugar for a much sweeter version 1 small onion, finely chopped, for a more savory version Which Ingredients Can You Replace? # Ingredient Alternatives Pumpkin: Butternut squash is a good alternative with a similarly mild, slightly sweet flavor.
Queso Paraguay: Mild fresh cheeses such as queso fresco, farmer cheese, or ricotta work well. Feta is saltier, while mozzarella can make the mixture stringy.
Cornmeal: Use finely ground cornmeal. Cornstarch is not a substitute, and coarse polenta will give the dish a different texture.
Gluten-free: The basic ingredients do not contain gluten. If you have celiac disease, make sure the cornmeal is labeled gluten-free.
Kitchen Equipment # large pot knife and cutting board slotted spoon and bowl potato masher or sturdy fork wooden spoon 👩‍🍳 Step-by-Step Preparation # Preparation # Peel the pumpkin, remove the seeds, and cut the flesh into cubes. Crumble the cheese or cut it into small pieces. Measure the cornmeal, milk, and remaining ingredients and have them ready. Cooking Instructions # Cook the pumpkin until soft: Place the pumpkin and water in a large pot. Bring to a boil, then cook over medium heat until the pieces are easy to mash with a fork.
Mash the pumpkin: Lift the pumpkin pieces out of the pot with a slotted spoon and save the cooking water. Mash the pumpkin as finely as possible with a masher or fork, then return it to the pot along with the cooking water.
Stir in the milk and seasonings: Stir the milk, oil, sugar, and salt into the pumpkin puree.
Add the cornmeal: Reduce the heat. Slowly sprinkle in the cornmeal, stirring constantly and vigorously to prevent lumps.
Cook the Kivevé: Continue cooking over low heat for about 10 to 15 minutes, stirring constantly, until the mixture is thick and creamy with the consistency of soft polenta.
Stir in the cheese: Remove the pot from the heat and stir in the Queso Paraguay. Taste and add a little more salt if needed.
💡 Tips for Making Kivevé # How to Get the Right Texture Reduce the heat: Once the cornmeal is in the pot, keep the heat low. The thick mixture can otherwise stick easily to the bottom of the pot.
Do not thicken it too soon: Kivevé thickens as it cools, so do not add extra cornmeal too soon.
If it gets too thick: If the mixture is too firm, gradually stir in about 60 to 120 ml of hot water or warm milk until it reaches the texture you want. You may need less depending on the pumpkin.
Nutrition Information # The values below are for one of eight servings of the basic recipe.
Calories: about 335 kcal Protein: about 10 g Carbohydrates: about 47 g Fat: about 13 to 14 g Fiber: about 5 g Sugar: about 8 g Note: These values are estimates and may vary depending on the ingredients and serving size.
🍽️ How to Serve Kivevé # Kivevé can be served in several ways, depending on how you prepare it.
Serving Drinks Classic: As a creamy side dish alongside Bife or Asado. For everyday meals: On its own as a light, warm meal. Merienda: Prepared a little sweeter or served with some milk. With a sweeter version: Unsweetened coffee or Cocido, a hot drink made with Yerba Mate, makes a pleasant contrast. For merienda: A glass of milk also goes well with it, especially if the Kivevé is only lightly sweetened. 🔄 Recipe Variations # Recipes vary from household to household. The main difference is how sweet or savory the dish is.
Common Variations # Semi-sweet: With a little sugar and mild cheese, the basic version falls somewhere between sweet and savory. It works both on its own and as a side dish.
More savory with onion: For a more savory version, finely chopped onion is sautéed in oil and less sugar is used. This version goes especially well with meat.
Sweeter: With a little more sugar, the dish becomes noticeably sweeter and works well as a dessert or for merienda. A little milk can soften the texture or be added when serving.

You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → 🇵🇾 Background on Kivevé # Name and Spellings # In Spanish, both Kivevé and Quibebé are used; in Guaraní, the name appears as kiveve. In English texts, the accent is often left out, and the name is written as Kiveve.
One common interpretation links the name to a reddish color, perhaps referring to the pumpkin’s hue. The exact origin of the word, however, is unclear.
Similar pumpkin dishes are also found in Argentina and Brazil, where they are often called Quibebé or Quibebe. Recipes can vary considerably. In Brazil, for example, Quibebe is often prepared as a more savory dish and is sometimes cooked with meat.
What Makes Kivevé Special? # The basic ingredients are simple and common in Paraguay: pumpkin, cornmeal, and fresh cheese. The pumpkin adds natural sweetness and color, while the cornmeal thickens the puree and gives it a creamy texture similar to soft polenta.
Queso Paraguay adds a mild, slightly tangy flavor. That sweet-savory balance is typical of Kivevé, which is why the dish does not fit neatly into either the side-dish or dessert category.
Kivevé in Paraguayan Food Culture # Kivevé is one of Paraguay’s traditional dishes and has been included since 2018 on an official list of the country’s gastronomic and culinary heritage. The DINAPI Resolution No. 05/2018 ↗ declares this list to be of national interest.
During the cooler months, Kivevé is especially comforting when served warm, which is why we also include it in our roundup of Paraguayan winter dishes. Depending on how it is prepared, it can be served on its own, as a side dish with Bife or Asado, or a little sweeter for merienda (a small afternoon meal or snack).
At traditional celebrations, Kivevé is sometimes offered among the typical foods served around San Juan.
During Semana Santa, the dish also has its place alongside Chipa, Sopa Paraguaya, and Mbaipy as part of traditional Holy Week cuisine. On Good Friday in particular, it offers a meat-free option made with pumpkin, cornmeal, and cheese.
Kivevé, Dulce de Calabaza, and Andai Kamby: Three Traditional Pumpkin Dishes # Kivevé, Dulce de Calabaza, and Andai Kamby represent three sweet or semi-sweet ways of preparing pumpkin in Paraguayan cuisine.
For Dulce de Calabaza, pumpkin is simmered with much more sugar and spices. The result is sweet and syrupy.
Kivevé, in contrast, is mashed and thickened with cornmeal. Fresh cheese adds a slightly savory contrast to the sweetness of the pumpkin.
Andai Kamby is a sweet dish made with pumpkin, milk, and sugar. Unlike Kivevé, it is not thickened with cornmeal.
If You Prefer Something Savory When the pumpkin harvest is plentiful, I do not use it only for sweet or semi-sweet dishes. I like to add pumpkin to Caldo de poroto (bean stew) or cook Guisos (stews) with plenty of pumpkin, ground meat, tomato, and sometimes other vegetables or rice. The pumpkin adds a little sweetness and helps thicken the stews.
For more ideas, browse our pumpkin recipes.
❓ Frequently Asked Questions # What is Kivevé? Kivevé is a creamy, usually semi-sweet Paraguayan dish made with pumpkin, cornmeal, and fresh cheese. Depending on the recipe, it is served as a side dish, light meal, merienda, or sweet dish. Is Kivevé a dessert or a side dish? It can be either. With less sugar or with onion, Kivevé leans more savory; with more sugar, it also works as a dessert or for merienda. Which pumpkin is best for Kivevé? Andai is traditionally used. Outside Paraguay, butternut squash is an easy-to-find alternative with sweet, orange flesh. What kind of cornmeal should I use for Kivevé? Use finely ground cornmeal for cooking. Cornstarch is not suitable. Coarse polenta will give the dish a noticeably different texture. What can I use instead of Queso Paraguay? Mild fresh white cheeses such as queso fresco, farmer cheese, or ricotta work well. Feta is much saltier, so it works best as a partial substitute rather than a full replacement. How thick should Kivevé be? The mixture should be creamy and spoonable, similar to soft polenta. It firms up slightly as it cools. How long does Kivevé keep? Cool leftovers quickly and store them in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Kivevé will keep for about 2 to 3 days. To reheat it, stir in a little milk or water and warm it slowly. Conclusion # With its simple combination of pumpkin, cornmeal, and cheese, Kivevé is a good introduction to Paraguayan cuisine. Depending on your taste, you can prepare it as a more savory side dish or make it a little sweeter for merienda.
Enjoy cooking, and buen provecho!
Have some pumpkin left over? Try Dulce de Calabaza next as a much sweeter option. Browse more traditional dishes and everyday favorites in our Paraguayan recipes.
Share & Support Know someone who would like to try something different with pumpkin?
Share the Kivevé recipe, or leave a like if you enjoyed the post.
summary: Creamy, lightly sweet, and versatile: discover a Paraguayan classic made with pumpkin, cornmeal, and cheese.

content:
In late August and early September, you may still need a jacket in the morning in Paraguay, then find yourself looking for shade by afternoon. At the same time, trees start putting out new growth, the first fruit trees begin to bloom, and some lapachos are already full of color.
These contrasts are exactly what define spring in Paraguay. Rather than a long stretch of consistently mild weather, it is a fairly quick shift from winter toward warmer and, in many places, more humid days. In daily life, you can see nature changing around you, the days become warmer and longer, but cool nights, thunderstorms, and heavy rain are still possible.
The most important points at a glance Spring runs from September to November: On the meteorological calendar, September, October, and November are spring in Paraguay.
Changeable rather than consistently mild: Cool mornings and cold fronts are still possible in September. October gets warmer, and November often already feels like summer.
Clear regional differences: The Región Oriental is wetter and greener, while the Chaco is drier and often hotter.
You can see nature changing: Lapachos may already bloom during winter. As temperatures rise, new shoots appear, more plants flower, fruit begins to set, and growth speeds up.
Rain plays a bigger role in daily life again: Thunderstorms, muddy roads, and standing water become more relevant. After rain, it is also worth checking for possible mosquito breeding sites.
When does spring begin in Paraguay? # Paraguay is in the Southern Hemisphere, so its seasons are the opposite of those in Europe. On the meteorological calendar, spring begins on September 1 and includes September, October, and November.
Astronomical spring starts a little later at the equinox. In 2026, it falls on September 22 at around 9:05 p.m. in Asunción. The exact date and time shift slightly from year to year.
In everyday life in Paraguay, spring has another date firmly marked on the calendar: September 21. On that day, Paraguay celebrates Día de la Primavera y de la Juventud, or Spring and Youth Day, with a variety of activities. This cultural observance should not be confused with the astronomical start of spring.
The weather in Paraguay does not follow any of these dates anyway. A warm August day can already feel like spring, while a cold air mass from the south can still bring noticeably cooler temperatures in September.
🌤️ How the weather changes from September to November # A single temperature range does not tell you much about spring in Paraguay. What matters more is how conditions change over the course of the three months.
Month Typical conditions What matters in daily life September Transition month with warm days, cool mornings, and possible cold spells Keep a light jacket handy and watch for sudden weather changes October Noticeably warmer and more humid, with thunderstorms becoming more frequent Plan outdoor work for the morning and keep rain and mosquitoes in mind November Already summery to hot in many areas, with warmer nights as well Shade, water, and midday heat become more important September: Between a winter jacket and a T-shirt # September in Paraguay shows especially well why averages only tell part of the story. A morning can be cool and the middle of the day pleasantly warm. A few days later, a north wind may bring much higher temperatures before another cold front moves through and leaves a few chilly mornings behind.
In our experience, frost is usually no longer an issue around this time where we live in rural Guairá. Temperatures can still drop below 10°C, though. Winter in Paraguay does not end overnight.
October: Heat and humidity increase # By October, the weather already feels noticeably different. Warm to hot days become more common. At the same time, humidity rises in many parts of the Región Oriental, and thunderstorms become more frequent again.
With warmth and rain, vegetation often takes off quickly. Around gardens and properties, this is the time when it can feel hard to keep up with all the growth.
November: Summer is already in the air # Meteorologically, November is still part of spring. In daily life, however, it can already feel very much like summer.
The midday sun gets stronger, hot days become more frequent, and nights stay warmer. At this point, I prefer to plan gardening or longer outdoor activities for the morning or later in the afternoon.
That is an important difference between the calendar and how the season actually feels: meteorological summer does not begin until December, but the hot season can make itself felt much earlier in Paraguay.
Spring varies across Paraguay: Eastern Region, south, and Chaco # There is no single version of “spring weather in Paraguay.”
In the Región Oriental, or Eastern Region, the climate is generally wetter. After rain, the landscape often turns green quickly, and thunderstorms become more common as temperatures rise. This includes departments such as Central, Guairá, Caazapá, and Alto Paraná, as well as large parts of the south and southeast. Asunción is also in this wetter part of the country.
In the south and southeast, nights and mornings can stay somewhat cooler during the transition. Especially in September, it is worth looking at more than just the daytime high.
The Chaco is generally drier and often hotter than the Eastern Region. High temperatures can already occur there in spring, while rainfall tends to be distributed more unevenly. If you travel to the Chaco in September or October, do not assume conditions will be the same as in Asunción or the greener east.
Even within the same region, the exact location makes a difference. An open pasture, a low-lying area, a densely built neighborhood, or a property with many large trees can feel very different on the same day, even at similar temperatures. Wind, humidity, sun, and shade all play a part.
🌸 When Paraguay turns green again # The most visible side of spring does not necessarily begin on September 1. Some plants are well ahead of the calendar.
Among the most noticeable are the lapachos, also called Tajy in Guaraní. Pink lapachos can bloom between July and September, while yellow species often flower somewhat later, into October. The blossoms frequently appear before the tree has fully leafed out again, making the colorful crowns stand out even more.
Around lapacho season, you will also hear people say that winter is now over, or at least that there will be no more frost. The bloom is a beautiful sign that the seasons are changing, but it is not a reliable weather rule. A cool spell or late cold front can still follow.
A blooming lapacho where we live in rural Guairá. Pink petals on red soil against all that green are some of my favorite splashes of color as spring approaches. Here in rural Guairá, this is one of the times when I notice the change of seasons most clearly. After the quieter winter weeks, warmer weather brings new shoots and blossoms to many other plants as well. Citrus and mango trees begin to flower and set their first small fruit, while the mulberry already has fruit hanging from its branches. Depending on the temperatures, rainfall, and plant species, the property can become much greener and more colorful within a short time.
Spring where we live in rural Guairá: blossoms, new shoots, and the first young fruit mark the shift toward the warm season. Our region stays relatively green even in winter. Still, the shift into spring is easy to notice. When driving through other parts of Paraguay at this time of year, you also see blooming lapachos and large mango trees with their striking flower clusters.
🌱 Garden and property in spring # Spring is a busy time around the garden and property. Many plants begin growing more vigorously again, and there is plenty to take care of after winter. Many trees and shrubs are also pruned during winter or toward its end, before new growth really gets going. When and how much to prune depends on the individual plant.
You can plant year-round in Paraguay if the species and current weather are suitable. Around here, new trees and shrubs are often planted in spring, especially in September and October. We also prefer planting at this time. Young plants can establish their roots before the intense summer heat and still have more time before the next winter. Planting in fall is possible too, but sensitive plants then have less time before the first cold spells of winter.
A few things have worked especially well for us:
Keep an eye on cool nights and wind: Protect sensitive and newly planted plants during late cold fronts, and stake them if needed. Use mulch: It helps the soil retain moisture as sunshine and temperatures increase. Expect fast growth: With warmth and rain, grass and weeds grow quickly too. Beds and planting areas need more attention again. Pick favorable planting weather: Mild days with moderate rain are useful. During intense heat, heavy rain, or a cold front, it is better to wait a little. ⛈️ Thunderstorms, rain, and mosquitoes # As temperatures rise, the weather also becomes more unsettled. Especially in the Eastern Region, warm and humid days can alternate with thunderstorms and heavy rain.
For daily life, the monthly rainfall total often matters less than how quickly the rain falls and how concentrated it is in one area.
In rural areas, unpaved roads can become much harder to drive after heavy rain. A road that was dry in the morning may look completely different after an afternoon thunderstorm. Heavy rainfall can also cause local problems in cities.
Spring 2026: El Niño For October through December 2026, Paraguay’s meteorological service expects above-average rainfall in parts of the Eastern Region, particularly in the east, southeast, and northeast. Above-average temperatures are also forecast across much of the country.
Meanwhile, El Niño continues to strengthen in the Pacific. According to NOAA’s October 8 assessment, a strong to very strong event is likely and could persist into early 2027.
This increases the risk of unusual weather conditions in Paraguay. However, seasonal forecasts cannot predict how much rain will fall in a particular location or when severe thunderstorms might occur. They describe general trends over several months, not the weather on individual days.
Updated: October 9, 2026
Sources: Dirección de Meteorología e Hidrología: October–December 2026 outlook · NOAA Climate Prediction Center
With rain and rising temperatures, mosquitoes also become more noticeable again. After rainfall, it is worth taking a quick look around the property. Water can collect in buckets, plant saucers, old containers, tires, or gutters and become a mosquito breeding site.
☀️ Is spring the best time to visit Paraguay? # Whether spring is the best time to visit Paraguay depends on what you want to do and how well you handle heat. For many people, however, spring and winter are among the more comfortable times to get to know the country. Especially in September and during part of October, outings and longer drives are often more pleasant than in the intense summer heat.
The landscape is another reason this time of year stands out. Paraguay stays green year-round in many regions, but spring brings fresh growth, and blooming lapachos and other plants add even more color.
Conditions are not the same everywhere, though. The Chaco can already be considerably hotter. In the wetter Eastern Region, rain, humidity, and thunderstorms become more noticeable as spring progresses.
The season also matters for things to do in Paraguay. Spring is often a comfortable time for outings, sports, or an afternoon outdoors with friends.

Meteorologically, spring in Paraguay runs from September 1 through the end of November. Astronomical spring begins around the September equinox and shifts slightly from year to year. How warm is Paraguay in spring? No single temperature range works for all of Paraguay. Cool mornings and cold fronts are still possible in September. October gets noticeably warmer, while November already feels summery to hot in many places. The region makes a big difference as well. Does it rain a lot during spring in Paraguay? Rain and thunderstorms become more common in many parts of the country as spring progresses. The Región Oriental is generally wetter. There is no clearly defined rainy season that begins at the same time across the entire country. When do lapachos bloom in Paraguay? Lapachos may begin blooming during winter. Is September 21 a public holiday in Paraguay? September 21 is legally established in Paraguay as Día de la Juventud y de la Primavera. It is not a national public holiday, however. What should you wear in Paraguay in spring? Light clothing is usually enough. In September, keep a jacket or sweater handy for cool mornings or a cold front. Sun protection is also useful, along with some rain protection depending on your travel plans. Conclusion: Spring in Paraguay is all about change # Spring in Paraguay brings together things that may seem hard to reconcile at first: cool mornings and hot afternoons, blooming trees and late cold fronts, dry days and strong thunderstorms.
From September to November, it steadily gets warmer and, in many places, more humid. At the same time, vegetation starts growing vigorously again and daily life shifts outdoors.

A golden-brown crust, moist corn batter, and small pieces of cheese and soft-cooked onions throughout: this is Sopa Paraguaya. It is a classic in Paraguay, but its name can be misleading at first. Despite the name, there is no soup involved. Instead, this savory corn cake is cut into pieces and served as a side dish. It is a staple at family meals and celebrations.
You only need a few ingredients to make Sopa Paraguaya. Fine cornmeal, cheese, onions, eggs, and milk form the base. The recipe is easy to prepare, and if you get the batter consistency and baking time right, the corn cake stays moist inside while still being firm enough to slice.
📝 Sopa Paraguaya Recipe: Step by Step # At a Glance Difficulty: Easy Preparation time: About 20 minutes prep + 40 to 45 minutes baking Servings: About 10 to 12 pieces as a side dish, depending on how large you cut them Baking pan: About 30 × 20 cm (12 × 8 inches) Oven temperature: 180°C (350°F), conventional oven Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 🛒 Ingredients for Sopa Paraguaya # Here is what you need to make a classic Sopa Paraguaya.
Main Ingredients # 500 g fine cornmeal (harina de maíz / avati ku’i) 500 ml milk 3 eggs 250 g Queso Paraguay 2 medium onions, about 300 g 150 ml neutral-flavored vegetable oil About 10 g salt, depending on the cheese you use A little oil for greasing the pan Optional: a little black pepper for extra flavor What Ingredients Can You Substitute? # Ingredient Substitutes The basic recipe is gluten-free and vegetarian.
Cornmeal: In Paraguay, use finely ground harina de maíz or avati ku’i. Cornstarch is not a substitute. Fine polenta can work, but it gives the Sopa a slightly coarser texture. Precooked cornmeal used for arepas behaves differently and is not a direct 1:1 substitute.
Queso Paraguay: Outside Paraguay, you can use queso fresco, mild farmer cheese, or feta that is not too salty. A mixture of mild feta and mozzarella gives you a good balance of saltiness and a soft texture.
Milk: You can use lactose-free milk in the same amount. Plant-based milk also works, but it changes the flavor slightly.
Fat: Instead of vegetable oil, you can use butter or, traditionally, lard. Sopa made with lard is no longer vegetarian.
Kitchen Equipment # Large bowl Skillet Cutting board and knife Whisk or wooden spoon Rectangular baking dish or baking pan, about 30 × 20 cm (12 × 8 inches) Kitchen scale and measuring cup 👩‍🍳 Step-by-Step Instructions # Preparation # Preheat the oven to 180°C (350°F), conventional setting, and lightly grease the pan. Peel and finely dice the onions. Crumble the Queso Paraguay or cut it into small pieces. Set out the eggs, milk, and remaining ingredients. Cooking # Add some of the 150 ml of oil to the skillet and cook the onions over medium heat until soft and translucent. Do not let them brown too much.
Whisk the eggs in a large bowl. Stir in the milk and the remaining oil.
Add the cornmeal in batches and mix everything into a smooth, thick batter. Then add the cooled onions and cheese.
Season with salt. Use less if your substitute cheese is already salty.
Pour the batter into the prepared pan and smooth the top.
Bake the Sopa for about 40 to 45 minutes, until the top is lightly golden brown and the center is firm. It should still be moist inside, but there should be no visible liquid batter.
Let it rest for about 10 minutes after baking. This makes it easier to cut into neat pieces.
Here is the finished Sopa:
Baked until golden brown and cut into pieces: the finished Sopa Paraguaya. 💡 Practical Tips for Sopa Paraguaya # For a Moist, Sliceable Sopa Check the consistency: The batter should be thick and creamy and spread easily in the pan. If your cornmeal absorbs a lot of liquid and the batter is very firm, gradually add a little more milk. Use the right pan: In a very large pan, the Sopa will be flatter and dry out faster. Muffin tins or other small oven-safe dishes work well for buffets or finger food. Since the Sopa cooks faster in smaller dishes, start checking it earlier. Do not rely only on the clock: The top should be golden brown and the center firm, but not dry. Adjust the salt to the cheese: The saltier the cheese, the less additional salt you need. Nutrition Information # The values are based on the amounts listed above, using vegetable oil, and calculated per piece when the Sopa is cut into 12 pieces.
Calories: About 360 kcal Protein: About 10 g Carbohydrates: About 37 g Fat: About 20 g Fiber: About 3.5 g The nutrition information is approximate and may vary depending on the cornmeal, cheese, fat, and serving size.
🍽️ What Goes Well with Sopa Paraguaya? # It is usually served as a side dish, but it works with many different foods depending on the occasion.
Side Dishes Drinks Classic: With Asado or other grilled meats Fresh: With tomato, cabbage, or green salad Hearty: On cooler days, with soups or stews such as Caldo de Poroto For larger gatherings: With cassava, salads, and other small dishes on a buffet On the go: Sopa Paraguaya also tastes good cold. Cut into pieces, it is easy to pack for a picnic, work, or a school snack. Paraguayan classic: Tereré, the cold yerba mate infusion, on warm days Simple: Water with lemon Fruity: Homemade lemonade or fruit juice For cooler days: Mate cocido, a hot yerba mate drink, or coffee 🔄 Recipe Variations # Besides the basic recipe, there are several variations of Sopa Paraguaya. One of the best known is the hearty Sopa so’o with a meat filling, but pumpkin can also add an interesting flavor to the corn mixture.
🥩 Sopa So’o: Sopa Paraguaya with Meat Filling # Sopa so’o is one of the best-known variations. So’o means “meat” in Guaraní. For this version, a seasoned meat filling is placed between two layers of Sopa batter. This makes it much more filling and suitable as a main dish.
Additional ingredients for the meat filling:
500 g ground beef 1 medium onion 1 Locote (bell pepper) 2 garlic cloves 1 green onion A little fresh parsley Salt, black pepper, and cumin to taste A little oil for cooking Optional: Some family recipes also add chopped hard-boiled eggs to the meat filling.
Quick preparation:
Finely chop the onion, Locote, and garlic and cook them in a little oil until soft. Add the ground beef and cook until browned and crumbly. Season with salt, pepper, and cumin. Finally, stir in the green onion and parsley. The filling should stay moist but not be runny. Let the meat filling cool for a few minutes before assembling the layers.
Pour about half of the prepared Sopa batter into the greased pan.
If you want clearly separated layers, you can pre-bake this first layer for about 5 minutes. However, this extra step is not necessary.
Spread the meat filling evenly over the first layer and add the chopped eggs if desired. Cover with the remaining Sopa batter and bake as described in the basic recipe, until the top is golden brown and the Sopa is fully baked.
🎃 Sopa Paraguaya with Pumpkin # If you prefer it without meat but still want to try something a little different, you can also make Sopa Paraguaya with pumpkin. Simply work a little pumpkin into the corn mixture for a slightly sweet and moist variation.
More posts like this? 🇵🇾 Did you enjoy this post and want to learn more about Paraguay? Get Paraguay4Life updates by email and stay connected. Get new posts by email Free. You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → 🇵🇾 Background Information about the Recipe # Why Is It Called Sopa Paraguaya? # The name Sopa Paraguaya literally means “Paraguayan soup,” which does not seem to fit a solid baked corn dish at all.
The best-known explanation is a legend from the time of Carlos Antonio López. According to the story, a corn dish at the home of then-president Carlos Antonio López accidentally became too thick and was then baked. There is no historical evidence that it happened this way, but the story is still often told today.
What Makes Sopa Paraguaya Special? # The texture of the finished Sopa is somewhere between a savory corn cake and moist cornbread. It is firm enough to slice but stays soft and slightly moist inside. The cornmeal gives it its compact, bread-like texture. Queso Paraguay adds moisture and a mild saltiness, while the soft-cooked onions add flavor and a light sweetness. The result is more savory than many American-style cornbreads.
It tastes good warm, at room temperature, or cold, and its firm texture makes it easy to take with you.
Sopa Paraguaya is often confused with Chipa Guasu. Both dishes combine corn, cheese, eggs, and onions, but there are two clear differences.
Sopa Paraguaya Chipa Guasu Corn base Fine cornmeal Fresh, chopped or blended corn (choclo) Texture Firmer and easy to slice Moister and more like a casserole What Role Does Sopa Paraguaya Play in Paraguay? # This corn and cheese classic works just as well for everyday meals as it does for larger family gatherings. At the asados we attend here in the countryside, Sopa is almost always part of the meal. Like Chipa Guasu, it can be prepared ahead of time and easily served with meat, salads, and other dishes.
It also regularly appears at traditional celebrations. Around San Juan, it is one of the typical San Juan dishes in Paraguay. It is also a traditional part of Easter cooking during Semana Santa.
Traditionally, Sopa Paraguaya can also be baked in a Tatakua, Paraguay’s wood-fired clay oven. When families bake Chipa, Sopa Paraguaya, or Chipa Guasu there for a large gathering, the preparation itself often becomes a shared activity. Of course, you do not need a Tatakua for this recipe at home. A regular oven works just as well.
Since 2017, the traditional preparation of Sopa Paraguaya and the related recipes, practices, and knowledge have been recognized as part of Paraguay’s intangible cultural heritage. The recognition is based on SNC Resolution No. 592/2017 issued by the Secretaría Nacional de Cultura ↗. The recognition also includes Vori Vori, Locro, and Jopará. However, this is not a UNESCO designation.
❓ Frequently Asked Questions # Is Sopa Paraguaya really a soup? No. It is a firm, savory corn and cheese cake that is baked and then cut into pieces. Why is Sopa Paraguaya called a soup? A common legend traces the name back to a corn dish that became too thick at the residence of Carlos Antonio López. However, there is no historical evidence that this origin story is true. What kind of cornmeal should I use for Sopa Paraguaya? Use finely ground cornmeal (harina de maíz / avati ku’i). Cornstarch is not a substitute. Fine polenta can work depending on the grind, but it gives the Sopa a slightly coarser texture. What can I use instead of Queso Paraguay? Good options include mild queso fresco, mild farmer cheese, feta that is not too salty, or mozzarella. A mixture of mild feta and mozzarella is often a practical solution. Is Sopa Paraguaya gluten-free and vegetarian? The basic recipe is gluten-free and vegetarian when made with vegetable oil or butter. If you need to follow a strict gluten-free diet because of celiac disease, make sure the cornmeal is labeled gluten-free. Sopa made with pork lard is not vegetarian. How long does Sopa Paraguaya keep, and can I reheat it? Store leftovers covered in the refrigerator and use them within three to four days if possible. Sopa tastes good cold, but it can also be reheated. What is the difference between Sopa Paraguaya and Chipa Guasu? Sopa is baked with cornmeal, which makes it firmer. Chipa Guasu is made with fresh, ground corn and stays moister and more like a casserole. Final Thoughts # For me, this combination of a few ingredients, hearty flavor, and simple preparation is exactly what makes Sopa Paraguaya a classic of everyday Paraguayan cooking. Served warm, it goes naturally with Asado or a big family meal. Cold, it is easy to take along for a picnic or when you are on the go. It is also a good example of how simple and versatile Paraguayan cuisine can be.
Have fun cooking and buen provecho!
If you would like to try more recipes with corn, try our Paraguayan corn tortillas. Or browse our collection of Paraguayan recipes.
Share & Support Do you enjoy Sopa Paraguaya as much as I do, or do you know someone who should definitely try it? Give this post a like and share it with others interested in South America. Together, we can help more people discover Paraguayan cuisine.
summary: Why Sopa Paraguaya is not a soup – and why this moist corn cake is a favorite at family meals and asados.
title: Sopa Paraguaya Recipe: Savory Paraguayan Corn Cake

Have some cooked cassava left over from lunch? In Paraguay, those leftovers do not have to come back to the table as the same side dish at dinner. With onions, eggs, and cheese, they can go straight back into the skillet and become Mandi’o Chyryry, a simple, hearty everyday dish.
It has become one of our favorite ways to use cooked mandioca, the term commonly used for cassava in Paraguay. It works just as well with freshly cooked cassava as with leftovers from the day before. The idea is a little like pan-fried potatoes with eggs, but cassava has its own flavor and a firmer, starchier bite.
And it does not take much to make. In this recipe, I will show you step by step how to turn cooked cassava into a quick, warm meal.
📝 Mandi’o Chyryry Recipe: Step by Step # At a Glance Difficulty: easy Prep time: about 10 minutes Cook time: about 15 minutes With fresh cassava: allow another 20 to 30 minutes for boiling Servings: 2 large or 3 smaller servings Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 🛒 Ingredients for Mandi’o Chyryry # Besides cooked cassava, the base recipe only needs eggs, cheese, onions, and a few fresh herbs.
Main Ingredients # 750 g cooked cassava, well drained 1 medium onion 1 garlic clove, optional 2 tbsp neutral oil 2 eggs 100 g Queso Paraguay 2 green onions 1 to 2 tbsp chopped parsley or cilantro salt black pepper a little ají, optional What Can I Substitute? # Ingredient Substitutions The base recipe is naturally vegetarian and gluten-free.
Cassava: You can use fresh cassava or frozen yuca. Cook it thoroughly until tender before frying, then drain it well.
Queso Paraguay: A mild queso fresco or another mild white cheese works well. A mix of mild feta and mozzarella is another good option.
Kitchen Equipment # large skillet pot, if using fresh cassava knife cutting board bowl for the eggs spatula or wooden spoon 👩‍🍳 Step-by-Step Instructions # Preparation # If using fresh cassava: Peel the root, wash it thoroughly, and cut it into large pieces. Boil in salted water for about 20 to 30 minutes until fully cooked and tender. Drain well and let the pieces cool briefly. Do not eat cassava raw. You can use cooked cassava from the day before without any additional preparation. Remove the tough center fiber and cut the cassava into bite-sized pieces. Pieces that are not too small hold their shape better while browning and when the eggs are folded in. Finely chop the onion and optional garlic. Chop the green onions and herbs. Lightly beat the eggs in a small bowl. Cut the Queso Paraguay into small pieces or crumble it coarsely. Cooking # Sauté the onions: Heat the oil in a large skillet. Sauté the onion and optional garlic over medium heat until translucent.
Brown the cassava: Add the cooked cassava pieces and spread them out in a single layer if possible. Cook over medium to medium-high heat until browned in several spots. Do not stir constantly. Let the pieces sit undisturbed for a few minutes at a time, then turn them carefully.
Add the eggs: Pour the beaten eggs over the browned cassava and gently fold everything together.
Add the cheese: Once the eggs have started to set, add the Queso Paraguay. Continue cooking just until the eggs are fully set and the cheese has softened. Do not cook it too long, or the dish can turn dry.
Finish the dish: Fold in the green onions and herbs, then season with salt and black pepper to taste. Serve the Mandi’o Chyryry hot right away.
Nutrition Information # The values are based on 1 of 3 servings of the base recipe.
Calories: about 550 kcal Protein: about 13 g Carbohydrates: about 81 g Fat: about 20 g Fiber: about 5 g The nutrition information is an estimate and may vary depending on the cassava, cheese, amount of oil, and serving size.
🍽️ What Goes Well with Mandi’o Chyryry? # Mandi’o Chyryry can easily be served on its own as a warm meal. If you would like to add something, there are a few simple options depending on when you are serving it.
Sides Drinks As a meal: Mandi’o Chyryry does not really need a side dish.
Paraguayan: Two simple Paraguayan options are Pan Casero and Galleta Cuartel, the latter being a firmer type of bread. Outside Paraguay, plain dinner rolls work well too.
Fresh: A tomato and onion salad or a simple green salad adds a fresh contrast.
As a side dish: A smaller serving also works well with grilled or pan-fried meat.
Paraguayan: Mate or Cocido are good choices when Mandi’o Chyryry is served in the morning or on a cooler day.
Refreshing: In warm weather, Tereré is a refreshing choice.
🔄 Recipe Variations # Like many simple everyday dishes, Mandi’o Chyryry can be adapted to whatever you have on hand. Recipes therefore vary from household to household.
Popular Variations # With vegetables: Diced tomatoes or Locote (bell pepper) add a little more moisture and freshness to the skillet.
With meat (Mandi’o Chyryry So’o): Ground beef, finely diced beef, or chorizo make the dish richer and more filling.
More posts like this? 🇵🇾 Did you enjoy this post and want to learn more about Paraguay? Get Paraguay4Life updates by email and stay connected. Get new posts by email Free. You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → 🇵🇾 Background on Mandi’o Chyryry # Name and Spelling Variants # The name points straight to the main ingredient. Mandi’o is the Guaraní word for mandioca, or cassava. Chyryry roughly means “fried” or “to fry.”
Sometimes, chyryry is also associated with the sizzling sound of food frying in a skillet. It is a useful image, but it should not be confused with the actual dictionary meaning.
We use the spelling Mandi’o Chyryry. Online, you will also find Mandi’o Chyryry with a straight apostrophe as well as the simplified spelling Mandio Chyryry.
Cassava and Mandi’o Chyryry in Everyday Paraguayan Cooking # Cassava, eggs, and Queso Paraguay are everyday staples in many Paraguayan households. They are versatile and show up in all kinds of everyday dishes.
Cassava itself is often served as a side dish in Paraguay. When cooked pieces are left over, they can easily be turned into another meal with just a few additional ingredients.
Mandi’o Chyryry is a good example of how simple that can be. The cassava stays in fairly large pieces and is browned in a skillet. When we first saw the dish, it immediately reminded us of pan-fried potatoes. The basic idea is similar, although cassava has a very different flavor and texture.
There is no strict rule about when Mandi’o Chyryry is eaten. It can be served as a hearty breakfast, as a warm meal on its own, or sometimes as a side dish or appetizer. There is no fixed season for it either. Because it is quite filling, however, it works especially well during the cooler months as a hearty winter dish.
Cooked cassava is also used for Pajagua Mascada, where it is combined with meat and shaped into savory patties. Pastel Mandi’o, on the other hand, is similar to an empanada: its dough is based on cooked cassava, then filled with a savory mixture and fried.
❓ Frequently Asked Questions # What is Mandi’o Chyryry? Mandi’o Chyryry is a Paraguayan skillet dish made with cooked cassava, eggs, cheese, and usually onions or green onions. It is especially handy for turning leftover cassava into a new meal. Can I use cooked cassava from the day before? Yes. Mandi’o Chyryry works especially well with leftovers from the day before. The cassava pieces become firmer in the refrigerator but soften again when heated in the skillet. What cheese can I use instead of Queso Paraguay? A mild queso fresco or another mild white cheese works well. You can also use a mix of mild feta and mozzarella. Can I use frozen yuca? Yes. Cook it until fully tender, drain it well, and then use it just like freshly cooked cassava. Is Mandi’o Chyryry gluten-free? The base recipe is naturally gluten-free. If needed, check the labels of processed ingredients and keep possible cross-contact in mind. How long can I store cooked Mandi’o Chyryry? Cool leftovers as quickly as possible and refrigerate them within two hours. Mandi’o Chyryry will keep in the refrigerator for about 3 to 4 days. If the temperature is above about 90°F (32°C), refrigerate it within one hour. Reheat leftovers thoroughly before eating. What is the correct spelling of Mandi’o Chyryry? We use Mandi’o Chyryry. The spelling Mandi’o Chyryry with a straight apostrophe and the simplified version Mandio Chyryry are also common online. Conclusion # For me, Mandi’o Chyryry is a great example of just how simple everyday Paraguayan cooking can be. Cooked cassava and a few other ingredients quickly turn into a completely new warm meal.
Enjoy cooking, and buen provecho!
You can find more Paraguayan recipes with cassava in our cassava recipe collection. You can find even more dishes to try in our collection of Paraguayan recipes.

summary: Leftover cooked cassava? Add eggs, Queso Paraguay, and onions to make Mandi’o Chyryry, a quick and hearty cassava skillet dish.

Chipa is one of those things you can hardly miss in Paraguay. You will find it in chiperías, at roadside stands, in markets, and along the country’s highways. People eat it for breakfast, as an afternoon snack, or simply on the go.
Once a year, this traditional savory cheese bread even gets a day of its own: the Día Nacional de la Chipa, also known as Chipa Ára. In 2026, National Chipa Day falls on Friday, August 14. It is always observed on the second Friday in August.
It is not a day off. Still, the occasion says a lot about the place chipa holds in Paraguay. It is simply part of everyday life and, for many people, part of Paraguay itself.
Quick Facts at a Glance Date in 2026: Friday, August 14 Annual date: second Friday in August Status: National Chipa Day, not an official public holiday Legal basis: Ley Nº 5267/2014 Meaning: chipa is recognized as the Alimento Nacional del Paraguay Possible activities: Chipa-Apo, tastings, school and cultural activities, and special promotions Places with a strong chipa tradition: Eusebio Ayala in Cordillera and Coronel Bogado in Itapúa In short: businesses, schools, and government offices generally operate as usual. Chipa becomes more visible through restaurants, media coverage, and local events. 🧭 Día Nacional de la Chipa in Paraguay: Date, Status, and Meaning # The Día Nacional de la Chipa takes place every year on the second Friday in August. In 2026, this is August 14. The exact date therefore changes from year to year.
The legal basis is Ley Nº 5267/2014. It declares chipa the Alimento Nacional del Paraguay and also establishes National Chipa Day. The law uses the name Día Nacional del Chipá. In everyday life, you may also hear the shorter name Chipa Ára, which roughly means “Chipa Day.”
National Chipa Day is not an official public holiday. In other words, it remains a normal work and school day and does not create a long weekend.
The following day, August 15, the Fundación de Asunción is an official public holiday throughout Paraguay.
Like the Día Nacional del Tereré, National Chipa Day is not about having a day off. Instead, it is about recognizing a part of Paraguayan culture that is woven into everyday life.
Why Does Chipa Have Its Own Day in Paraguay? # If you have never tried chipa, think of it as a savory cheese bread. Typical ingredients include cassava starch, Queso Paraguay, eggs, and fat. Some recipes also use corn flour, milk, or anise. But that only tells you what is on the plate.
Chipa is eaten all year round in Paraguay. People have it for breakfast, as a merienda, or as something to take on the road. Along many highways, chiperías and chiperos and chiperas are a familiar sight. Chiperías are small shops that specialize in chipa, while chiperos and chiperas are the people who sell it.
Chipa on the Road One place where this roadside tradition really stands out to us is around Caacupé. Along Ruta PY02, roughly between kilometers 52 and 59, you will find several chiperías, but especially women selling warm chipa right by the roadside to passing travelers. Cars often pull over briefly with their hazard lights on, buy chipa, and continue on their way. For us, this stretch is often a quick stop when we visit Caacupé.
Chipa also carries a strong cultural tradition. Recipes, techniques, and knowledge about the dough, shaping, and baking are often passed down within families. Since 2015, the knowledge and techniques involved in making chipa have been recognized as national intangible cultural heritage.
Today’s chipa is also the result of a long history. Earlier forms made from cassava and corn came from Indigenous cooking traditions; cheese, milk, and eggs were added later. So calling any one person the “inventor of chipa” would be an oversimplification.
🪅 How Is the Día Nacional de la Chipa Celebrated in Paraguay? # There is no single nationwide program. Typical activities include Chipa-Apo, tastings, school events, restaurant specials, music, and folklore. What actually takes place depends on the location and the year.
One concrete example from 2026 comes from Eusebio Ayala: on August 9, the XVI Fiesta Nacional del Chipá was held at Plaza Independencia. Held every August, the festival traditionally combines chipa with music and a cultural program.
Events like these do not necessarily fall on the second Friday in August itself. Elsewhere, National Chipa Day may be marked much more quietly.
Chipa-Apo: Baking Together # Chipa apo loosely means making chipa. It is often about more than the recipe itself. Preparing the dough, kneading, shaping, and baking are all part of how techniques and family recipes are passed down.
Traditionally, chipa is often baked in a Tatakua, a dome-shaped clay oven. Banana leaves, known as pakova rogue, may be used as a baking surface.
Chipa-Apo is especially closely tied to Semana Santa in Paraguay, or Holy Week. Many families prepare large batches of chipa for the holidays.
We have not taken part in a Chipa-Apo ourselves yet. At Easter, though, we get homemade chipa every year from the man who works for us. His family bakes so much for the holidays that there is enough to share with amigos and the patrón as well.
On the Día Nacional de la Chipa, Chipa-Apo can also be seen beyond family kitchens, for example at public demonstrations, school activities, or cultural events.
If You Join a Chipa-Apo # You do not need any special experience. If you join a Chipa-Apo, feel free to ask about the family recipe (¿Cómo hacen la chipa en tu familia? – “How does your family make chipa?”), individual steps (¿Cómo se hace esto? – “How is this done?”), or the type of chipa: ¿Qué tipo de chipa es esta? – “What kind of chipa is this?”
If you are invited to join in, watch first and let someone show you how the dough is shaped and handled. Techniques and quantities vary from family to family.
When the chipa comes out of the oven hot and fresh and everyone sits down together, mate or Cocido is the classic accompaniment. An ¡Feliz Día Nacional de la Chipa! (“Happy National Chipa Day!”) is a natural thing to say, too.
Not All Chipa Is the Same # There are many different types of chipa. Recipes, ingredients, and shapes vary from family to family, from region to region, and between chiperías.
Some of the best-known varieties include:
Variety What is typical? Chipa almidón / aramirõ classic variety made with cassava starch and cheese Chipa mestiza also contains corn flour Chipa so’o chipa filled with meat Chipa manduvi variety made with peanuts Chipa asador / kavure (also caburé) cooked on a stick over hot coals There is no single fixed shape either. Besides the common rings, you can also find sticks, braids, and crescent-shaped chipa.
Classic chipa should not be confused with Chipa Guasu. Despite the name, Chipa Guasu is a different dish: a moist casserole made with fresh corn and cheese, often served as a side with asado or other meals.
You can find more dishes from Paraguay in our Paraguayan recipes.
What Does National Chipa Day Mean for Everyday Life? # Because August 14, 2026, is not an official public holiday, Friday is basically a normal working day.
Stores, supermarkets, and shopping centers: generally regular business hours, with occasional chipa-related promotions Chiperías and restaurants: generally regular business hours; local tastings or special events may take place Schools: regular classes; cultural projects or Chipa-Apo activities may take place Banks, government offices, and public institutions: regular business day Buses, taxis, and ride-hailing services: generally normal Friday service Areas around local events may be busier, with minor traffic changes possible.
Good to Know The following day, Saturday, August 15, 2026, the Fundación de Asunción is an official public holiday. Keep the two dates separate when planning errands, government office visits, or travel.
Where Is the Chipa Tradition Especially Visible? # Chipa is easy to find across Paraguay. Eusebio Ayala and Coronel Bogado are especially well known for their chipa traditions.
Eusebio Ayala / Chipa Barrero # Eusebio Ayala in the Department of Cordillera was once known as Barrero Grande. Chipa Barrero is still closely associated with the town today.
Chiperías along Ruta PY02, together with the Chipa Rape and the annual Fiesta Nacional del Chipá in August, make this tradition especially visible.
Chipa as Cultural Heritage in Eusebio Ayala Since March 2026, chipa has also had official recognition at the local level. Through Resolución I.M. Nº 433/2026, the municipality declared it Patrimonio Cultural Inmaterial de interés distrital. The recognition highlights local production, the way knowledge is passed down, and cultural activities connected with chipa.
Coronel Bogado # Coronel Bogado in the Department of Itapúa also has a strong chipa tradition. SENATUR tourism materials refer to the town as the Capital Nacional de la Chipa. Chiperías and roadside chipa sales have long been part of the local scene.
Together, Eusebio Ayala and Coronel Bogado represent two distinct and especially well-known chipa traditions.
Chipa and UNESCO: Where Does the Nomination Stand in 2026? # In 2026, Paraguay is moving forward with the nomination of chipa for inscription on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
The nomination is not just about the food itself. It also covers the know-how involved in making chipa, how that knowledge is passed from one generation to the next, and chipa’s cultural significance.
Not Yet Recognized by UNESCO As of August 2026, chipa has not yet been added to UNESCO’s Representative List. Paraguay is currently working on the nomination.

You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → ❓ Frequently Asked Questions About the Día Nacional de la Chipa # When Is the Día Nacional de la Chipa in 2026? In 2026, the Día Nacional de la Chipa falls on Friday, August 14. It is always observed on the second Friday in August, so the exact date changes from year to year. Is the Día Nacional de la Chipa a Public Holiday in Paraguay? The day is legally established as the Día Nacional del Chipá, but it is not an official public holiday. Stores, schools, banks, and government offices generally operate as usual. What Does Chipa Ára Mean? Chipa Ára can roughly be understood as “Chipa Day” and is a common shorter name for the Día Nacional de la Chipa. What Is the Difference Between Chipa and Chipa Guasu? Classic chipa is a savory cheese bread usually made with cassava starch and shaped into rings or other forms. Chipa Guasu, by contrast, is made with fresh corn and is a moist casserole. Our Chipa Guasu recipe gives you a closer look at the dish. Is Paraguayan Chipa Gluten-Free? Many classic chipa varieties are based on cassava starch and do not contain wheat flour. However, store-bought chipa is not automatically gluten-free. Recipes may vary, and cross-contamination is possible. If you have celiac disease, always ask about the ingredients and preparation. Is Chipa Already Recognized by UNESCO? No. Traditional chipa-making is nationally protected as intangible cultural heritage in Paraguay. In 2026, Paraguay is moving forward with the UNESCO nomination of chipa, but it has not yet been added to the list. Conclusion # Chipa is such a natural part of life in Paraguay that it is easy to forget how much tradition is wrapped up in it. You pick it up at a chipería in the morning, buy it along the highway while traveling, and see it baked together by many families at Easter.
Once a year, the Día Nacional de la Chipa gives this familiar everyday tradition a moment of its own. It is also a good reason to take a closer look during your next chipa stop, try a new variety, or ask how it was made.
If you would like to discover when chipa is most closely tied to family and tradition in Paraguay—and baked in large quantities—continue with our article on Holy Week in Paraguay.

summary: Why Paraguay celebrates chipa, how National Chipa Day is observed, and the traditions behind the country’s national food.

On August 15, Asunción remembers its founding in 1537. However, a city in the formal sense did not yet exist at that time. First, a fortified casa fuerte was established on the Río Paraguay. Asunción only received city status four years later.
Paraguay commemorates these beginnings with the Día de la Fundación de Asunción. The nationwide public holiday falls on Saturday, August 15, in 2026, and the capital celebrates its 489th anniversary.
You will also learn why it is a nationwide public holiday, how it is celebrated today, and what to know about opening hours, events, and traffic.
Quick Facts at a Glance Date in 2026: Saturday, August 15 Status: nationwide fixed public holiday (feriado inamovible) Commemorates: the establishment of the casa fuerte in 1537 Anniversary: 489 years of Asunción Celebrations in 2026: A central event at the Costanera has been announced. Everyday life: Government offices and banks remain closed. Private businesses decide their own opening hours. 🧭 Founding Day of Asunción in Paraguay: Date, Status, and Meaning # The Día de la Fundación de Asunción, literally “Day of the Founding of Asunción,” is celebrated every year on August 15. It is one of Paraguay’s fixed legal public holidays and remains tied to the calendar date as a feriado inamovible. In 2026, it falls on a Saturday, so it will not be moved to Friday or Monday.
The holiday commemorates the events of 1537, when a fortified outpost was established on the Río Paraguay. This settlement later developed into today’s capital.
Ley Nº 7544/2025 lists the day as a national public holiday. It therefore applies not only in Asunción, but throughout the country. In years when a new president takes office, the presidential inauguration also takes place on this date.
For 2026, this means there will be no additional long weekend. Anyone who normally works on Saturdays should check how the public holiday is handled under their employment terms.
And there is another special date just one day earlier: On August 14, Paraguay observes Día Nacional de la Chipa, another cultural day with strong ties to everyday life. Unlike August 15, however, it is not an official public holiday.
The Founding of Asunción: From a Casa Fuerte to a City # August 15, 1537, is considered the founding date of Asunción. On that day, Juan de Salazar de Espinosa did not establish a fully organized colonial city on the bay of the Río Paraguay. Instead, he set up a casa fuerte, or fortified outpost. At first, it served as a supply point and a base for further expeditions.
Spanish expeditions explored the region and searched for Juan de Ayolas and routes farther inland.
Why Was the Outpost Established Here? # The Río Paraguay was the most important transport route into the interior. People, messages, and supplies could be moved along the river. The bay also provided a suitable landing place, while the higher riverbanks offered strategic advantages.
Access to supplies also mattered. Cario-Guaraní communities were already living in the surrounding area, and the Spanish encountered their settlements, routes, and cultivated land.
The Cario-Guaraní Were Here Before 1537 # The Cario-Guaraní had already settled the area around the Río Paraguay before the arrival of the Spanish. Their encounter with the newcomers and the power relations that developed from it are part of Paraguay’s early colonial history.
Early contact included trade, supplies, and political agreements. Some Cario-Guaraní formed connections with the Spanish based on their own interests. However, these relationships were not equal or permanently peaceful.
As Spanish rule expanded, systems of dependency and forced labor emerged, later including the Encomienda system, which controlled Indigenous labor and tribute. Resistance and violence were also part of the colonial process. Describing this as a harmonious shared founding would ignore these power relations.
1537 or 1541: When Did Asunción Become a City? # The publicly celebrated founding date and the formal creation of the city are several years apart.
Year What happened? Meaning 1537 A fortified casa fuerte was established on the Río Paraguay Beginning of the permanent Spanish settlement 1541 The Cabildo was established on September 16 Asunción received a city government and formal city status A Cabildo was the municipal government of a Spanish colonial city. When it was established, Asunción formally became a city on September 16, 1541. However, the publicly celebrated founding date remained August 15, 1537.
Why Is the City Called Asunción? # The founding date fell on the Catholic feast of the Assumption of Mary. In Spanish, it is called Asunción de María. The new settlement was named after this feast.
Two similar Spanish words should not be confused:
Asunción refers to the Assumption of Mary. Ascensión refers to the Ascension of Christ. For this reason, the feast of Nuestra Señora de la Asunción is also celebrated on August 15, alongside the city anniversary.
Why Is Asunción Also Called “Madre de Ciudades”? # After the first Spanish settlement of Buenos Aires was abandoned in 1541, Asunción became the political and logistical center of the Spanish presence in the interior.
Further expeditions set out from here. They explored river routes, established settlements, and helped create other cities. The best-known example is the second founding of Buenos Aires in 1580.
For this reason, Asunción is known as the Madre de Ciudades, or “Mother of Cities”. The name refers to the city’s role as the starting point for later city foundations in the Río de la Plata region.
🪅 How Is August 15 Celebrated in Paraguay Today? # The public holiday is observed throughout the country, but the most visible celebrations take place in Asunción. The city anniversary, cultural events, and the religious feast of Nuestra Señora de la Asunción come together there.
Depending on the year, the program may include concerts, exhibitions, crafts, city tours, or performances. Larger events often have food stands as well. However, there is no known traditional dish specifically linked to the Fundación de Asunción.
Outside the capital, in the so-called Interior, the day is generally quieter. Many people follow the anniversary mainly through news reports and social media.
Fundación de Asunción 2026 # The Municipalidad de Asunción has announced a central celebration at the Costanera de Asunción for August 15. A special part of the 2026 program is the inauguration of a new monument to Nuestra Señora de la Asunción at the Costanera Norte. The inauguration also falls in the year marking the 75th anniversary of the Virgen de la Asunción being named Patroness of Paraguay and Mariscala de las Fuerzas Armadas. You can find current information about other city events from the Municipalidad, its cultural department, and local media.
Alongside the city celebrations, August 15 is also observed as a religious feast day. Around the Catedral Metropolitana, church services, a novena, and processions may take place. The religious program is organized separately from the city events and is announced by the Catedral Metropolitana or the archdiocese.
Where Can You Discover Asunción’s History Today? # Anyone in the capital around August 15 can discover the history of Asunción in several places.
The Catedral Metropolitana recalls Nuestra Señora de la Asunción and points to the religious origin of the city’s name. The Centro Cultural de la República El Cabildo represents the city’s political and urban development. The Manzana de la Rivera shows different periods of Asunción’s architecture.
At the Bahía and the Costanera, it becomes clear how important the Río Paraguay was for the location and supply of the early settlement.
Ahead of Asunción’s 500th anniversary in 2037, restoration and revitalization projects are already underway in the historic center.
🧩 What Does the Holiday Mean in Everyday Life? # As the holiday falls on a Saturday in 2026, it has less effect on the regular workweek. Its effects may still be noticeable around event venues in Asunción.
Opening Hours, Shopping, and Medical Care # Large supermarkets, shopping centers, and restaurants may be open, sometimes with adjusted hours. Small stores, despensas, and market stalls decide individually. Check the opening hours in advance, even if a business is normally open on Saturdays.
Museums and attractions may also have different opening hours because of the celebrations.
Regular doctors’ offices may be closed. In a medical emergency, call SEME free of charge at 141. The service is available 24 hours a day. To find an open pharmacy, look locally for a farmacia de turno.
Practical Shopping Tip Stock up on essential groceries and medication, and withdraw some cash in advance. A small pantry reserve makes you less dependent on last-minute changes to opening hours.
Schools, Government Offices, and Banks # Government offices, public institutions, banks, and schools do not operate normally on the holiday. In 2026, this matches the usual Saturday closure for many places. School projects or cultural programs usually take place in the days before.
Traffic and Travel # Buses may run on weekend or holiday schedules. For long-distance trips, check connections and your return journey in advance. Taxis and ride services are usually available, but they may be busier after larger events.
Depending on the event program, road closures, detours, and heavier traffic are possible around the Costanera and the Centro Histórico. Allow extra time. Anyone traveling from the Interior should fill up early and book accommodation in advance.
🤝 As a Visitor or New Resident: What Is Good to Know? # A few simple rules can help at public and religious celebrations.
✅ What Is Appreciated # A friendly anniversary greeting. Modest clothing at church services and processions. Asking permission before taking close-up photos of people. ⛔ What You Should Avoid # Interrupting religious ceremonies for photos. Blocking routes during a procession. Taking close-up photos of people or religious images without asking. At larger events, keep an eye on your personal belongings and agree on a meeting point with your group.
💬 Cheat Sheet: Useful Phrases for This Day # A few simple phrases you may hear or use around the Fundación de Asunción.
🇪🇸 Spanish 🇵🇾 Guaraní Phrase Meaning ¡Feliz aniversario, Asunción! Happy anniversary, Asunción! ¿Dónde se hacen los festejos por la Fundación de Asunción? Where are the Fundación de Asunción celebrations taking place? ¿Esta calle está cerrada por los festejos? Is this street closed because of the celebrations? Phrase Meaning Vy’apavẽ! Congratulations! 🗓️ At a Glance: What to Plan # The Fundación de Asunción falls on Saturday, August 15, in 2026, and will not be moved to Friday or Monday. Take care of government errands and banking beforehand, and get any needed medication or cash in good time. The day before, check the opening hours of stores, restaurants, museums, and attractions, as well as the current event program. If you are driving to Asunción, allow extra time around the Costanera and the Centro Histórico for the trip and parking. Keep possible road closures and detours in mind. Anyone traveling from farther away should book accommodation early and check tickets, schedules, and the return journey in advance when traveling by bus. You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → ❓ Frequently Asked Questions About the Fundación de Asunción # What is the Fundación de Asunción, and when does it take place in 2026? The Fundación de Asunción commemorates the establishment of a casa fuerte on August 15, 1537. In 2026, the holiday falls on Saturday, August 15, and marks the 489th anniversary. Is August 15 a holiday only in Asunción? No. August 15 is a legal public holiday throughout the country. However, the larger public celebrations are concentrated in Asunción. Will the August 15, 2026 holiday be moved? No. August 15 is a fixed holiday and remains on Saturday in 2026. A regular move to Friday or Monday is not planned. What happened in 1537, and why is 1541 also important? In 1537, Juan de Salazar de Espinosa established a fortified casa fuerte on the Río Paraguay. Only when the Cabildo was established on September 16, 1541, did Asunción receive a city government and formal city status. Are stores and supermarkets open on August 15? Many larger stores, shopping centers, and restaurants may be open, sometimes with adjusted hours. Small businesses decide individually, so you should check opening hours in advance. Conclusion # The Fundación de Asunción is more than a city birthday. It connects the area’s Indigenous history before 1537, the beginning of the Spanish settlement, and Asunción’s later role as the Madre de Ciudades.
If you are in the capital on August 15, it is worth combining the anniversary with a visit to the historic center, the Catedral Metropolitana, or the Costanera. Check the current program, opening hours, and possible road closures the day before.
If you would like to place Asunción’s founding in the broader context, our overview of the history of Paraguay takes you from the early colonial period to the present day.
Share and Support Did you know that Asunción began as a fortified outpost in 1537 and only received city status in 1541?
Then feel free to like and share this article with other people interested in Paraguay. This helps make the history and meaning of Paraguayan public holidays easier to understand.
