What do a cheese bread, a melancholic music style, a hydroelectric power plant, and a figure from folk beliefs have in common? Each one tells part of Paraguay’s story.
From A for Asunción to Z for zebu cattle, this Paraguay alphabet takes you through daily life and culture, language and history, as well as a few features that do not appear in every country guide.
And because Paraguay cannot really be explained without Ñ, this alphabet includes one extra letter.
🏙️ A for Asunción, Asado, and Ao po’i # Asunción is the capital, economic center, and the first contact many travelers have with Paraguay. Paraguay commemorates the founding of Asunción in 1537 every year on August 15. Historic buildings, modern office towers, green squares, simple residential neighborhoods, and the Río Paraguay are often surprisingly close together here.
An Asado is about more than grilled meat and sausages. On Sundays with family, at birthdays, around a football match, or together in the park, the grill quickly becomes a meeting place.
Ao po’i shows another side of the country. This fine cotton fabric is traditionally embroidered and is especially connected with Yataity in the Departamento Guairá.
🏞️ B for Balnearios and Being Landlocked # When the summer heat becomes intense, a weekend trip often leads to an arroyo, river, or one of the many balnearios. Some are simple swimming spots, while others offer barbecue areas, small restaurants, sports facilities, or places to stay. They are as much a part of free time in Paraguay as football, dancing, Tereré, and spontaneous trips into nature.
Paraguay is also landlocked, so a beach holiday by the ocean is not possible. That does not mean the country is cut off. The Río Paraguay and the Paraná provide navigable waterways all the way to the Atlantic.
🧀 C for Caacupé, Chaco, and Chipa # On December 8, the country’s attention turns to Caacupé. Around the celebration of the Virgen de los Milagros, many pilgrims travel to the basilica on foot, by bicycle, bus, or car.
The Chaco covers more than half of Paraguay’s land area but is only sparsely populated. Dry thorn scrub, large estancias, wetlands, indigenous communities, and Mennonite colonies shape the west of Paraguay.
And then there is Chipa. This bread made from cassava starch, cheese, and eggs is sold at gas stations, bus terminals, street stalls, in chiperías, and family kitchens. Especially during Semana Santa in Paraguay, larger amounts are baked in many different shapes.
Chipa even has its own national day: Día Nacional de la Chipa is observed on the second Friday in August.
🤝 D for Día de la Amistad and Danza paraguaya # Día de la Amistad, celebrated on July 30, is more than just another date on the calendar in Paraguay. The initiative for an International Day of Friendship began in Paraguay in 1958 and came before its later recognition by the United Nations.
Danza paraguaya brings together music, movement, and traditional clothing. Well-known examples include the Galopera and performances in which dancers balance bottles or other containers on their heads.
🎭 E for Encarnación # On the Paraná River, Paraguay shows a particularly lively side in summer. In Encarnación, the Costanera and beaches are as much a part of the city as trade, border traffic, and views across the river to Argentina.
Things become especially festive during Carnival, when the Sambadrom, music, and colorful costumes shape the city. At the same time, Encarnación is a good starting point for trips to the Jesuit sites of Trinidad and Jesús de Tavarangue.
⚽ F for Fiestas and Football # There are many reasons for fiestas: official and cultural holidays in Paraguay, patron saint celebrations and memorial days, weddings, birthdays, public festivals, or local anniversaries. Music, shared meals, and time with family, friends, or neighbors are often part of them.
Whether in the town square, at the stadium, or in front of the television, football in Paraguay is sport, leisure, and a topic of conversation all at once. In North American English, of course, it is usually called soccer. Those who do not play themselves follow La Albirroja, support a favorite club, or at least have an opinion about the last match.
📜 G for Guaraní and Guarania # Guaraní refers both to one of the country’s two official languages and to Paraguay’s currency. The language is not a remnant of the past but remains alive in many families, regions, and everyday situations.
The similarly named Guarania, on the other hand, is a Paraguayan music style. Its calm, often melancholic melodies tell of love, home, and longing. Polca paraguaya has a much livelier sound.
🎶 H for History and Harp # Paraguay’s history has been shaped by deep breaks. After independence in 1811 came, among other events, the War of the Triple Alliance, the Chaco War, and Alfredo Stroessner’s dictatorship from 1954 to 1989. These and other periods still shape the history of Paraguay today.
The Paraguayan harp, the arpa paraguaya, is one of the country’s best-known instruments. Together with the guitar, it shapes Guarania, Polca paraguaya, and many folk music pieces.
Its bright, flowing sound can be heard at concerts, celebrations, and dance performances: sometimes calm and gentle, sometimes so fast that it is hard to follow the musician’s fingers.
⚡ I for Independence, Indigenous Peoples, and Itaipú # Paraguay’s independence prevailed during the night of May 14 to 15, 1811. Today, both days are celebrated together with flags, events, and historical remembrance.
May 15 is also Mother’s Day in Paraguay. This makes the connection between national history and family celebrations especially visible during the long holiday weekend.
Alongside the Spanish- and Guaraní-speaking majority, Paraguay is home to many indigenous peoples and communities with their own languages and cultural traditions. They are not one single group and do not live only in the Chaco.
Itaipú is much more than a large dam on the border with Brazil. This binational hydroelectric power plant stands for Paraguay’s energy production, international cooperation, and a major technical project that has changed the entire region. Paraguay also has another large binational power plant: Yacyretá.
🏛️ J for Jopará, Jesuits, and Jasy Jateré # In everyday life, Spanish and Guaraní do not always remain clearly separate. Jopará refers to the common mixture or switching between the two languages, sometimes even in the middle of a sentence.
The Jesuit reductions tell the story of another period. The ruins of Trinidad and Jesús de Tavarangue are now UNESCO World Heritage Sites and among the country’s most impressive historic places.
Jasy Jateré comes from Guaraní folk stories. This small guardian of the siesta is said to wander around especially at midday, luring children away with his whistling or a magical staff.
🍲 K for Karai Octubre # On October 1, many kitchens prepare Jopará. This time, it does not mean the language mixture, but a hearty dish made from corn and beans.
Behind it is the story of Karai Octubre, who checks whether a household has prepared for the traditionally lean month. The custom recalls times when an empty food store was a serious problem.
August also begins with a special custom: On August 1, some people drink Carrulim, a mixture of caña, rue, and lemon that, according to folk belief, is meant to keep bad luck and illness away.
But customs and folk beliefs in Paraguay are not limited to these two dates. They are also part of family life, shape how people connect, and appear in small everyday habits. You can find more examples and the stories behind them in our overview.
🌸 L for Lapacho and Lomito árabe # When the Lapacho rosado blooms, its pink flowers can be seen from far away. The Lapacho, called Tajy in Guaraní, is legally recognized as Paraguay’s national tree. The pink variety is one of the most striking splashes of color during the drier season and often blooms as spring in Paraguay begins.
Late in the evening, a Lomito árabe from a lomitería is an easy meal: thinly sliced meat, vegetables, and sauce wrapped in soft flatbread. Its form is reminiscent of dishes from the Middle East. In Paraguay, it has long become a street food classic of its own.
🌱 M for Mandi’o and Mercado 4 # Mandi’o is called mandioca in Spanish and cassava in English. This cooked root naturally appears on the plate alongside Asado, meat dishes, soups, and stews—and you hardly miss bread or potatoes.
Mercado 4 in Asunción is a market, shopping district, and everyday experience all at once. Between fruit, meat, clothing, household goods, electronics, food stalls, and heavy traffic, you can find almost anything—just rarely in peace and quiet.

You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → 🌳 N for National Parks # Paraguay’s national parks show how different the country’s landscapes can be. Ybycuí stands for forests, streams, and waterfalls, while Cerro Corá combines nature with an important setting in Paraguayan history.
In Defensores del Chaco National Park, however, a dry, vast, and much harder-to-reach world begins. Anyone planning to visit such protected areas should check access, weather, and road conditions in advance.
🧵 Ñ – A Paraguayan Extra: Ñandutí and Ñai’ũpo # Ñandutí means roughly “spider web” in Guaraní. This delicate lace is especially associated with Itauguá and can be found on clothing, tablecloths, jewelry, and decorations.
Ñai’ũpo refers to a traditional ceramic craft in which containers and figures are shaped by hand. In 2025, this technique was added to UNESCO’s List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding.
Together with Ao po’i, both traditions represent Paraguay’s diverse handicrafts, which also include woodwork, leatherwork, and other ceramic crafts.
🎻 O for Orquesta de Cateura # What is waste for others becomes a musical instrument for the Orquesta de Cateura. Violins, guitars, cellos, and other instruments are made from reused materials.
The orchestra connects music with the everyday lives of children and young people from Cateura and nearby communities. That is why its story is more than an unusual recycling idea.
🌿 P for Pohã ñana and Pombero # Pohã ñana are plants and herbs traditionally used in daily life. Many are known as yuyos, freshly crushed or cut and added to the cold water for Tereré. Knowing which plant is used for what is knowledge passed down over generations.
The Pombero is one of the best-known figures in Paraguayan folk beliefs. He is said to roam through gardens and forests at night, making himself known through whistling or unusual sounds. The stories also include Jasy Jateré, Luisón, and Ao Ao.
🪵 Q for Quebracho and Queso Paraguay # Several quebracho trees grow in the Chaco. Their name is often derived from quiebra hacha, meaning “axe breaker.” Their especially hard wood played an important economic role for a long time.
Queso Paraguay is a mild, fresh cheese and a key ingredient in many kitchen classics. It is used in Chipa, Sopa Paraguaya, Mbejú, and the small cornmeal dumplings in Vori Vori soup. These classics are just a few examples from the diverse world of Paraguayan recipes.
🌊 R for Radicación, Railways, and Río Paraguay # Anyone who wants to live in Paraguay for a longer period will sooner or later come across the word Radicación. It refers to residency status or the related process. Requirements and documents can change, so the latest information should always be checked.
In 1861, the first train ran on a newly opened section of Paraguay’s railway. Later, the rail network connected Asunción with many towns inland and eventually with Encarnación. Today, old stations, workshops, and historic locomotives in places such as Sapucái and Pirayú recall this period.
Passenger rail service has not disappeared completely: a cross-border train still runs between Encarnación and Posadas in Argentina. Other railway projects, however, are still in different planning stages.
The Río Paraguay divides the country into the more densely populated eastern region and the vast Chaco. At the same time, it is a transport route, habitat, economic factor, and an important part of the country’s history.
🔥 S for San Juan Ára, Sopa Paraguaya, and Spanish # During San Juan Ára in June, things become loud, hot, and sometimes a little chaotic. Fire, traditional games, music, and foods such as Pastel Mandi’o or Pajagua Mascada are part of many celebrations around Saint John’s Day.
Despite its name, Sopa Paraguaya is not a soup. This moist corn casserole with cheese and onions is a classic side dish for Asado and festive meals. Chipa Guasu, made with fresh corn, is also often served.
Spanish is an official language alongside Guaraní and plays an important role especially in administration, media, education, and trade. In daily life, however, it often meets Guaraní and quickly becomes Jopará.
🧉 T for Tereré and Tranquilo # Tereré is not an iced tea that everyone drinks on their own. The guampa is filled, passed around, and belongs to conversations, breaks, family visits, leisure time, and long car trips.
The traditional practice surrounding Tereré and Pohã ñana is on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage List. The Día Nacional del Tereré is also celebrated on the last Saturday in February.
Depending on the situation, tranquilo can mean “everything is fine,” “stay calm,” or “don’t stress about it.” You also often hear a friendly tranquilo pa in everyday life: sometimes as reassurance, sometimes as a reminder to take something a little more calmly.
🏅 U for UNESCO Heritage # Paraguay’s UNESCO-recognized heritage ranges from historic ruins to living traditions. The Jesuit Missions of Trinidad and Jesús de Tavarangue are World Heritage Sites.
Guarania and the traditional practices surrounding Tereré and Pohã ñana are included on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Ñai’ũpo appears on the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding.
🍲 V for Vori Vori # Vori Vori is one of Paraguay’s best-known and most popular soups. This hearty broth is usually cooked with chicken and sometimes with beef.
It gets its name from the small balls made of cornmeal and Queso Paraguay. Especially on cooler days, Vori Vori is one of those dishes that fits naturally into Paraguayan home cooking.
📱 W for WhatsApp & Co. and Winter # An appointment, an order, or a question for a repair worker in Paraguay often first arrives through WhatsApp. Voice messages are practical when explaining an address, sending a photo, or arranging something at short notice. Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok are also part of everyday digital life.
When cold air arrives from the south with a Surazo, temperatures can drop noticeably within a short time. Damp weather and homes built mainly for summer often make winter in Paraguay feel colder than the thermometer suggests. It is usually short, but local frost (escarcha) and even freezing temperatures (helada) are possible on clear nights.
🎪 X for eXpo Paraguay # For X, a little creative spelling is allowed. Agriculture, cattle ranching, trade, food, concerts, and a fairground come together at the eXpo Paraguay.
The large exhibition in Mariano Roque Alonso is especially well known. Other expos are also held in different regions, with a stronger focus on agriculture, cattle ranching, or the regional economy.
⛰️ Y for Ypacaraí and Ybytyruzú # Lake Ypacaraí is known far beyond Paraguay through the song “Recuerdos de Ypacaraí.” San Bernardino and Areguá make it a popular destination for a short break. However, the long-standing environmental and water-quality problems are also part of the full picture.
The Cordillera del Ybytyruzú shows a more mountainous side of Paraguay. This area in the Departamento Guairá is home to Cerro Tres Kandú, the country’s highest elevation. Hiking trails, rocks, forests, and wide views make the region an interesting nature and excursion destination.
🐂 Z for Zebu Cattle # Zebu cattle are easy to recognize by the hump above their shoulders. Breeds such as Brahman and Nelore cope well with hot conditions and play an important role in Paraguay’s cattle ranching.
Together with crossbreeds such as Brangus and Braford, they can be found on large estancias as well as smaller agricultural farms. Cattle ranching shapes rural landscapes, regional expos, and an important part of the country’s economy.
🧭 The Journey Continues After Z # Of course, Paraguay does not end at Z. Behind many of these terms, the real story is only beginning: at the next Tereré, in a language that can change in the middle of a sentence, or in a place that classic travel guides barely mention.
Maybe one letter made you especially curious. Maybe it was H for History. Then you can dive deeper into the history of Paraguay and learn more about the background that still shapes the country today – whether you are just discovering Paraguay, are new to the country, or have lived here for a while.
Share & support Which letter surprised you or made you curious?
Then feel free to give this article a like and share it with other people interested in Paraguay and South America. This helps make Paraguay’s many sides more visible.
summary: From Asunción to zebu cattle, this Paraguay alphabet brings together daily life, culture, history, food, and surprising details.

content:
Free time in Paraguay often does not begin with a big outing plan. It can be sharing tereré in the shade, a soccer game on the cancha, a dance class after school, or a Sunday by the arroyo with family. Balnearios, fishing, markets, concerts, and a shared meal are also part of it.
Your options depend greatly on where you live. In Asunción and larger cities, the range of activities is wider and easier to find. In rural areas, local sports fields, dance schools, nature, clubs, and community events play a bigger role. Some activities are professionally advertised, but you often learn about them through WhatsApp, social media, or personal contacts.
This overview shows you which activities are part of everyday life in Paraguay, how cities and rural areas differ, and what to consider when planning.
📌 Things to Do in Paraguay at a Glance # The most important points Especially important in everyday life: family, friends, tereré, shared meals, and soccer Very visible in local culture: Danza Paraguaya, dance schools, music, and performances at celebrations Popular in summer: balnearios, swimming pools, arroyos, and other swimming spots Easier to find in larger cities: gyms, padel, running groups, movie theaters, and concerts Often more important in rural areas: local canchas, celebrations, fishing, cabalgatas, and nature destinations What do Paraguayans do on weekends and in their free time? # In Paraguay, free time is not always organized as a regular hobby. It is often closely connected to family, friends, and the neighborhood. People visit each other, sit together in the patio, the yard or outdoor area of a home, drink tereré, barbecue, or meet at the plaza, the town’s central square. Especially on Sundays and holidays, a shared lunch can take up a large part of the day.
That does not mean there are no clubs, classes, or modern activities. They are simply distributed very unevenly. What is easy to book in Greater Asunción is often organized through schools, private instructors, or personal contacts in smaller towns.
Searching also works differently than many people may be used to. Not every club has a well-maintained website. You can often find current activities through Facebook, Instagram, local WhatsApp groups, and by asking municipalities, schools, clubs, or people you know directly.
Spending time together: Tereré and Asado # If you only look for activities you can book, you miss an important part of Paraguayan everyday life. Sitting together and talking is not a break between activities, it is often the activity itself.
A tereré gathering is rarely only about the drink. People sit together, exchange news and sometimes gossip, pass around the guampa, and often stay longer than planned.
Tereré is Paraguay’s national drink and part of everyday social life. Its cultural importance is also reflected in Día Nacional del Tereré, celebrated on the last Saturday in February.
With an asado, the preparation, conversations, and time spent together are just as important as the food. Whether it is the traditional Sunday barbecue in front of the house, in a park, or near a soccer field, families, young people, and neighbors often get together in the late afternoon and evening as the summer heat eases.
For newcomers, this is one of the easiest ways to make connections. You do not need perfect Spanish or a special hobby. Often, accepting an invitation, bringing something to share, or watching a local game is enough.
Sports in Paraguay: Which sports are especially popular? # Soccer is the most visible sport in Paraguay. Futsal, Piki Vóley, volleyball, and dance are also part of everyday life in many places. In larger cities and regional centers, there are also gyms, running groups, martial arts, tennis, and padel. Which activities are available locally depends on where you live, the sports facilities, and local groups.
Playing soccer and following the games # Soccer is played in clubs and soccer schools, but also in schoolyards, simple sports fields, and rented canchas. Small-sided versions such as Fútbol 5 are especially common. In rural areas, local leagues and tournaments are often not only sporting competitions but also meeting places for families, friends, and neighbors.
If you would like to play yourself, you will often find a group through neighbors, coworkers, schools, or a local cancha rather than through an official club website. Many groups are privately organized and arranged on short notice through WhatsApp.
You will also encounter soccer in Paraguay almost everywhere as a spectator. Games of La Albirroja, major clubs such as Olimpia and Cerro Porteño, or the local team are watched at home, in bars, and with neighbors.
Futsal, Piki Vóley, and other ball sports # In addition to soccer, futsal, also called Fútbol de Salón, and volleyball play an important role in many places. They are easier to organize in schools, municipalities, and multipurpose courts than sports that require their own facilities or expensive equipment.
You will also often come across Piki Vóley in Paraguay. The ball is played over a net without using hands. This mix of soccer technique and volleyball is especially common on simple courts, in private groups, and at smaller tournaments.
Basketball, handball, and tennis are also available. How easily you can play them locally depends more on schools, clubs, and the facilities available.
Dance: from Danza Paraguaya to modern styles # Dance is especially widespread among children and teenagers in Paraguay. Many start at an early age in a dance school or group and later perform at school events, patron saint festivals, cultural programs, or competitions. This means dance is not only an activity offered through classes, but is also visible at celebrations and in public life.
Danza Paraguaya, Paraguayan folk dance, has a special place. It is offered by dance schools, cultural groups, and sometimes municipalities. Depending on the location, classical ballet, contemporary and urban dance, Zumba, and partner dances such as salsa and bachata are also part of the program.
Dance schools and groups can be found not only in large cities but also in many smaller towns.
Fitness, running, and padel # In larger cities and regional centers, you can find gyms, martial arts, cross-training, and private padel courts. There are also running and cycling groups, as well as organized road races and trail events. Based on our observations, running groups and local competitions are more visible in our area today than they were a few years ago. This is not a nationwide statistic, but an everyday observation.
In rural areas, these groups are often organized through WhatsApp or social media. It is worth asking at gyms, municipalities, and among people you know.
Outdoor Activities: Water, Exercise, and Outings # Which activities are suitable at any given time depends greatly on the climate and weather in Paraguay. During the hot summer, balnearios, swimming pools, and shady places by the water are especially popular. The cooler months are often more pleasant for hiking and longer outings.
Balnearios, swimming pools, and swimming spots # Balnearios are popular destinations, especially in summer. Some are simple swimming areas with shade and barbecue spaces, while others offer pools, slides, food service, restrooms, or accommodations.
Good to know: The name “balneario” says nothing about its facilities, water quality, or supervision. MADES lists water testing, safety measures, restrooms, and safe access among the requirements for approved facilities. Especially when traveling with children, a beautiful arroyo is not automatically a safe place to swim.
Public and private swimming pools are mainly found in larger cities and regional centers. They are often part of sports clubs, swim schools, hotels, cooperatives, or municipal facilities. Traditional indoor public pools, like those found in many cities in Europe, are less common. Many pools are outdoors and can be used through classes, memberships, or day passes.
Fishing, horseback riding, and cabalgatas # Fishing is common at rivers, lakes, and private fishing ponds. For beginners, Pesque y Pague facilities are often uncomplicated because access and rules are explained on site. At natural bodies of water, however, there are rules on fishing methods, minimum sizes, and the annual veda pesquera, a temporary fishing ban.
Horseback riding is mainly arranged through estancias, private groups, and personal contacts. Cabalgatas, organized group horseback rides, are often easier to find. They take place as separate events or as part of patron saint festivals, expos, and regional celebrations.
Hiking, cycling, camping, and nature watching # First, it is important to know that marked and maintained hiking trails are not a given outside well-known nature destinations. An outing can therefore be more adventurous than expected.
Depending on where you live, you may find nature and excursion destinations in Paraguay nearby, which can be combined with bird and plant watching or nature photography.
For a day trip or weekend outing, options include Cerro Tres Kandú in Guairá, waterfalls along the Ruta de los Saltos, or the Chaco’s salt lagoons during the cooler months. The Jesuit Missions in Itapúa can also be combined well with a stay in Encarnación.
Based on our experience, cycling has also become more popular in our area over recent years. Quiet side roads are usually more pleasant for rides than heavily traveled main roads. Heat, dust, heavy traffic, missing shoulders, and unpaved roads can make a trip more difficult.
Camping is possible at some nature destinations, private facilities, and sometimes at posadas or estancias. Facilities range from simple tent areas to cabins and permanent accommodations.
Eating out and spending the evening # Sharing a meal is part of how people spend their free time. In the evening, lomiterías, pizzerias, ice cream shops, and simple restaurants with outdoor tables become popular meeting places.
The options differ greatly between cities and rural areas. Asunción and its surroundings, as well as Ciudad del Este and Encarnación, offer more restaurants, bars, cafés, movie theaters, and nightlife options. Smaller towns usually have only a few places to eat, and things are especially busy on weekends or special occasions.
Events and cultural activities # Popular celebrations such as San Juan festivities, expos, markets, dance performances, competitions, and regional festivals shape everyday activities in Paraguay throughout the year. Music, food, crafts, sports, and socializing often come together at these events.
Religious and cultural dates are also part of family life and free time. During Semana Santa in Paraguay, many people travel to visit relatives, while processions, performances, and other activities take place in different towns. Around December 8, the pilgrimage to Caacupé attracts many visitors. Traffic and events in the area are often affected in the days before.
One of the best-known major events is Expo Paraguay in Mariano Roque Alonso. There are also many local celebrations, markets, and performances.
How easy it is to find current events depends on where you live. Larger cities usually have more concerts, theater performances, museums, and cultural programs. In rural areas, schools, municipalities, churches, and local organizers often share upcoming dates.
Check the schedule and start time At local celebrations, the announced start time is not always when the main program begins. If you are traveling for a particular performance, ask about the detailed schedule beforehand.
🧭 Which activity fits your day? # If you … Then you could try … Check beforehand only have a few hours a park, café, local game, swimming pool, or a short tereré gathering opening hours, heat are out with children a park, playground, swimming pool, balneario, movie theater, market, or expo shade, restrooms, safety want to be active soccer, dance class, gym, running group, or padel class times, registration, costs are looking for nature an arroyo, hiking trail, fishing pond, or viewpoint access, weather, trail conditions want to get to know Paraguay better a local celebration, market, soccer game, dance performance, or outing program, start time, return trip have a full day free a balneario, cabalgata, nature destination, or trip to a nearby town travel time, road access, food ✅ Practical Tips for Activities and Outings # Ask in advance # Many businesses, sports groups, and organizers announce changes on Facebook, Instagram, or WhatsApp rather than on a regularly maintained website. Municipalities and neighbors are also often good sources of information about activities and events. Before you go, check opening hours, prices, class times, reservations, and the current daily schedule.
Check access and facilities # For nature destinations, balnearios, and outings, these questions are especially important:
Is the destination open and publicly accessible? What is the access road like after rain? Are there parking spaces, shade, and restrooms? Can you bring your own food or barbecue there? Is swimming allowed, and is there a designated swimming area? Is there cell phone coverage or someone to contact on site? Plan for travel time and cash # Distances often look shorter on a map than they are in reality. Road conditions, passing through towns, and construction can make a trip take longer. If you do not know a destination, it is sensible to visit for the first time during daylight.
Card payments are widely accepted in cities. For smaller events, rural destinations, parking areas, and vendor stands, you should also bring cash and small bills.
Keep school breaks and holidays in mind # During long weekends, school vacations, and major holidays in Paraguay, popular destinations are often crowded or fully booked early. At the same time, there are often additional programs for families.
🗣️ Useful activity vocabulary in Paraguay # Term Meaning cancha sports field, often a soccer or multipurpose field balneario swimming and recreation area with widely varying facilities arroyo creek or small stream plaza central public square, often with green areas and seating cabalgata organized group horseback ride veda pesquera temporary fishing ban seña deposit or reservation fee patio yard or outdoor area of a home ❓ Frequently asked questions about activities in Paraguay # Is dancing popular in Paraguay? Yes. Children and teenagers in particular often start early at a dance school or in a group. Depending on the location, Danza Paraguaya, ballet, urban dance styles, Zumba, salsa, and bachata are offered. What is a balneario in Paraguay? A balneario is a swimming and recreation area. It can be a simple swimming spot by an arroyo or a larger facility with pools, food service, and accommodations. What activities are available outside Asunción? In rural areas, local sports fields, dance groups, balnearios, fishing, horseback riding, nature destinations, and regional celebrations play an important role. Many activities are announced through municipalities, schools, WhatsApp, or personal contacts. What can you do with children in Paraguay? Depending on where you live, options include parks and playgrounds, farms, animal parks, and other family-friendly destinations. There are also sports and dance activities, balnearios, movie theaters, indoor play areas, and local events. Larger cities offer more weather-independent options, while activities with children in rural areas more often take place outdoors. With younger children, pay particular attention to short travel distances, shade, restrooms, and an easy return trip. Where can you find current activities in Paraguay? Check the Facebook and Instagram pages of municipalities, sports groups, and organizers. In rural areas, WhatsApp groups, schools, radio stations, and personal recommendations are also important sources. Can you hike or fish in Paraguay? Yes, both are possible. However, many paths, shore areas, and access roads are on private land or difficult to use after rain. Fishing is also subject to regulations and seasonal fishing bans. Conclusion # Things to do in Paraguay are not limited to well-known attractions and major events. Often, it is the local cancha, a dance school, the nearest balneario, a local celebration, or an invitation for tereré that shapes a free afternoon or weekend.
Anyone who lives in Paraguay for a while quickly notices that soccer and dance are part of everyday life in many families and communities.
In Asunción and larger cities, it is easier to find padel courts, movie theaters, concerts, and organized classes. In rural areas, activities are often closer to local life: at the cancha, by an arroyo, on a cabalgata, or at a community event. When you get to know Paraguay this way, you quickly notice that free time here is often much more closely connected to everyday and social life than you might expect.
Soccer is a particularly good example: it shows how closely free time, community, and everyday life are connected in Paraguay. If you want to get to know this side of the country better, read on about soccer in Paraguay.

content:
Soyo, called So’o Josopy in Guaraní, is a thick beef soup made with finely ground beef, a little rice, and vegetables. This traditional Paraguayan soup is a firm part of the country’s local cuisine and is often served hot on cool days, usually with Paraguayan tortilla or boiled cassava.
When I tried my first bowl, I immediately noticed its unusually fine texture. Unlike a typical ground beef soup, the meat does not stay crumbly but spreads evenly throughout the broth.
In this recipe, you will learn step by step how to achieve this fine texture. You will also find practical cooking tips, simple ingredient substitutions, and several variations.
📝 Soyo Recipe: Step-by-Step Instructions # At a Glance Difficulty: medium Total time: about 60 minutes including 20 minutes of preparation and 40 minutes of cooking Servings: 6 servings as a main dish or 8 smaller servings Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 🛒 Ingredients for So’o Josopy # You probably already have most of the ingredients at home. Here is what you need for the basic recipe and how you can add more flavor.
Main Ingredients # 500 g carnaza negra (roughly top round), finely ground twice; alternatively, use another lean cut from the beef round or lean ground beef 2 liters cold water 2 tbsp rice 1 large onion 1 red or green bell pepper (locote) 1 large tomato 2 garlic cloves 3 green onions 2 tbsp vegetable oil (or pork lard / grasa de cerdo) 1 tsp dried oregano Salt and black pepper 2 tbsp chopped parsley Optional Ingredients # 1 level tbsp all-purpose flour (for additional thickening) ½ tsp ground cumin (comino) A little fresh cilantro (kuratũ) for serving Ingredient Substitutions and Dietary Options Locote: Outside South America, simply use a regular green or red bell pepper.
Fresh tomato: Two to three tablespoons of canned diced tomatoes are a practical substitute when tomatoes are out of season.
Gluten-free: Without the optional flour, the basic recipe is gluten-free. The rice and finely distributed meat already provide light thickening.
Kuratũ: If you do not like fresh cilantro or cannot find it, use flat-leaf parsley instead.
Milder flavor: Vegetable oil has a more neutral flavor than pork lard. For a lower-fat version, you can also reduce the amount slightly.
Kitchen Equipment # Large pot Large bowl for the cold mixture Cutting board and sharp knife Wooden spoon or wooden spatula (patulá) Whisk Meat grinder, blender, or food processor 👩‍🍳 Step-by-Step Preparation # Preparation # Dice the onion, bell pepper, tomato, and garlic as finely as possible. Cut the green onions into thin rings and chop the parsley or cilantro. Rinse the rice briefly and let it drain. Working in batches, pulse the meat and rice with a little cold water in a blender until both are very finely chopped. Do not blend for too long, or the meat may turn into a tough paste. If the meat has already been finely ground twice, you can blend only the rice with a little water and then mix it into the meat.
Cooking Process # Prepare the cold mixture: Mix the meat and rice with 500 ml of the cold water in a large bowl. Gradually whisk in the remaining cold water until the meat is evenly distributed without large lumps. The mixture will look cloudy and milky.
Cook the vegetable base: Heat the oil or pork fat in the pot. Cook the diced onion over medium heat until translucent, then add the garlic and bell pepper and cook for another three minutes.
Build the flavor: Stir in the diced tomato and half of the green onions. Cook for a few minutes until the vegetables soften and the tomato releases its juices. For more thickening, add the optional flour now and cook it for one minute.
Add the meat mixture: Slowly pour the cold meat and rice mixture into the pot in a steady stream. Important: From this point on, stir continuously with a wooden spoon while slowly bringing the Soyo to a boil. This keeps the meat evenly distributed and prevents it from sticking to the bottom.
Simmer: Once the soup begins to boil, reduce the heat. Let the Soyo simmer gently without a lid for about 25 to 30 minutes, stirring regularly.
Season: Season with salt, pepper, oregano, and optional cumin. Remove the pot from the heat and stir in the remaining green onions and fresh parsley.
💡 Practical Tips for Soyo # How to Get the Beef Soup Right Make Soyo without a mortar: Ask your butcher to grind the beef twice, or briefly blend regular ground beef with a little cold water.
Prevent lumps: Distribute the meat and rice completely in cold water. Stir continuously while heating until the soup begins to boil.
Use the right amount of rice: Two tablespoons are enough. Too much rice absorbs the liquid and makes the Soyo much thicker.
Adjust the consistency: If the soup is too thin, let it simmer uncovered for a few more minutes. If it becomes too thick, add a small amount of hot water.
Storage and reheating: Cool leftovers quickly and store them covered in the coldest part of the refrigerator. Try to eat the Soyo within two to three days. The soup usually thickens when reheated, so add a little water if needed.
Nutrition Information # The values are based on one of six main-dish servings without any side dishes.
Calories: about 230 kcal Protein: about 18 g Carbohydrates: about 10 g Fat: about 13 g Fiber: about 1.5 g Note: These nutrition values are estimates and may vary depending on the meat, fat, and serving size used.
🍽️ What Goes Well with Soyo? # Locally, this Paraguayan beef soup is usually eaten as a filling meal rather than a light appetizer. These sides go especially well with it:
Sides Drinks Paraguayan tortillas: Soyo with freshly fried tortilla is the classic combination. Crisp on the outside and soft inside, it is perfect for dipping.
Boiled cassava: In Paraguay, it is often served with savory dishes instead of bread.
Baguette or bread: Both are also simple everyday options to serve with the soup.
Lime water: Its fresh acidity provides a pleasant contrast to the rich soup.
Tereré: This cold yerba mate drink is part of everyday life for many people, even on sunny winter days.
Mate Cocido: This hot mate tea goes especially well with the soup on cold mornings or evenings.
🔄 Recipe Variations # As with many Paraguayan everyday dishes, this recipe varies from family to family. Herbs, amounts of vegetables, and thickening methods can all differ. However, the cold mixture made with finely ground meat remains its defining feature.
Traditional Variations # Soyo con Huevo: In one traditional rural variation, eggs are poached directly in the gently simmering soup at the end. One egg per person makes the dish even more filling. Cook until the egg white is completely set.
With thin soup noodles: One traditional version uses thin soup noodles (fideíto fino) instead of rice. They are also mixed with the meat in cold water.
Modern Everyday Variations # Soyo de Pollo: For this modern variation, very finely chopped chicken is mixed with cold water using the same basic method. The flavor is milder, and the result feels a little lighter than the beef version.
With more vegetables: Carrot or squash gives the soup a light sweetness and makes it a little thicker, but it also changes its meat-focused character.
Quick ground beef version: In this version, the vegetables and ground beef are browned directly in the pot and then covered with water or broth. It is easy to prepare, but the result is closer to a regular ground beef soup than the finely textured So’o Josopy.
You can find more side dishes and other savory classics in our collection of Paraguayan recipes.

You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → 🇵🇾 So’o Josopy in Paraguay: Name, Meaning, and Tradition # What Does So’o Josopy Mean? # The name comes from Guaraní:
So’o means meat, josopy (from joso) means pounded or crushed. So, So’o Josopy roughly means “pounded meat.”
You may also see spellings such as So’o Josopy, So’o Yosopy, or the shortened form Sojo.
The name refers directly to its traditional preparation: Beef and rice were pounded together in an angu’a, a large wooden mortar, until they formed a fine mixture.
The Secret of the Cold Mixture # Why is raw meat stirred into cold water?
Cold water allows the finely chopped meat to spread evenly. In hot liquid, it would immediately set and form larger lumps. Slowly heating and stirring the mixture creates its typical fine, thick texture.
Cultural Role in Paraguay # Soyo belongs to traditional Paraguayan home cooking and is a popular Paraguayan winter dish.
When nights become cold during winter in Paraguay and unheated homes feel uncomfortable in the morning, a hot bowl of Soyo is a welcome meal. The soup is usually eaten at lunchtime, but sometimes also in the late morning as a media mañana.
Since living here, I have noticed how naturally soups and stews are served as complete meals during the colder season. Classics such as Vori Vori, Puchero, Sopa de Locro, and the fish soup Pira Caldo also appear on the menu more often.
The dish also received official recognition in 2025: The Paraguayan Senate declared So’o Josopy a national food. Its traditional preparation in the angu’a was also recognized as culturally important. Declaration No. 294 ↗ also calls for steps toward recognizing the preparation process as part of Paraguay’s intangible cultural heritage.
The Defining Ingredients # Lean beef forms the base of the dish. Traditional recipes call for carnaza negra, also known as nalga in Paraguay. This cut comes from the beef round and is roughly equivalent to top round in the United States. Outside Paraguay, another lean cut from the beef round works well, while lean ground beef is the easiest alternative.
The remaining ingredients are intentionally simple and are mostly part of the basic food supplies found in many Paraguayan households. The small amount of rice is not used like a regular soup filling. Instead, it is ground together with the meat and helps provide light thickening. The refrito made with onion, locote, tomato, and garlic adds flavor. Oregano, parsley, and cilantro (kuratũ) are added near the end so their fresh flavor remains.
❓ Frequently Asked Questions # Why does my Soyo become lumpy, and how can I prevent it? The meat was probably added to liquid that was too warm, or the mixture was not stirred enough while heating. First distribute the meat completely in cold water, then stir continuously until the soup begins to boil. Can I freeze Soyo? Yes. Let the Soyo cool completely and freeze it in individual portions. It will keep for about two to three months in the freezer. The rice may become slightly softer after thawing. Reheat the soup slowly and add a little water if needed. Is Soyo gluten-free? Without the optional all-purpose flour, the basic recipe is gluten-free. Can I make Soyo with regular ground beef? Yes. For the traditionally fine texture, ask for the beef to be finely ground twice, or briefly blend it at home with a little cold water. Regular ground beef also works, but it produces a coarser texture. Does traditional Soyo always contain rice? Rice is used in many traditional recipes and helps provide light thickening. One traditional variation uses thin soup noodles instead. A little flour may also be added separately for extra thickening. Is So’o Josopy recognized as UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage? No. In 2025, the Paraguayan Senate declared So’o Josopy a national food and recognized it as culturally important. The declaration calls for national steps toward recognizing the preparation process as part of Paraguay’s intangible cultural heritage. It has not been recognized by UNESCO. Conclusion # Soyo is a simple but distinctive dish for cold days. The cold mixture needs a little attention, but it rewards you with a finely textured, thick soup that tastes rich and warms you up.
For me, Soyo clearly shows what makes many traditional recipes from Paraguay special: A few everyday ingredients create a dish with a character of its own. Served with tortilla or boiled cassava, it becomes a filling meal that also works well outside Paraguay.
Have fun cooking and buen provecho!
Want to try a very different Paraguayan soup? Vori Vori, with its corn-and-cheese dumplings, is one of the country’s best-known classics. You’ll find more in our collection of Paraguayan soups and stews.
Share & Support Did this traditional So’o Josopy recipe inspire you and make you curious about Paraguay?
Give this post a like and share it with others interested in Paraguay and South America. Together, we can help make Paraguayan cuisine better known.
summary: This thick Paraguayan beef soup is comforting on cool days. Easy to follow, with practical tips, substitutions, and variations.
title: Soyo Recipe from Paraguay: So’o Josopy Soup

At Paraguay4Life, our recipes primarily use grams, milliliters, and degrees Celsius. These metric measurements are precise and commonly used in Paraguay and many other countries.
This guide provides practical conversion tables and reliable reference tools for readers who normally cook with US measurements.
Celsius to Fahrenheit for cooking # Temperatures can be converted reliably. In our English recipes, the Fahrenheit temperature therefore appears directly after the original Celsius measurement:
180°C (350°F) Here are some common oven temperature conversions:
Celsius Fahrenheit 150°C 300°F 160°C 320°F 170°C 340°F 180°C 350°F 190°C 375°F 200°C 400°F 220°C 425°F The Fahrenheit values are rounded to commonly used oven settings. Since ovens can heat differently, check the dish a little earlier the first time you prepare a recipe.
Milliliters, teaspoons, tablespoons, and US cups # Milliliters can be converted into common US volume measurements such as teaspoons, tablespoons, fluid ounces, and cups.
Metric measurement Approximate US measurement 5 ml 1 tsp 10 ml 2 tsp 15 ml 1 tbsp 30 ml 2 tbsp or about 1 fl oz 50 ml about 1.7 fl oz 60 ml 1/4 cup 80 ml about 1/3 cup 100 ml about 3.4 fl oz 120 ml 1/2 cup 125 ml about 1/2 cup 150 ml about 5 fl oz 180 ml 3/4 cup 200 ml about 6.8 fl oz 240 ml 1 cup 250 ml about 1 cup 480 ml 2 cups 500 ml about 2 cups 1 liter about 4 1/4 cups The abbreviations mean:
tsp: teaspoon tbsp: tablespoon fl oz: fluid ounce cup: US measuring cup One US cup is approximately 240 ml. Common metric quantities such as 250 ml and 500 ml are therefore slightly more than one or two US cups. The original metric quantity in the recipe remains the more precise measurement.
Grams, ounces, and pounds # Grams and kilograms measure the weight of an ingredient. They can be converted to ounces or pounds regardless of the type of ingredient.
Metric measurement Approximate US measurement 28 g 1 oz 50 g 1.8 oz 100 g 3.5 oz 150 g 5.3 oz 200 g 7.1 oz 250 g 8.8 oz 300 g 10.6 oz 500 g 17.6 oz or 1.1 lb 750 g 1.65 lb 1 kg 2.2 lb oz is an ounce by weight. fl oz is a fluid ounce and measures volume. The two units are not interchangeable.
Why we do not automatically convert grams to cups # Grams measure the weight of an ingredient, while cups measure its volume. A reliable conversion therefore depends on the specific ingredient being measured.
One cup of cassava starch does not weigh the same as one cup of sugar, cornmeal, shredded cheese, or cooked cassava. Moisture, texture, processing, and the way an ingredient is placed in the cup can also change the result.
For that reason, a general conversion such as “100 grams equals half a cup” would not be reliable.
Our tip: Use a digital kitchen scale for flour, starch, and other dry ingredients whenever possible. It is usually easier and more accurate than converting the quantities to cups.
Which measurements should you use in our recipes? # The metric measurements are the original and most precise quantities in our recipes. Use them whenever you have a kitchen scale or a measuring cup marked in milliliters.
Fahrenheit is provided alongside Celsius for relevant cooking and oven temperatures. The conversion tables on this page offer practical guidance for liquids and weights, but rounded values may differ slightly from the original metric quantities.
When accuracy affects the texture of a dough or batter, follow the metric measurement.
Ready to start cooking? Explore our Paraguayan recipes.
External cooking measurement references # The following independent third-party references may help with additional conversions. Paraguay4Life is not affiliated with either provider.
NIST Metric Kitchen # The National Institute of Standards and Technology provides an official reference for milliliters, teaspoons, tablespoons, cups, fluid ounces, and other common kitchen measurements.
NIST Cooking Measurement Equivalencies ↗
Ingredient-specific conversion chart # The King Arthur Ingredient Weight Chart provides cup, ounce, and gram measurements for many individual ingredients.
King Arthur Ingredient Weight Chart ↗
For regional ingredients, check that the listed ingredient and preparation are comparable. Cassava starch, cooked cassava, cornmeal, and Paraguayan cheese can vary in moisture, texture, and processing.
Frequently Asked Questions # How many milliliters are in one US cup? One US measuring cup is approximately 240 ml. A metric quantity of 250 ml is therefore slightly more than one US cup.
This small difference usually has little effect in soups, sauces, or drinks. For baking and other recipes that require precision, follow the original milliliter measurement.
Can I convert grams directly to cups? Not without knowing the ingredient. Grams measure weight, while cups measure volume. The number of grams in one cup varies considerably between ingredients.
A cup of sugar, flour, cassava starch, shredded cheese, and cooked cassava will each have a different weight. Use an ingredient-specific conversion chart or, preferably, a kitchen scale.
Do I need a kitchen scale for Paraguayan recipes? A kitchen scale is not required for every recipe. Eggs, onions, teaspoons, and tablespoons can be measured without one.
A digital scale is especially helpful for cassava starch, cornmeal, flour, cheese, and other ingredients where accurate quantities affect the texture of the dish.
Are US cups the same as metric cups? Not exactly. A US customary cup contains approximately 236.6 ml and is commonly rounded to 240 ml for cooking. A metric cup contains 250 ml.
The difference often has little effect in everyday cooking, but it can matter in baking and dough-based recipes. Use the original metric measurement when accuracy is important.
summary: Practical conversion tables for temperatures, liquids, and weights used in our Paraguayan recipes.

Expo Paraguay in Mariano Roque Alonso is the country’s largest fair and a major event on the regional calendar. Every July, the grounds of the Asociación Rural del Paraguay (ARP) become a mix of livestock show, business exhibition, public festival, and entertainment program. According to the organizers, more than 800,000 people visited the fair in 2026.
For people who live in Paraguay, are planning to move here, or simply want to understand the country better, the Expo brings many sides of Paraguay together in one place: livestock farming and agriculture, industry and trade, food, culture, public institutions, and a family day out.
This guide explains what Expo Paraguay is, what you can usually expect there, and what to know when planning a future visit. The completed 2026 edition serves as a clear example.
📌 Expo Paraguay 2026: A look back # The 2026 edition at a glance Official name: Expo Paraguay ARP 2026 Edition: 43rd Expo Feria Internacional and 80th Exposición Nacional de Ganadería Dates: July 11 to 26, 2026 Venue: Asociación Rural del Paraguay (ARP) fairgrounds, Mariano Roque Alonso Address / getting there: Ruta PY03, still known to many as Ruta Transchaco, Km 14 Motto: “Lo que mueve al país” (What moves the country) Visitors: more than 800,000 Exhibitors: 200 exhibitors representing 1,500 brands Animal exhibition: More than 2,400 animals of different species and breeds had been announced for the opening. Admission: Regular admission cost Gs. 25,000. Special admission rules applied to certain groups and school visits. Program examples: concerts, Expo Asador, Expo Empleo, animal judging, motocross shows, and family activities These figures and prices apply only to 2026. At the time of this update, no date for the next edition had been confirmed.
What is Expo Paraguay? # Expo Paraguay ARP is a large multi-sector fair. It brings together livestock farming, business, trade, services, culture, food, and entertainment. Locally, it is also called Expo Mariano Roque Alonso, Expo MRA, or simply Expo Py.
The fair brings together areas that often seem separate in everyday life:
Agriculture & livestock farming (Ganadería) National industry & international trade Services & technology Food, crafts & music Public institutions, organizations & job opportunities This mix makes the Expo both a trade fair and an event for the general public. Producers and companies use it for contacts, presentations, and business. For many families, it is also a traditional winter outing.
When and where does Expo Paraguay take place? # Expo Paraguay usually takes place in July. The exact dates, opening hours, admission prices, and special activity days are set separately for each edition. The fair often overlaps with the receso de invierno, Paraguay’s winter school break. Weekends and family days can therefore get especially busy.
The venue is the Campo Ferial Mariano Roque Alonso, the fairgrounds of the Asociación Rural del Paraguay. It is located in Mariano Roque Alonso, a city in the Departamento Central just north of Asunción.
The grounds are on Ruta PY03, which many people still call Ruta Transchaco. The reference to “Km 14” can be confusing because the road name may suggest the Chaco. However, the venue is in the Greater Asunción area.
Why is Expo Paraguay important? # In everyday life in Asunción or along common travel routes through eastern Paraguay, the agricultural economy can remain in the background. The fair shows how important livestock farming, agriculture, and food production are to the country. It is not only about animals, but also about breeding, investment, farm technology, trade, and new business contacts.
Industrial companies, service providers, public institutions, banks, and smaller businesses also present their work. Together, they offer a broad view of Paraguay’s economic and social life.
While industry professionals look at breeding animals, machinery, and products, concerts and shows in the Ruedo Central, food areas, and amusement rides attract families and the wider public. This combination makes the Expo more than an agricultural fair.
Why the awards matter Animals that receive awards during the Juzgamiento can become much more valuable for breeding farms. At the auctions that follow (Remates), the focus is not only on individual animals, but also on genetics, quality, and the reputation of each Cabaña.
Who is Expo Paraguay worth visiting for? # The fair offers a direct look at daily life and the economy in Paraguay. A visit can be useful for several groups:
For immigrants, future expats, and people new to Paraguay: In one day, you can get an overview of companies, brands, public institutions, and economic sectors that shape the country. For families and children: Animal areas, large machines, food stands, shows, and amusement rides make the Expo a varied day out. Activities for children and admission rules change with each edition. For industry professionals and investors: Livestock farming, agriculture, technology, industry, and services are important parts of the fair. There are also auctions, product presentations, and opportunities to make contacts. For travelers: If you want to experience Paraguay beyond its sights, the Expo shows where the country’s urban and rural sides meet. What can you see at Expo Paraguay? # The fairgrounds cover around 25 hectares, so expect longer walking distances if you want to visit several areas. The exhibitors, animals, and special events change from year to year, but the main sections remain similar.
🐂 Animals, genetics, and livestock farming (Ganadería) # Although the Expo is not only an agricultural fair, livestock farming and animal exhibitions are central parts of it. Depending on the edition, visitors may see cattle, horses, sheep, goats, and other animals. Cattle breeds suited to conditions in Paraguay often receive particular attention:
Brangus & Braford: These crossbreeds are widely represented in Paraguay. Nelore: These strong, usually white zebu cattle play an important role in the Chaco’s livestock industry. Visitors can watch animal judging and awards. Auctions, genetics, and contact between the different Cabañas are also important for breeders and industry professionals.
🚜 Industry, technology, and business # Alongside agriculture, companies present products and services from many industries. These range from utility vehicles, cars, tractors, and farm machinery to food, energy and solar technology, telecommunications, and financial services.
If you are new to the country, you will also see many providers and brands that are part of everyday shopping in Paraguay. Public agencies and institutions often have information stands as well.
🍴 Food and gastronomy # Food is also part of the Expo experience. Common options include Lomitos (steak sandwiches), Asaditos (meat skewers), Empanadas (filled pastries), Churros with Dulce de Leche, and larger grill stations known as Parrilladas.
Special food events change from year to year. In 2026, the program included Expo Asador and the Tereré Road, with products related to Tereré, mate accessories, and Yerba Mate.
If you would like to prepare typical dishes yourself, you can find more ideas in our collection of Paraguayan recipes.
🎶 Music, shows, and supporting program # Concerts, shows, and competitions often take place on the fairgrounds after the trade program. Depending on the edition, there may also be job opportunities, family days, food events, and other special activities.
In 2026, examples included the Expo Empleo job fair, motocross shows, the Miss Expo competition, and several national and international concerts. The detailed daily program is created again for each edition.
Small glossary: words you may hear at the Expo # At the Expo, you will hear and read specific Spanish terms. Some of them are especially useful.
Term Meaning Ganadería Livestock farming. Remate Auction, usually for animals. Juzgamiento Evaluation of animals by a jury. Cabaña Breeding farm. Ruedo Central Main arena for shows and awards. Campo ferial Fairgrounds. Feria multisectorial Multi-sector fair for business, agriculture, culture, and leisure. Practical tips for your visit # 🚗 Plan for traffic # Traffic around the Expo can be heavy, especially in the afternoon, on weekends, and before major evening events. Allow enough time when traveling via Ruta PY03.
Ride-hailing apps such as Bolt or Muv can save you from looking for parking. If you drive, use official or guarded parking areas whenever possible and check in advance which entrances are open.
🏨 Staying nearby # Mariano Roque Alonso has fewer accommodation options than Asunción. If you are traveling from farther away, it is a good idea to book early.
Practical alternatives in the Greater Asunción area include:
Luque / near Silvio Pettirossi Airport: You can reach the fair without driving through central Asunción. Northern Asunción (Aviadores del Chaco / Carmelitas area): This area has a wider choice of hotels, restaurants, and shopping centers. 🧥 Clothing for the Paraguayan winter # Winter in Paraguay is often underestimated. July days can be sunny and mild, while evenings may become much cooler after a cold front from the south. Since many parts of the Expo are outdoors, a jacket or sweater is useful. On sunny days, sunscreen and a hat are also important.
💵 Bring cash # Many permanent stands accept cards or QR-code payments. Cash in Guaraníes is still useful at smaller stalls, parking areas, and places selling snacks or drinks.
⏱️ Allow enough time # Plan at least half a day for a first overview. If you are visiting with children or want to combine the animal areas, exhibitors, and evening program, a full day may be better. Comfortable shoes are important because of the long walking distances.
📅 Check the daily program # Concerts, animal judging, auctions, and special events do not take place every day. Before you visit, check the date, opening hours, admission prices, and daily schedule on the official Expo website.
For international visitors The Expo is lively, loud, and very crowded at peak times. This mix offers a direct look at the economic, cultural, and social topics that come together in Paraguay.
Does Expo Paraguay have anything to do with the Chaco? # Yes and no. The venue is in Mariano Roque Alonso in the Departamento Central, not in the Chaco. However, the fair has strong links to the region because the Chaco plays a major role in Paraguay’s cattle breeding and agricultural industry.
This is especially clear in two areas:
Genetics & products: Cattle breeds suited to the hot climate and products from well-known Chaco cooperatives are represented at the fair. Technology: Many machines and four-wheel-drive vehicles are also designed for businesses with unpaved roads and difficult conditions in western Paraguay. If you would like to visit agricultural events in the Chaco itself, there are separate fairs:
Expo Pioneros del Chaco: It usually takes place near Loma Plata and has a strong focus on agricultural technology. Expo Rodeo Trébol: It is held near Filadelfia and is an important livestock and agricultural show for the region. More posts like this? 🇵🇾 Did you enjoy this post and want to learn more about Paraguay? Get Paraguay4Life updates by email and stay connected. Get new posts by email Free. You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → ❓ Frequently asked questions about Expo Paraguay # When does Expo Paraguay take place? Expo Paraguay usually takes place in July. The 2026 edition ran from July 11 to 26. The exact dates are announced separately for each year. What are the opening hours of Expo Paraguay? Opening hours and the start times of individual events can differ by day. Check the official daily program before your visit. How much does admission to Expo Paraguay cost? The admission price is set for each edition. In 2026, regular admission cost Gs. 25,000. Special rules applied to children, students, and certain groups, while some events could require separate tickets. Where does the Expo take place, and is it in the Chaco? The fair takes place at the Asociación Rural del Paraguay grounds in Mariano Roque Alonso in the Greater Asunción area. It is not in the Chaco. The name Ruta Transchaco for the access road sometimes causes this confusion. What is the best way to get to the Expo, and where can you park? The main access route is Ruta PY03. Because of traffic and the search for parking, allow extra time or use a ride-hailing service. If you drive, official or guarded parking areas are the best choice. Is Expo Paraguay safe to visit? Security and traffic officers are present during the Expo. As at other large events, you should still watch your valuables, bag, and phone and use marked entrances and parking areas whenever possible. How much time should you plan for Expo Paraguay? Half a day is enough for a first overview. If you are visiting with children or want to include the animal areas and evening program, plan closer to a full day. Can you eat and drink at Expo Paraguay? Yes. The grounds have food stands, food areas, grills, snacks, and drinks. Popular stands can get busier on weekends and during evening events. Does the Expo take place during Paraguay’s winter school break? The fair usually takes place in July and often overlaps with the receso de invierno. However, both the school break and Expo dates can change each year. Where should you stay if you are traveling from farther away? Practical options include Luque, the area near the airport, or northern Asunción. Mariano Roque Alonso is easy to reach from these areas, and they have more accommodation choices than the area directly around the fairgrounds. How is Expo Paraguay different from Expo Pioneros or Rodeo Trébol? Expo Paraguay in Mariano Roque Alonso is a national multi-sector fair for livestock farming, business, trade, culture, and entertainment. Expo Pioneros and Expo Rodeo Trébol take place in the Chaco and have a stronger agricultural focus. Conclusion: Expo Paraguay shows the country at work # When people think of Paraguay, they may first picture nature, Tereré, moving to the country, or a more relaxed way of life. All of this is part of everyday life. The Expo also shows another important side: the productive Paraguay of livestock breeders, farmers, traders, companies, cooperatives, and family businesses.
Modern farm machinery stands beside award-winning breeding animals, while families, school groups, businesspeople, craftspeople, and public institutions share the same grounds. This mix may seem a little confusing at first, but it reflects many facets of Paraguay.
Expo Paraguay is therefore neither only a trade fair nor simply a public festival. If you want to understand how agriculture, business, and everyday culture come together in Paraguay, Mariano Roque Alonso offers a particularly clear example.
The Expo is just one of many ways to experience Paraguay beyond the classic sights. You’ll find more ideas for day trips, nature, sports, and everyday activities in Things to Do in Paraguay.
Did this article help you? Then feel free to give it a like and share it with friends, acquaintances, or in your Paraguay group. This helps other people find practical information about everyday life, culture, and events.

summary: Expo Paraguay brings together livestock, business, food, and entertainment. Learn what to expect, how to plan a visit, and what happened in 2026.
