Go to the Telegram channel → ❓ Frequently asked questions about Paz del Chaco in Paraguay # When is Paz del Chaco in Paraguay in 2026? Paz del Chaco is on June 12. In 2026, the day falls on a Friday and creates a long weekend in daily life. Is Paz del Chaco an official public holiday in Paraguay? Yes, Paz del Chaco is a nationwide statutory public holiday. It is one of Paraguay’s movable public holidays (feriados movibles) and may be moved by decree to the Monday before or after the original date. In 2026, June 12 falls on a Friday and remains on its regular date. Is June 12 a public holiday in Paraguay? Yes. June 12 is the Peace of the Chaco (Paz del Chaco) and a nationwide legal public holiday in Paraguay. Are banks, public offices, and schools closed on Paz del Chaco? Yes. Since it is a national public holiday, schools, public offices, and banks are usually closed. Do important appointments or payments in advance. Are stores open on Paz del Chaco? It depends on the place and the chain. Large supermarkets, shopping centers, and gas stations are often open, while smaller shops, offices, and businesses usually close. What is Paz del Chaco in simple words? This day of remembrance honors the peace protocol of June 12, 1935. Two days later, on June 14, the fighting between Paraguay and Bolivia ended. What was the Chaco War in simple words? It was a war between Paraguay and Bolivia (1932–1935) over the Chaco Boreal region. For Paraguay, it is still a central part of national history. Is Paz del Chaco celebrated with big events in Paraguay? No, there are no large folk festivals. The day has a memorial character, shaped by official acts, school programs, flags, and honors for veterans (Excombatientes). Conclusion # Paz del Chaco is much more than a day off. It is deeply connected to national identity. Its meaning becomes clearer when you know the historical background and understand why it is not a festival, but a moment of remembrance.
In practical terms, this means: since public life slows down, it is best to handle banking and public office errands in advance. If you visit memorial sites, a calm and respectful attitude shows that you take the meaning of the day seriously.
If you want to understand life in Paraguay in the long term, you should see June 12 for what it is: an invitation to better understand the connection between history, family, and land.
If you would like to understand the Chaco War and its significance in the context of the country’s wider history, our overview of the history of Paraguay provides the bigger picture.

When the smell of freshly fried Pastel Mandi’o fills the street, it is hard not to get hungry for this savory classic from Paraguayan cuisine.
At first glance, they look like classic empanadas. But the dough made with cassava (Mandioca) makes the big difference. It is rustic, filling, and a great gluten-free alternative to wheat flour.
As a hearty snack for the cooler season or as part of traditional dishes for the San Juan festival: Pastel Mandi’o is authentic Paraguayan cuisine you can hold in your hand. In this recipe, I show you step by step what matters for the cassava dough, the filling, and the frying.
📝 Pastel Mandi’o Recipe - Step by Step # At a glance Difficulty: medium Preparation time: about 90 minutes Servings: about 12 to 14 pieces Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 🛒 Ingredients You Need # Here is what you need for the recipe:
Main ingredients # For the cassava dough:
1 kg peeled mandioca, cooked and well drained 1 egg 180 to 250 g fine corn flour (Harina de Maíz), plus a little more for rolling 1 tbsp oil, butter, or pork lard 1 tsp salt Oil for frying For the meat filling:
500 g ground beef 1 large onion, finely chopped 1 small green bell pepper or locote, finely diced 2 garlic cloves, finely chopped 2 hard-boiled eggs, chopped 2 tbsp oil Salt, pepper, and cumin to taste Optional ingredients # Green onions or parsley 1 bay leaf for the meat filling 1 pinch of paprika A splash of orange juice. Traditionally, Apepú or bitter orange is used, but regular orange also works. It makes the dough softer and more aromatic. Which ingredients can you replace? # Flexible alternatives for availability or diet This recipe is naturally gluten-free. Just check bouillon cubes or spice mixes for hidden gluten sources.
Mandioca: Fresh cassava is ideal. In Paraguay, this is easy to find. In Europe and North America, you can often find it fresh or already peeled in the freezer section of Asian, Afro, or Latino markets. It is often labeled as yuca or cassava.
Corn flour: Fine corn flour (Harina de Maíz) is standard. Very finely ground polenta also works. Add it little by little, because the moisture of the cassava can vary.
Fat: Pork lard tastes the most traditional. Oil is more neutral.
Meat filling: Instead of beef, you can also use chicken, pork, soy granules, lentils, or just vegetables.
Kitchen tools you need # Large pot, sieve Potato masher, meat grinder, or mortar Pan, bowl, rolling pin or a smooth bottle Deep pot or pan for frying, slotted spoon, paper towels 👩‍🍳 Step-by-step preparation # Preparation # Cassava
Fresh: Peel, wash, and cut into pieces. Frozen: Thaw completely and pat dry well. This helps avoid too much moisture. Cooking: Cook the pieces in salted water until soft. Remove the woody fiber from the center. Mash or crush the cassava while it is still warm. Filling
Peel and chop the hard-boiled eggs. Finely dice the onion, bell pepper or locote, and garlic. Cooking process # Filling: Heat oil in a pan. Sauté onion, locote, and garlic until soft and translucent.
Meat: Add the ground beef and fry it well. Season with salt, pepper, and cumin. At the end, fold in the eggs and, if you like, green onions or parsley.
Let the filling cool completely. If it is still warm, the cassava dough can tear more easily while shaping or frying.
Dough: To make the cassava dough, work the still warm cassava very finely with a meat grinder, mortar, or potato masher. These traditional methods give the best texture.
Kneading: Mix the cassava with egg, salt, and fat. Add the corn flour little by little until you get a smooth, flexible dough that no longer sticks too much.
Shaping: Divide the dough into small portions. Roll it out on a surface dusted with corn flour, but not too thin, or press it flat with your hands.
Filling: Put some filling in the center, fold the dough over, and press the edges closed. You can use your fingers or a fork.
Frying: Heat oil in a deep pot and fry the empanadas in batches until golden brown.
Test the oil temperature: Put a small piece of dough into the oil. If it bubbles right away, the temperature is good. If the oil is too cold, the cassava dough absorbs too much oil instead of becoming crispy. Do not fry too many empanadas at once, so the temperature stays stable.
Serving: Drain briefly on paper towels and serve warm if possible.
💡 Practical tips for Pastel Mandi’o # Tips for good cassava dough Work the cassava right away: Process the cassava right after cooking and draining. If the mixture cools down, it becomes tough and is harder to shape.
Avoid the “rubber effect”: Do not use a food processor. The rotating blades can make the mixture sticky like glue. A potato masher or meat grinder is the better choice.
Avoid a temperature shock: Do not fry Pastel Mandi’o straight from the fridge. The sudden temperature change can make the dough tear in the hot oil.
The right thickness: Do not roll the dough too thin. It is delicate, and a little more dough gives it the stability it needs when closing.
First aid for cracks: No panic. Close small cracks with damp fingers and dust them with a little corn flour.
Storage: Leftovers keep covered in the fridge for up to 2 days. A pan is ideal for reheating them so they become crispy again.
Nutrition facts for Pastel Mandi’o # The values refer to one piece, based on a total amount of about 12 to 14 Pastel Mandi’o.
Calories: about 290 to 360 kcal Protein: about 10 to 13 g Carbohydrates: about 30 to 40 g Fat: about 12 to 18 g Fiber: about 2 to 4 g Note: These are average values. The actual values can vary depending on the filling, the size of each piece, and how much oil is absorbed during frying.
🍽️ What goes well with Pastel Mandi’o? # Cassava empanadas work well as a snack between meals or as a small hearty main dish. But what can you serve with them?
Sides Drinks Classic: Serve them plain with a little hot sauce or a simple garlic dip (Salsa de Ajo). They are also often served with Paraguayan pan (white bread), galleta (firm bread roll, sometimes with anise), or coquito (dry, crispy mini bread rolls).
Traditional mix: With Mbejú, Pajagua Mascada, Tortillas paraguayas, Chipa Guasu or Sopa Paraguaya, it fits well with typical platos tradicionales.
Fresh contrasts: A tomato salad, cabbage salad, or a tangy herb sauce such as chimichurri makes the dish feel lighter.
Paraguayan: On warm days, Tereré is the absolute classic.
For cool evenings: A hot Cocido or Mate Cocido goes perfectly with these hearty empanadas.
Refreshing: Cold water with lime or a light fruit juice is a good contrast to this fried snack.
🔄 Variations: How to fill Pastel Mandi’o # Pastel Mandi’o is very easy to change. The important thing is this: the filling should be well seasoned and not too wet, so the cassava dough stays stable when shaping and frying.
Classic with meat (Guiso): Traditionally, cooked beef is often used. It is crushed in a mortar or meat grinder and mixed with onion, locote, and egg. Chicken or pork also work well.
Pastel Mandi’o de Queso: For a meatless version, fill the empanadas with Queso Paraguay, cream cheese, or a mix of mild and stronger cheese. This gives the filling more flavor and helps it melt better.
Pastel Mandi’o de Jamón y Queso: This modern snack version with ham and cheese is easy to make and very popular when things need to be quick.
Chilena-inspired filling: If you like the taste of Paraguayan empanadas, you can add olives (aceitunas) and, if you like, raisins (pasas de uva) to the meat filling. This gives it a sweet and savory note.
Vegetarian or vegan: Lentils, soy granules, or a savory vegetable and mushroom mix work well. For a vegan version, leave out the egg and cheese and make the cassava dough smoother with a little oil if needed.
Pastel Mandi’o al horno or from the air fryer: In the oven or air fryer, Pastel Mandi’o is less traditional and usually a little drier, but it has fewer calories. Brush the empanadas lightly with oil so they get some color and crispness, and do not make them too large.
Mini Pastel Mandi’o: Small empanadas are great as finger food for guests, buffets, or a Paraguayan recipe table.

You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → 🇵🇾 Background information about the recipe # What makes Pastel Mandi’o special? # Pastel Mandi’o is often described as a Paraguayan cassava empanada. In Spanish, you may also see the names Empanada de Mandioca or Pastel de Mandioca. It is a highlight of local cuisine. The name already tells you a lot: “Mandi’o” is the Guaraní word for cassava, which is an essential everyday basic ingredient in Paraguayan food.
Corn flour gives the dough the structure and binding it needs. Compared to wheat flour empanadas, the dough is more rustic, denser, and wonderfully crispy when fried. The filling gets its character from typical spices and ingredients such as cumin (Comino), green onions (Cebollita de verdeo), onion (Cebolla), green bell pepper (Locote), and garlic (Ajo). They season the filling well without covering the taste of the cassava.
Urucu for the golden-orange color The color comes from Urucu, also called Annatto. Traditionally, the seeds are heated in hot fat, which then colors the dough. If you do not have Urucu, paprika powder or turmeric can give a similar visual effect.
This dish shows very well what Paraguayan cuisine is about: a few simple ingredients become hearty food that makes you full.
What role does Pastel Mandi’o play in Paraguay? # These fried empanadas are much more than a simple snack. In Paraguay, they are part of everyday food culture and also a piece of Paraguayan identity.
Festivals and celebrations: Especially in June, around the San Juan celebrations and San Juan Ára on June 24, Pastel Mandi’o is very present as Paraguayan street food. Together with Mbejú, Pajagua Mascada, Chipa Guasu, or Sopa Paraguaya, this fried cassava pocket is part of the typical San Juan dishes from Paraguay.
Resolution No. 370/2026 also specifically names Pastel Mandi’o as one of the culinary expressions of the Fiesta de San Juan – San Juan Ára, which has been recognized as national intangible cultural heritage since 2026.
Winter snack: Pastel Mandi’o is not only eaten at festivals. Because of the strong dough, the savory filling, and the frying, it is a hearty snack that fits well into the cooler season. As real comfort food, it is a perfect addition to the collection of winter dishes from Paraguay.
Pastel Mandi’o from Coronel Oviedo: In Coronel Oviedo, in the department of Caaguazú, this dish has special regional meaning. The local Pastel Mandi’o is even recognized as intangible cultural heritage of Paraguay. What is honored here is mainly the traditional technique: the meat is crushed in a mortar. The empanadas are cooked with the maimbe method, meaning in a pan lightly greased with pork fat. They are turned “vuelta y vuelta”, meaning briefly turned and browned on both sides.
❓ Frequently asked questions # Can I prepare Pastel Mandi’o ahead of time? Yes. You can prepare the filling and the cooked mandioca one day before and keep them in the fridge. But it is best to shape and fry the empanadas fresh, because the cassava dough loses moisture while stored and can crack. Why does my cassava dough tear? Most of the time, the dough is too dry, rolled too thin, or the filling is too wet. Let the filling cool completely. If the dough cracks, knead in a little fat or a few drops of water. Can I freeze Pastel Mandi’o? Yes, ideally raw and already shaped. Place the empanadas one by one on a board to freeze them briefly first, then put them in a bag. You can fry them straight from the freezer in hot oil. Be careful: the oil may splatter. Can I make Pastel Mandi’o vegan or vegetarian? Yes, this works well.
Vegetarian: Replace the meat with cheese, lentils, or a vegetable and mushroom mix. You can keep the egg in the dough.
Vegan: Leave out the egg in the dough. Cooked cassava usually binds well enough. For the filling, use savory soy granules or lentils instead of meat and cheese.
Are Pastel Mandi’o gluten-free? Yes, Pastel Mandi’o is usually gluten-free if you make the dough with cassava, corn flour, and egg. Just check spice mixes for hidden gluten and do not replace corn flour with wheat flour. Conclusion # Pastel Mandi’o shows how good Paraguayan home cooking can be with very simple ingredients. Whether for the San Juan festival or as a hearty snack between meals, these empanadas are real comfort food. Try different fillings and enjoy the result. Your guests may never see cassava as just a simple “side dish” again.
Do not be afraid of the dough. If it cracks a little at first or the shape is not perfect, that is completely fine. It is part of learning by doing. In the end, the taste is what matters.
Have fun cooking and buen provecho!
Like savory cassava bites? Mbejú has no filling, cooks quickly in a skillet, and tastes especially good fresh and warm. You’ll find more easy bites among our Paraguayan snacks and small bites.
Share and support Did this traditional Pastel Mandi’o recipe inspire you and make you curious about Paraguay?
Then feel free to like and share this post with other South America fans. This helps make Paraguay’s culinary variety more visible.
summary: Savory and crispy: Pastel Mandi’o is Paraguayan comfort food with cassava dough and many filling ideas.

When Paraguay plays, the rhythm of the country changes. After a late match, the next morning often starts more slowly: People continue discussing the game on the radio, and the result is the main topic at the supermarket. Soccer in Paraguay is everywhere.
But soccer is much more than a sport watched on television. It is part of daily life and a popular activity that brings people together and starts conversations. This sense of unity is especially clear when La Albirroja plays.
Whether over Tereré or on the Cancha, understanding the meaning of soccer helps you connect more easily. This article explains La Albirroja, major clubs and local structures. You will also learn how soccer shapes life in Paraguay and helps you meet people.
At a Glance Soccer is part of daily life and leisure in Paraguay and quickly brings people into conversation. The Paraguayan national soccer team is known as La Albirroja. Along with the major clubs, local teams and the UFI play an important role in the Interior. At the 2026 World Cup, Paraguay reached the Round of 16 after defeating Germany and was then eliminated by France. Why Is Soccer So Popular in Paraguay? # Soccer is a topic almost everyone can talk about. Even people who rarely watch matches usually know when La Albirroja is playing or which club everyone is discussing. The sport brings families, neighbors and entire communities together.
With the Paraguayan national team, it is about more than results. It is about pride and the feeling that: “We may be a small country, but we do not back down.” One expression that captures this perfectly is garra guaraní.
The expression describes fighting spirit and the will not to give up, even against stronger opponents. It stands for strength, heart and determination and is closely linked to both La Albirroja and Paraguayan identity.
The history of Paraguay also helps explain why garra guaraní has such a strong meaning in the country.
What Does “La Albirroja” Mean, and Why Is Paraguay’s National Team Called That? # La Albirroja is the nickname of the Paraguayan national team, the Selección Paraguaya de Fútbol. The name means “the red-and-white team” and refers to its traditional jersey colors.
During matches, however, all three national colors are often visible: red, white and blue. Flags, jerseys and car stickers appear everywhere, and the country seems to glow in these colors.
You may also hear the name Los Guaraníes, which puts more focus on cultural identity. This fits daily life in Paraguay, where Spanish and Guaraní often exist side by side and are naturally mixed as Jopara.
Info In Guaraní, soccer or a ball can be called vakapipopo. In daily conversation, however, most people simply say fútbol.
🪅 La Albirroja at the 2026 World Cup: A Return to the Round of 16 # After 16 years without a World Cup appearance, Paraguay returned to the world stage in 2026. Under coach Gustavo Alfaro, La Albirroja qualified in September 2025. The celebration was so great that the government declared September 5 a national holiday.
The first group match on June 12 also fell on a special date. While Paraguay played the United States, the country also observed Día de la Paz del Chaco, the day that marks the end of the Chaco War.
Paraguay’s Group Stage at the 2026 World Cup Group D: United States, Paraguay, Turkey and Australia
June 12, 2026: United States vs. Paraguay – 4–1 June 19/20, 2026: Turkey vs. Paraguay – 0–1 June 25/26, 2026: Australia vs. Paraguay – 0–0 Record: 1 win, 1 draw and 1 loss – 4 points and 3rd place.
Paraguay advanced as one of the best third-place teams and faced Germany. After a 1–1 draw following extra time, La Albirroja won 4–3 on penalties. Reaching the Round of 16 was so important that the government briefly declared June 30 a national holiday.
For the first time since 2010, Paraguay was among the final 16 teams. The journey ended on July 4 with a 1–0 loss to France.
Looking Ahead to the 2030 World Cup Paraguay will be one of six host countries in 2030 and will stage one of the three centenary matches in South America. The other two will take place in Argentina and Uruguay, while most of the tournament will be held in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. All six host countries qualify automatically.
⚽ How Is Soccer Organized in Paraguay? # Organized soccer is overseen by the Asociación Paraguaya de Fútbol (APF). It manages competitions including the Primera División (the top division), the División Intermedia (the second division), the Copa Paraguay (the national cup), the Super Cup and women’s soccer.
The best-known clubs include Olimpia, Cerro Porteño, Libertad, Guaraní and Sportivo Luqueño. Many major clubs are based in Asunción and the surrounding area.
The season usually consists of two separate championships: the Torneo Apertura during the first half of the year and the Torneo Clausura during the second half.
The Clásico paraguayo between Olimpia and Cerro Porteño is especially famous. When La Albirroja plays, however, club rivalries usually pause and the national team takes center stage.
Soccer in the Interior: The Importance of the UFI # In the Interior, the Unión del Fútbol del Interior (UFI) plays an important role. It is connected to the APF and oversees regional leagues and local clubs outside the greater Asunción area.
Soccer in the Interior is often a social and community event. People support their local club or their own team (Equipo), help maintain the field or organize small Asaditos to raise money for travel or jerseys.
At clubs and league events, you may also see Madrinas or Reinas: women who represent the club at festivals and special competitions. In many places, this is also part of club culture.
Women’s Soccer in Paraguay # Women’s soccer is also growing through competitions such as the Campeonato Anual Femenino and the Copa Paraguay FEM. There are also more opportunities for girls and youth teams.
Even so, women’s soccer is still less visible than men’s soccer in daily life and the media.
At a glance: How soccer is organized in Paraguay 🧩 How Does Soccer Appear in Daily Life? # Soccer is not limited to stadiums. It is both a hobby and a meeting point, making it an important part of free time in Paraguay.
Playing Soccer in Paraguay # Children play in the street, teenagers meet after school, and adults gather for their weekly game on the Cancha. Fútbol 5 and other small-sided formats are especially popular.
Competition is not the only thing that matters. The match is often followed by the Tercer Tiempo, the “third half.” People share Tereré, have a beer or eat together afterward.
Along with these relaxed and mostly private games, there are organized competitions in local leagues and through the UFI, ranging from friendly and school tournaments to larger championships.
Watching a Match Spontaneously # People who do not play often watch instead. Large public broadcasts are most common in Asunción and during special matches. Most people, however, watch in smaller groups: at a bar, in someone’s yard or even in front of a television at the supermarket.
Tip When Paraguay plays late, do not schedule the next morning too tightly. After important matches, many people start the day more slowly.
Community: Neighbors or friends often gather spontaneously for evening matches. One person provides the television, while someone else brings Tortillas paraguayas, empanadas or peanuts. Larger gatherings may also include an Asado, for example with Chipa Guasu. Tereré or beer is usually close at hand.
Atmosphere: People cheer, discuss the match and eat together. You may hear the neighbors celebrating before you see the goal on your own television. The next morning, even a conversation at the checkout may begin with the question: “¿Viste el partido?”
Radio and Jerseys # Despite smartphone streams, traditional radio is still common during farm work or in workshops. Jerseys from Olimpia or Cerro Porteño are also part of the street scene. On match days, they show clear support and provide an easy conversation starter.
💡 Expats and Visitors: Why Soccer Opens Doors # You do not have to be a major soccer fan (Hincha) or play yourself to use the sport as a way into social life in Paraguay.
An icebreaker: You do not need perfect Spanish. A simple question such as “¿Cómo salió el partido?” is often enough to start a conversation. → Here are more useful phrases for match day.
Understanding the local mindset: Soccer shows part of Paraguay’s resiliencia (resilience). After a loss, people first discuss and complain about the match, but soon they begin looking ahead to the next one. Seeing this can teach you a lot about pride, disappointment and unity.
Leaving the expat bubble: Watching or playing soccer puts you in the middle of local life and can help you go from being “the foreigner” to being “the neighbor.”
Tip To play soccer yourself in Paraguay, ask your neighbors or the local Municipalidad about the town team.
Practicing Spanish: The short and often repeated phrases are ideal for using Spanish in daily life and learning the local way of speaking. 🗣️ Useful Soccer Phrases for Daily Life # Here are a few simple phrases for the next match day:
Questions to Start a Conversation # “¿Cómo salió el partido?” – How did the match end? “¿A qué hora juega Paraguay?” – What time does Paraguay play? “¿Hay partido este fin de semana?” – Is there a match this weekend? Phrases for the Atmosphere # “¡Dale, dale!” – Come on! / Let’s go! “¡Qué partido!” – What a match! “¡Vamos, Albirroja!” – Let’s go, Albirroja! 📺 TV Guide: Where Can You Watch Soccer in Paraguay? # Whether it is a league match, the Clásico paraguayo or an appearance by La Albirroja, people who cannot attend the stadium can almost always follow the game on television, through an app, on the radio or with others at a bar. The broadcaster depends on the competition and current media rights.
Paraguayan Club Soccer # For the Primera División and many other APF competitions, Tigo Sports is one of the main broadcasters. Depending on the agreement, matches are available on cable television or through an app.
You can usually find the current broadcaster in the APF schedule, through Tigo Sports or from the club involved.
La Albirroja Matches # Broadcasters may change for international matches. The APF usually names the channel in its match announcement. Some recent matches were shown through Tigo Sports and APF TV.
Radio and Watching Together # Radio remains a useful alternative when traveling, in rural areas or where the internet connection is weak. Without the right subscription, you can often still find the match at a bar, with friends or at a neighbor’s home.
Outside Paraguay # Outside Paraguay, broadcast rights vary by country and competition. Before the match, check the official channels of the APF, the competition and local broadcasters.
Warning Broadcast rights and platforms may change. Research last updated: July 21, 2026.

Go to the Telegram channel → ❓ Frequently Asked Questions About Soccer in Paraguay # Why Is Paraguay’s National Team Called La Albirroja? La Albirroja is the well-known nickname of the Paraguayan national soccer team, the Selección Paraguaya de Fútbol. The name means “the red-and-white team” and refers to its traditional red-and-white jerseys. The 2026 World Cup jersey also included blue details inspired by the Paraguayan flag. How Far Did Paraguay Go at the 2026 World Cup? Paraguay reached the Round of 16 at the 2026 World Cup. After finishing third in Group D, La Albirroja defeated Germany 4–3 on penalties in the Round of 32. Paraguay was eliminated in the Round of 16 after a close 1–0 loss to France. Which Soccer Clubs in Paraguay Are the Best Known? The best-known Paraguayan soccer clubs include Olimpia, Cerro Porteño, Libertad, Guaraní and Sportivo Luqueño. The Clásico paraguayo between Olimpia and Cerro Porteño receives attention across the country. What Is the UFI in Paraguayan Soccer? The UFI is the Unión del Fútbol del Interior. It is connected to the APF and organizes regional leagues and clubs outside the greater Asunción area. Can You Play Soccer in Paraguay? Yes. Many towns have local teams, sports fields or recreational groups. To join, ask people in the area, contact a local club or check with the Municipalidad. Where Can You Watch La Albirroja and Paraguayan League Matches? Many Paraguayan club matches are shown through Tigo Sports. Broadcasters for La Albirroja may change depending on the competition. Before a match, check announcements from the APF, Tigo Sports and the clubs involved. Where Can You Buy Tickets for Soccer Matches in Paraguay? For major league matches and national team games at the Estadio Defensores del Chaco in Asunción, buy tickets in advance through the official channels of the APF or the clubs involved. For smaller clubs and matches in the Interior, tickets are often available directly at the venue. Conclusion # Soccer in Paraguay is sport, leisure and community. You find it on local fields and in major stadiums, on the radio and in daily life, especially when La Albirroja plays.
Understanding what soccer means to people also helps you understand Paraguay. The sport starts conversations, creates connections and reveals much about the Paraguayan way of life.
The 2026 World Cup showed this once again: The victory over Germany and the Round of 16 appearance are now part of the country’s recent soccer history. But the sport’s power to bring people together can be seen every week, far from the world stage.
Soccer is, of course, only one part of how people spend their free time in Paraguay. If you’d like to explore more, Things to Do in Paraguay has ideas ranging from balnearios and nature outings to dancing and events.

The smell of cheese melting in the pan, mixed with the aroma of roasted cassava starch, is the taste of Paraguay for me. Mbejú is one of those Paraguayan dishes that shows very clearly why simple ingredients are so important in the local kitchen. A little cassava starch, cheese, fat and milk are enough to make something that feels warm, easy and comforting. This specialty tastes best straight from the pan, when the cheese is still soft and the edges are crispy.
Mbejú, also written as Mbeju, Mbeyú or Mbejú de almidón in everyday life, looks simple at first. But it is surprisingly flexible. It fits almost any time of day: in the morning with coffee or a traditional Cocido, in the evening as a quick main meal, as a side dish with hearty stews or in small pieces as finger food for guests.
The traditional Mbejú recipe is simple, but it needs a little feeling. The secret? The dough is not kneaded. It is mixed into crumbs and then gently pressed together in the hot pan. This gives Mbejú its typical light texture. If you want to make Mbejú yourself, I will show you step by step how this classic cheese cassava flatbread works, what to watch out for with the texture and which versions are most popular in our home.
📝 Easy Mbejú Recipe from Paraguay - Step by Step # At a glance Difficulty: easy to medium Preparation time: about 30 minutes Servings: 4 large Mbejú or 6 smaller flatbreads Typical for: Paraguayan breakfast, quick dinner, side dish Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 🛒 Ingredients you need # You probably already have most of the ingredients at home. The following overview shows what you really need for the basic recipe and what you can add if you like.
Main ingredients # For about 4 large Mbejú, you need:
500 g cassava starch In Paraguay, it is usually sold as almidón de mandioca, sometimes also as fécula de mandioca.
250 g Queso Paraguay or another mild, slightly salty cheese 100 g butter, pork fat or margarine 150 to 200 ml milk or water, as needed 1 level teaspoon salt Important shopping tip Make sure you use real cassava starch and not coarse cassava flour. The difference between cassava flour and cassava starch is important: the fine starch creates the typical binding and texture, while coarse cassava flour would make the Mbejú dry and crumbly.
Optional ingredients # a little grated hard cheese for more flavor pepper or dried herbs for aroma Which ingredients can you replace? # Flexible alternatives for availability or diet Naturally gluten-free: As a gluten-free recipe from Paraguay, Mbejú is made without wheat flour in the basic version. Just make sure that the cassava starch you use was processed gluten-free.
Replacing cassava starch:
If you cannot find almidón or fécula de mandioca, tapioca starch, pure starch from the cassava root, is usually the best substitute. Replacing Queso Paraguay:
Mild feta, white cheese or young farmer’s cheese work well. Mozzarella makes the inside of the Mbejú softer and more elastic. A mix of mozzarella and a little feta comes closest to the original Paraguayan taste. Replacing the fat:
Butter gives a round, fine flavor. Pork lard tastes more traditional and adds a hearty note. Margarine works as a plant-based option, but tastes more neutral. Replacing milk:
Water is enough if you want to make the recipe simpler or lactose-free. Milk makes the flatbread a little richer and softer. Kitchen tools you need # large bowl non-stick pan or well-seasoned iron pan spatula kitchen scale or measuring cup 👩‍🍳 Step-by-step preparation # Preparation # Let the butter soften in time or melt it gently over low heat. Crumble the cheese roughly with your hands or grate it. Measure the milk or water and keep it ready. Cooking process # Put the cassava starch and salt into a bowl and mix them briefly. Add the soft butter or lard in small pieces. Rub the fat into the starch with your fingertips until you get a fine, slightly sandy texture. Add the crumbled cheese and mix it in evenly. Now add the liquid little by little. Important: The mixture must not become smooth or elastic. It should stay moist and crumbly. If you press a handful together firmly, it should hold its shape, but fall apart again with light pressure. Heat the pan over medium heat. It should be hot, but not smoking. You usually do not need extra fat for the pan because the mixture already contains enough fat. Add a generous portion of the crumbly mixture to the pan and spread it evenly into a round shape. Press it down gently with the back of a spoon or a spatula. Cook the Mbejú for about 3 to 5 minutes on each side, until the edge becomes lightly golden and the flatbread holds together. Turn the flatbread carefully. If you are unsure, place a flat plate on the pan, turn it over with one quick movement and slide the Mbejú back into the pan. Serve the dish hot, straight from the pan, while the cheese is still soft. 💡 Practical tips for Mbejú # How to make the flatbread work well Use the liquid carefully: Too much liquid makes the mixture heavy and sticky. Too little liquid makes the Mbejú crumble in the pan. The goal is a moist crumb mixture, not a smooth dough ball.
Keep the heat medium: If the heat is too high, the outside burns while the starch inside stays dry or crumbly.
Press gently: Press the mixture lightly in the pan at the beginning, but not so hard that the flatbread becomes compact and hard like a stone.
Small size for guests: It is easier to cook smaller Mbejú rounds. They are much easier to turn and work very well as small bites.
Nutrition overview # The values refer to 1 smaller Mbejú when the basic recipe makes 6 portions.
Calories: about 530 to 590 kcal Protein: about 9 to 12 g Carbohydrates: about 70 to 80 g Fat: about 18 to 24 g Fiber: about 1 to 2 g The nutrition values are average values and can vary depending on the ingredients, amount of cheese, fat and portion size.
🍽️ What goes well with Mbejú? # To make your meal feel complete, here are a few ideas for side dishes and drinks that go well with it.
Side dishes Drinks Classic: Mbejú plain, with a fried egg or scrambled eggs. Hearty: with ham, cheese or fried vegetables. Paraguayan: with soups, stews or rustic dishes. Fresh: with tomato salad, coleslaw or avocado cream. Authentic: Hot traditional Cocido or strong coffee go perfectly with it. Refreshing: On warm days, ice-cold Tereré is an ideal drink with it. Mild: A light herbal tea or a glass of milk, especially if children are eating too. 🔄 Recipe variations # Mbejú is easy to change. Some versions are well known in Paraguay, others are good for guests or modern cooking.
Well-known variations # Mbejú relleno with ham and cheese: First add a thin layer of Mbejú mixture to the pan, then cheese and ham, then another thin layer of mixture. Cook it as usual and turn it carefully. This version is richer, very filling and works especially well as a warm dinner.
Comfort food: When a cold south wind blows on a cool winter morning and the fire is burning inside, this version is popular here in Paraguay as a typical winter dish. Add a hot Cocido, and the morning already feels a little warmer.
Mbejú mestizo: In this version, a little cornmeal is added to the mixture. This makes the flavor more rustic and the texture a bit heartier. Start with only 1 to 2 tablespoons of cornmeal so the Mbejú does not become too dry.
Mbejú cuatro quesos: A version with several types of cheese. It tastes more intense and becomes softer inside. A mix of mild cheese such as Gouda, mozzarella, a little stronger hard cheese such as Parmesan and a small amount of blue cheese, for example Gorgonzola, works well.
Mbejú with anise: A little anise gives the flatbread a special aroma that is also known from other traditional Paraguayan recipes. Not everyone likes it, but if you enjoy anise, it adds a warm and pleasant note.
Modern variations # Mbejú bites Caprese style: Bake small Mbejú rounds and top them while still warm with half a cherry tomato, a little balsamic reduction and fresh basil. Alternatively, you can place tomato and basil between two thin layers of Mbejú mixture and make a filled vegetarian Mbejú. This is not classically Paraguayan, but it looks beautiful and works well as an elegant starter for special days like a Valentine’s Day menu.
Mbejú with avocado cream: A small spoonful of avocado cream with lime and salt makes Mbejú fresher. Small, not too thick Mbejú rounds work well as a summer dish on warm days and also as finger food for a buffet or for guests.
Mbejú with honey or fruit: A sweet modern variation: served warm with a little honey, banana or fresh fruit, Mbejú becomes an unusual breakfast or a small dessert.

You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → 🇵🇾 Background information about the recipe # What makes Mbejú special? # Mbejú is neither a classic pancake nor bread. The secret is its structure: the crumbly mixture only comes together through the heat and the melting cheese in the pan. A fine crust forms on the outside, while the center stays soft.
The starch from the cassava root is the key. It binds differently from wheat flour and gives the flatbread its typical structure.
From my everyday experience here: moisture is the key to success. If the mixture keeps its shape for a short moment when you press it together in your hand, the ratio is usually just right.
What role does Mbejú play in Paraguay? # In Paraguay, Mbejú is a fixed part of the kitchen and culture. You can find it in a cozy café in the city as well as in a simple kitchen in the countryside. Because it is made without an oven, the dish is quick, affordable and flexible.
This fits an everyday kitchen where cassava and products made from it, such as flour or starch, are among the most important basic foods in daily life. Mbejú is served on special occasions or as a traditional comida típica at the San Juan festival, but it tastes just as good on a normal weekday.
Mbejú is also specifically named in Resolution No. 370/2026 as one of the culinary expressions of the Fiesta de San Juan – San Juan Ára, which has been recognized as national intangible cultural heritage since 2026.
Which ingredients shape Mbejú? # Cassava starch and Queso Paraguay in Paraguayan cooking # Cassava, called mandioca in Paraguay and also yuca in other Spanish-speaking countries in Latin America, is one of the most important basic ingredients in daily life. If you live in Paraguay or visit the country, you will hardly find a meal where it does not appear in some form. In most cases, the root is served boiled as a side dish. But there are also many cassava recipes where the root itself or the starch made from it is used, for example Mandi’o Chyryry, Pastel Mandi’o or Chipa.
Queso Paraguay is a traditional cheese made from cow’s milk. It is mild, slightly salty and not as firm as many European hard cheeses. It gives the dish flavor, moisture and binding.
❓ Frequently asked questions # Why does my Mbejú fall apart in the pan? This happens when the mixture is too dry or was not pressed together enough in the pan. Add a very small amount of liquid, tablespoon by tablespoon, and check the texture. When adding the mixture to the pan, press it gently but firmly into one even surface with a spoon. Which pan is best for Mbejú? A good non-stick pan is easiest for beginners because nothing sticks. Experienced cooks often like a well-seasoned, heavy cast-iron pan because it stores heat more evenly and creates a very nice crust. Can I prepare the dough in advance? The dry mixture of cassava starch, salt and fat can be prepared well in advance. But you should add the freshly grated cheese and the liquid shortly before cooking, so the mixture does not become unevenly moist or lumpy. Can I make Mbejú with tapioca starch instead of cassava starch? Yes, tapioca starch usually works well as a substitute for cassava starch. It is important to use fine starch and not coarse cassava flour. The texture should stay moist and crumbly so the Mbejú holds together in the pan. How do I store leftovers and make them fresh again? You can store cooked flatbreads covered in the fridge for 1 to 2 days. They become firm and dry when they cool down, so it is best to warm them again in a pan over low heat with a tiny splash of water and a lid on top. This makes them soft again. What is the difference between Mbejú and Chipa? Although both recipes are based on cassava starch and cheese, the preparation is very different. Chipa is made into a smooth, kneadable dough, shaped and baked in the oven, traditionally in a Tatakua. Mbejú stays crumbly and is cooked directly in the pan. Conclusion # Mbejú shows beautifully how much flavor can come from only a handful of simple basic ingredients. The dish is easy, wonderfully flexible and brings a real piece of South American joy to the table.
Have fun cooking and buen provecho!
Mbejú already shows how versatile cassava can be. If you’d like to try it in a completely different and much heartier form, Pajagua Mascada with beef is a great option. You’ll find more Paraguayan recipes with cassava in our cassava recipe collection.
Share & support Did this traditional Mbejú recipe inspire you and make you more curious about Paraguay? Then feel free to give this post a like and share it with other South America fans, helping to make Paraguay’s culinary diversity more visible.
summary: Golden from the pan: Mbejú is a simple but wonderful dish. Here is the recipe for Paraguay’s cheese flatbread.

If you live in Paraguay, you encounter the country’s history surprisingly often — even without setting foot in a museum. Guaraní and Spanish are part of everyday life, streets are named after historical figures, and holidays such as Heroes’ Day or Chaco Peace Day go back to defining moments in the country’s past.
Many issues that still matter in Paraguay today - national identity, political structures, or the importance of the Chaco - also become easier to understand once you know how the country developed.
This article takes you through the main stages of Paraguay’s history: from Indigenous cultures and the Spanish colonial period to independence, wars, dictatorship, and today’s democracy.
Paraguay History in Brief # Paraguay’s history has been shaped by very different influences and major turning points. Indigenous cultures and Spanish colonization, political independence in 1811, two major wars in the 19th and 20th centuries, and the long Stroessner dictatorship all left lasting marks on the country.
The timeline below gives you a quick overview of the main periods.
Indigenous cultures before 1500 Guaraní-speaking communities and other Indigenous peoples live in the area of present-day Paraguay long before Europeans arrive. Spanish colonial period from 1537 A Spanish fortified outpost is established at the site of present-day Asunción in 1537. From there, Spanish influence expands further into the interior. Jesuit reductions 17th and 18th centuries Jesuit missions shape parts of Paraguay and neighboring regions. Visible traces remain in southern Paraguay today. Independence 1811 Paraguay breaks from Spanish rule and develops as an independent state. War of the Triple Alliance 1864 to 1870 The war against Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay becomes the greatest catastrophe in Paraguayan history. Chaco War 1932 to 1935 Paraguay fights Bolivia over the disputed Chaco region and gains military control over much of the contested territory. Stroessner dictatorship 1954 to 1989 Alfredo Stroessner rules Paraguay as an authoritarian leader for almost 35 years. Democratic transition since 1989 After Stroessner’s fall, Paraguay begins the transition toward its present democratic system. Before the Europeans arrived: the Guaraní and the land between the rivers # Long before the Spanish arrived in South America, different Indigenous peoples lived in the area of present-day Paraguay. Various Guaraní-speaking communities were especially influential.
Their ways of life were not all the same, but many were closely connected to rivers, forests, farming, hunting, and fishing. Crops included corn, cassava (manioc), and sweet potatoes.
The Guaraní are not simply a chapter from the distant past. Their language and cultural influence remain clearly visible in Paraguay today.
Language is perhaps the most obvious example. Guaraní is an official language alongside Spanish, and both are widely used. In everyday conversation, you will also often hear Jopara, which combines elements of Guaraní and Spanish.
This linguistic reality sets Paraguay apart from many other Latin American countries and shows how strongly Indigenous influences have remained part of the country’s culture.
The Spanish colonial period: Asunción and the development of a distinct culture # A new chapter began with the arrival of the Spanish in the 16th century.
On August 15, 1537, Juan de Salazar y Espinosa established a fortified casa fuerte on the Paraguay River. Asunción developed from this outpost and formally received city status in 1541.
These events are commemorated every year on August 15 with the Founding of Asunción.
Asunción became an important base for Spanish expansion into the interior of South America. Relationships and families formed between Spanish settlers and Guaraní women, and over time a society developed in which European and Indigenous influences were closely intertwined.
This process, however, took place within unequal colonial power structures. Missionary activity, dependency, coercion, and social inequality were just as much a part of the colonial period as cultural exchange and intermixing.
Paraguay therefore did not simply become a Spanish copy in South America. Its distance from major coastal centers and trade routes also helped distinct social and cultural structures develop in the interior.
The Jesuit reductions: missions, Guaraní, and historical traces # The Jesuit reductions are among the most visible legacies of Paraguay’s colonial period.
These were mission settlements in which Jesuits converted Indigenous communities to Christianity and organized life in permanent settlements. The reductions were religious centers, but they were also places of farming, craftsmanship, music, and economic production.
For the Guaraní communities living there, the system meant major changes to religion, society, and everyday life. At the same time, the missions could offer some protection from other forms of colonial exploitation and allowed certain local structures to continue.
Numerous reductions were established in present-day Paraguay and neighboring regions during the 17th and 18th centuries. After the Jesuits were expelled from Spanish territories in 1767, many missions lost their previous organization. Some were abandoned, while others continued as settlements.
Today, Paraguay’s best-known Jesuit sites are the historic ruins of Trinidad and Jesús de Tavarangue. San Cosme y Damián is another place where this chapter of Paraguayan history remains visible.
Ruins of the Jesuit mission of Trinidad: a visible legacy of the Jesuit reductions in southern Paraguay. At these sites, history becomes more than a list of dates. Walls, church ruins, and entire settlement layouts still show how religion, Indigenous communities, and European colonial rule were connected.
Independence: Paraguay becomes its own state # Paraguay became independent in 1811.
The break was not only about separating from Spain. Paraguay also wanted to preserve its political autonomy from Buenos Aires rather than become part of a larger political project in the Río de la Plata region.
The political structure of the new state continued to develop gradually over the following years. In 1811, Congress initially established a Junta Superior Gubernativa. Its members included Fulgencio Yegros, José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, and Pedro Juan Caballero. In 1813, the Junta was replaced by a consulate led by Yegros and Francia; with the new system of government adopted on October 12, Paraguay was explicitly described as a republic.
By 1814, Francia had become the sole head of state. Under José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, Paraguay then became highly centralized and largely isolated from the outside world. Francia ruled in an authoritarian manner and limited many contacts with other countries. As a result, Paraguay remained internationally isolated, while at the same time strengthening its political independence from its neighbors.
After Francia’s death in 1840, Paraguay gradually opened up under Carlos Antonio López. State institutions, transport infrastructure, the military, and the economy were expanded. Paraguay increasingly sought to adopt technological developments from Europe and modernize its infrastructure.
Did you know? Paraguay’s first train left Asunción in 1861. The railway network was expanded over the following decades. The later main line from Asunción through places such as Pirayú and Sapucai to Encarnación eventually reached around 376 kilometers. Old stations and railway workshops still recall this period of infrastructure development.
The importance of independence is especially visible every year on May 14 and 15. During the Fiestas Patrias and Independence Day, schools, families, and public institutions commemorate the events of 1811.
The War of the Triple Alliance: the great national catastrophe # Only a few decades after independence, Paraguay entered the most devastating war in its history.
The War of the Triple Alliance lasted from 1864 to 1870. Under President Francisco Solano López, Paraguay fought Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay.
The causes cannot be reduced to a single event. Power struggles in the Río de la Plata region, the political crisis in Uruguay, Brazilian intervention, regional rivalries, and decisions made by the Paraguayan government under López all played a role.
These conflicts developed into a war whose consequences were especially severe for Paraguay.
The country lost a significant share of its population. Towns, farms, and economic structures were destroyed, territory was lost, and reconstruction took decades. The exact number of deaths remains the subject of historical debate and widely differing estimates. What is not disputed is the enormous scale of the disaster.
The war fundamentally changed Paraguay’s population, economy, state, and society.
For Paraguay, it is therefore not simply a closed chapter of the 19th century. Many places, memorial days, and national symbols still refer to the conflict.
This is especially visible on Heroes’ Day on March 1. The day commemorates, among other things, the death of Francisco Solano López at Cerro Corá in 1870 and the country’s war dead.
Paraguayan Women’s Day on February 24 also has a connection to this period. The memorial day refers to a women’s gathering in 1867, when women donated jewelry and other valuables to support the national cause.
Places such as Cerro Corá, Humaitá, and Piribebuy still represent some of the most important and painful events of this war.
After the war: reconstruction and political unrest # After 1870, Paraguay had to rebuild its political, economic, and social structures under extremely difficult conditions.
Brazilian troops remained in the country for several more years, political institutions had to be reorganized, and major economic changes followed.
The party system that would later shape Paraguayan politics for generations also began to take form during this period. Political power struggles, frequent changes of government, and military influence repeatedly caused instability.
The late 19th and early 20th centuries were therefore not simply a quiet period between Paraguay’s two major wars. They were decades in which a severely weakened country tried to rebuild state institutions while continuing to navigate a politically unstable region.
The Chaco War: the conflict with Bolivia # From 1932 to 1935, Paraguay fought Bolivia over the Chaco Boreal, a large and sparsely populated region in the west.
The war followed decades of disagreement over the border. Large parts of the Chaco were only lightly settled, and the boundary between the two countries had never been clearly established. The region also had strategic importance, including access to the Paraguay River.
Conditions for the soldiers were extreme. Heat, lack of water, disease, and the enormous distances made the fighting even more difficult and deadly.
One of the best-known early battles was the Battle of Boquerón (Batalla de Boquerón) in September 1932. After weeks of fighting, Paraguayan forces captured the Bolivian-held position on September 29.
Boquerón became important not only militarily but also as a powerful symbol in Paraguay’s memory of the war. September 29 is still commemorated today.
As the conflict continued, Paraguay gained control of large parts of the disputed territory. The peace protocol was signed on June 12, 1935, and the fighting ended two days later. The final border settlement between Paraguay and Bolivia followed several years later.
Día de la Paz del Chaco on June 12 and the Día de la Batalla de Boquerón on September 29 show how strongly the war remains part of Paraguay’s national memory.
If you travel through the Chaco today, you will come across names such as Boquerón, Fortín Toledo, and Mariscal Estigarribia. They are reminders that the history of this region goes far beyond its landscape and agriculture.
Stroessner and the long dictatorship # One of the defining chapters of Paraguay’s more recent history is the dictatorship of Alfredo Stroessner.
Stroessner came to power in 1954 and ruled Paraguay until 1989. For almost 35 years, the country was shaped by authoritarian government, close ties between the state, the military, and the Colorado Party, and extensive political control.
At the same time, the government carried out major infrastructure projects and benefited during some periods from economic growth and international support in the context of the Cold War.
Alongside this were repression, censorship, political persecution, torture, exile, and serious human rights abuses.
The memory of this period is not the same for everyone in Paraguay. In family and public conversations, you still hear different views: some associate the era mainly with economic development, infrastructure, or a sense of order. For others, political violence, fear, and the lack of freedom stand at the center of their memories. Both perspectives are therefore part of how the period is remembered.
Did you know? Itaipú also belongs to this historical period. The enormous hydroelectric power plant on the border with Brazil was planned and built during the Stroessner era. It still plays a central role in Paraguay’s electricity supply, economy, and relationship with Brazil.
The effects of the long dictatorship did not disappear automatically when Stroessner fell. Political networks, party structures, and personal continuities remained influential during the democratic period that followed.
Since 1989: democracy, changes of power, and political continuity # In February 1989, Stroessner was overthrown in a military coup.
This marked the beginning of Paraguay’s transition toward democratic government. An important institutional milestone was the 1992 Constitution, which still provides the framework for the country’s political system. Paraguay commemorates it on Constitution Day.
The democratic transition, however, was not a straight path.
The Colorado Party, which had been closely connected to the state during the Stroessner era, remained Paraguay’s dominant political force for many years.
A major change came in 2008, when Fernando Lugo became the first president in decades who did not belong to the Colorado Party.
His presidency ended in 2012 after a controversial impeachment process. The proceedings took place within a very short period and drew international criticism over the way they were carried out.
Vice President Federico Franco then took over the presidency.
In 2013, the Colorado Party returned to power under Horacio Cartes. He was followed by Mario Abdo Benítez, who served as president from 2018 to 2023.
Since August 15, 2023, Santiago Peña has been president of Paraguay.
Paraguay today is a constitutional democracy with regular elections. At the same time, strong political parties, local power structures, economic interests, and personal networks continue to play an important role in political life.
The country has also changed economically and socially in recent decades. Services, the financial sector, digital payments, construction, and new developments in energy and agriculture have become more visible.
For younger generations, the internet, digital communication, and international connections are a much more natural part of everyday life than they were only a few decades ago. Education, work, and periods spent abroad also play a greater role for many people.
At the same time, regional differences, traditional ways of life, and strong local ties remain important.
This combination of change and continuity is itself part of Paraguay’s recent history.
What does this history mean for everyday life in Paraguay? # In Paraguay, history is not limited to books and museums.
Many streets, towns, schools, and public squares are named after historical figures. Holidays commemorate independence, wars, and political turning points. Monuments and historic sites refer to many of the same events.
Historical symbols also appear on banknotes, in public buildings, and during state ceremonies.
History in everyday life: the 10,000 guaraníes banknote and the Panteón Nacional de los Héroes make Paraguay’s past visible in daily life. | Symbolic image The country’s two major wars are particularly present. The War of the Triple Alliance and the Chaco War appear again and again in place names, memorial days, and national narratives.
The Stroessner era is also still relatively recent history. Many people experienced the dictatorship themselves or know its effects through their own families.
Language is another visible example. The strong presence of Guaraní alongside Spanish makes much more sense when Paraguay’s Indigenous and colonial history is taken into account.
History does not explain every modern habit or automatically explain how individual people behave. But it does provide important context for understanding why certain subjects, symbols, and political developments have particular significance in Paraguay.
This perspective also helps avoid seeing the country only through romanticized images or only through its problems.
Paraguay faces real challenges, including corruption, social inequality, political entanglements, and major regional differences. At the same time, it has developed a remarkably distinct culture and has repeatedly rebuilt itself after deep historical disruptions.
Knowing that background makes many things you encounter in Paraguay easier to place in context.

Go to the Telegram channel → ❓ Frequently Asked Questions About Paraguay’s History # When was Paraguay founded, and when did it become independent? Paraguay does not have a single founding date in the same way a city does. The area of present-day Paraguay had been inhabited long before Spanish colonization; in 1537, Asunción began as an important Spanish outpost from which colonial rule expanded further into the interior. Paraguay became an independent state in 1811. The revolution of May 14 and 15 set the break from Spanish rule in motion, and in June of that same year a congress chose its own governing authorities without Spanish participation. Where does the name Paraguay come from, and what does it mean? The name Paraguay has Guaraní-language roots and was already used for the Paraguay River. Its original meaning, however, is not fully settled. Historical interpretations include a connection to the Payaguá people as well as meanings such as “river that gives rise to a sea” or “crowned river.” There is therefore no single generally accepted translation of the name. Why is Guaraní so important in Paraguay? Guaraní is an official language alongside Spanish and remains widely used in everyday life. The two languages are also often combined in what is known as Jopara. This makes Indigenous influence especially visible in Paraguay’s language today. What was the War of the Triple Alliance, and how did it affect Paraguay? In the War of the Triple Alliance from 1864 to 1870, Paraguay fought Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay. For Paraguay, the conflict became the greatest catastrophe in its history: the country lost a significant share of its population and suffered severe economic, political, and social damage. The exact number of deaths remains disputed, but the enormous scale of the consequences does not. What was the Chaco War, and how did it end for Paraguay? In the Chaco War from 1932 to 1935, Paraguay and Bolivia fought over the Chaco Boreal. Paraguay gained military control over large parts of the disputed territory during the conflict. The peace protocol was signed on June 12, 1935, and the fighting ended two days later. The final border settlement followed several years later. Events such as the Battle of Boquerón remain part of Paraguay’s national memory today. Who was Alfredo Stroessner, and how long did he rule Paraguay? Alfredo Stroessner ruled Paraguay from 1954 to 1989, almost 35 years, as an authoritarian leader. His time in power included major infrastructure projects and economic changes, but the regime was also marked by political control, censorship, persecution, exile, and serious human rights abuses. The effects of the long dictatorship are still felt in Paraguay’s politics and society today. Is Paraguay a democracy today? Yes. After Stroessner’s fall in 1989, Paraguay began its transition toward democratic government. The 1992 Constitution remains the foundation of the country’s political system. Paraguay holds regular elections and has elected state institutions, although strong parties, political networks, and local power structures continue to play an important role. Which historical places can you visit in Paraguay? Important historical places include Asunción, the Jesuit ruins of Trinidad and Jesús de Tavarangue, Cerro Corá, Humaitá, and Piribebuy, as well as sites in the Chaco such as Boquerón and Fortín Toledo. Some are well-known visitor attractions, while others become especially interesting once you know the history behind them. Which holidays and memorial days commemorate Paraguay’s history? Important historical dates include May 14 and 15 for independence, Heroes’ Day on March 1, Chaco Peace Day on June 12, and the Battle of Boquerón on September 29. Constitution Day on June 20 and the Founding of Asunción on August 15 are also closely connected to the country’s history. Paraguayan Women’s Day on February 24 also has a historical link to the War of the Triple Alliance, although it is a memorial day rather than a regular nationwide public holiday. Conclusion: Paraguay is easier to understand when you know its history # Paraguay’s history brings together Indigenous and European influences, early political independence, two devastating wars, a dictatorship that lasted for decades, and a democratic transition that continues to shape the country today.
Many of these chapters remain visible in modern Paraguay — in language, holidays, street names, monuments, political structures, and national symbols.
You do not need to memorize dates to understand the country. But knowing the basic history makes it easier to place current events, public debates, and many things you encounter in everyday life in context.
Our Paraguay A to Z shows how history, culture, and everyday life come together today — from Guaraní and tereré to many of the small details that make Paraguay distinctive.

Be honest: who would have thought that in a country like Paraguay, you might one day crave a hot stew? But when the south wind, the Surazo, moves across the country and temperatures in Paraguay drop noticeably, one thing is clear: winter in Paraguay has arrived.
Then it is less about the pool, Tereré and summer salad, and more about a warm oven, Mate and dishes that warm you from the inside and give you enough energy for cool days. Since these warming dishes are back on our table right now, I have put together 14 winter dishes from Paraguay for this article – dishes that have been loved here for generations and are now also regular favorites among many of us immigrants.
Some of these dishes are more than everyday food: Sopa Paraguaya, Vori Vori and Locro are among the dishes whose traditional preparation was officially recognized in Paraguay as intangible cultural heritage in 2017. The language also shows how diverse Paraguayan cuisine is – Spanish words, Guaraní words and local everyday language often come together very naturally in the names of many dishes.
🧉 The Power Start: Breakfast for Cold Mornings # In Paraguay, breakfast in winter is often warm and very hearty, so people have enough energy for working outside.
Mbejú: When it is rainy and uncomfortable outside, there is hardly anything better than a freshly made, steaming Mbejú, also often written Mbejú. This flatbread made from manioc starch and lots of cheese is the perfect comfort food and quick to prepare. For an extra filling version, I recommend Mbejú relleno – a modern version filled with extra cheese and ham.
Tortillas Paraguayas: Not to be confused with Mexican corn tortillas: the Paraguayan tortilla is a savory fried dough cake made with wheat flour, lots of cheese and spring onions. They are wonderfully flexible and can be prepared with meat (Tortilla So’o) or other vegetables, for example corn (Tortilla avatiky). In our home, they are not only served on a winter morning for breakfast, but also often as a quick snack or as a crispy side dish with a hot soup.
Revido: This rustic classic is made from a simple dough of flour, water and salt, which is broken up in hot fat in a pan until golden, crispy crumbs form. In the past, it was an important basic energy source for forest workers because it was cheap and kept people full for a very long time. Even today, it is still the ultimate “campo worker’s breakfast”. If you want to enjoy it in an authentic way, eat it with a fried egg.
Like many Paraguayan families, we traditionally drink Mate or Cocido Quemado (caramelized Yerba Mate) with milk with it. On weekends, we sometimes have the sweeter version too – Mate dulce, with sugar and, depending on your appetite, milk instead of water.
🍲 The “Soul Warmers”: Hearty Soups & Stews # At lunchtime in winter, there is really only one rule: it has to be hot and steaming in the pot.
Vori Vori (Bori Bori): The name Bori comes from the Spanish word “bolita” (small ball) – in Guaraní, this becomes “Vori”, so here it means something like little ball-little ball. This rich chicken soup with hand-rolled corn and cheese balls again ranked number 1 among the world’s best soups by TasteAtlas in 2026. For many immigrants, it is a good first dish to try because it can remind you of dumpling soup or marrow dumpling soup from home. We tried it for the first time when our first Capataz offered it to us during our first winter here; since then, it has become a regular dish in our meal plan.
Soyo (So’o Josopy): The name says it all: “So’o Josopy” means crushed meat in Guaraní. In this warming soup, finely pounded beef and vegetables come together into a thick, smooth dish. It is a fixed part of everyday winter cooking and is almost always served with fried tortillas.
Sopa de Locro & Puchero: When the south wind blows, it is time for Sopa de Locro. This thick stew made from white corn and beef simmers for hours until the broth becomes wonderfully creamy. If you prefer something a little lighter, choose Puchero, a clear beef broth with large pieces of vegetables such as corn on the cob, pumpkin and potatoes. Both dishes have real “grandma’s kitchen” vibes and are also easy for us immigrants to adapt with extra spices.
Pira Caldo: When the weather turns cooler in Paraguay, this hearty fish soup appears on the table more often. Made with surubí from the country’s great rivers, vegetables, and a rich broth, it brings a very different side of Paraguayan winter cuisine to the table.
🍴 Hearty Fillers & Side Dishes # These dishes work as a meal on their own or as a strong side dish with Asado.
Sopa Paraguaya & Chipa Guasu: These two corn and cheese dishes are a must. While Sopa Paraguaya is more firm and compact, Chipa Guasu stays especially juicy because of the fresh corn. In winter, both are often eaten as a main meal with boiled manioc or as a hearty side dish with Asado. They develop their full flavor best when baked in the traditional clay oven, the Tatakuá.
Arroz Kesu / Arroz con Queso: This is the Paraguayan answer to “Mac and Cheese”. Rice, lots of local cheese and a splash of milk make a simple, filling dish that feels especially good on gray days.
Mandi’o Chyryry: “Mandi’o” means cassava and “Chyryry” roughly means fried or to fry. This typical manioc dish is also our favorite way to use boiled manioc from the day before. Fried in a pan with egg, cheese and onions, it gets a very savory flavor and always reminds us of hearty fried potatoes – just in a Paraguayan way.
Pastel Mandi’o: These heavy pastries made from manioc and corn flour are much more filling than normal empanadas. Filled with beef and egg, they are ideal food for a cold winter night by the fire.
Pajagua Mascada: The name is often connected with the Payaguá, a historical Indigenous group from the Río Paraguay area. Today, many people know Pajagua Mascada mainly as hearty food for the San Juan festival in Paraguay. Together with Pastel Mandi’o, it is one of the typical classics there, when fire, games and traditional foods are at the center of the celebrations in June.
The base is a strong dough made from boiled manioc, minced meat, garlic and spring onions, which is fried in hot oil until crispy. Fresh from the pan, Pajagua Mascada reminds you a little of a meat patty, but with much more manioc. Crispy on the outside, soft on the inside and really filling, it is exactly the kind of snack that tastes especially good on a cool evening.
🍯 Desserts: A Sweet Finish for Cold Days # Mazamorra (Kaguyjy): White locro corn, milk, and a little sugar come together in a simple, creamy dessert that is especially comforting served warm on cold days, but tastes just as good chilled. Add a little miel de caña or a pinch of cinnamon for an easy feel-good treat. The soft corn kernels may remind you a little of rice pudding, but they have a texture all their own.
Kivevé: This creamy pumpkin dish made with Andai, cornmeal, and Queso Paraguay combines the natural sweetness of the pumpkin with the mild, slightly tangy cheese. Depending on how it is prepared, Kivevé can be served semisweet as a light meal or merienda, or made a little more savory as a side dish with bife or asado. This meat-free dish also has its place in the traditional cuisine of Holy Week.
More sweet ideas for cold days If you like sweet winter dishes, Arroz con Leche and Dulce de Calabaza also fit well into the cold season. Both remind you of Mazamorra and Kivevé through their ingredients and are easy to prepare ahead of time.

Go to the Telegram channel → ❓ Frequently Asked Questions # Can I make Paraguayan specialties outside Paraguay? Yes. With a few simple substitutions, many Paraguayan specialties are easy to make outside the country as well.
Cassava starch (Almidón de Mandioca) is often available in Asian or African grocery stores, usually labeled as “Tapioca Starch.”
As a substitute for Queso Paraguay, different mild cheeses work better depending on the dish. For baked dishes such as Sopa Paraguaya or Chipa Guasu, a combination of mild feta and a little mozzarella can work well. For creamy dishes such as Kivevé, Queso fresco, Farmer’s Cheese, or ricotta are better options.
You can replace Andai squash in Kivevé with butternut squash. It also has mildly sweet, orange flesh and can be prepared in a similar way.
What do people eat in Paraguay when it is cold? When the south wind, the Surazo, moves through the country and temperatures drop, simple and filling dishes often come to the table in Paraguay. Many of them are part of traditional Paraguayan cuisine and warm you exactly when it gets uncomfortable outside. Especially popular are hot soups and stews such as Vori Vori, Locro or Puchero, but also fresh-from-the-oven classics like Chipa Guasu and Sopa Paraguaya.
Warm pan dishes like Mbejú, Tortillas Paraguayas or Pajagua Mascada also fit well. If you like something sweet, choose Mazamorra, Kivevé or Arroz con Leche – best with hot Cocido or Mate.
Which winter dishes from Paraguay are especially easy for beginners? For a first step into Paraguayan winter cooking, Mbejú, Tortillas Paraguayas, Arroz con Queso and Mandi’o Chyryry are a good choice. They do not need complicated techniques and can be adapted well with ingredients you can also find outside Paraguay. Which dishes are good meat-free options? Mbejú, Sopa Paraguaya, Chipa Guasu, Arroz con Queso, Mazamorra and Kivevé are made without meat or can easily be prepared without meat. Kivevé is especially good if you are looking for a filling dish without meat. Which ingredients are especially typical for Paraguayan winter dishes? When cooking in Paraguay, simple basic ingredients such as manioc, corn, Queso Paraguay, milk, eggs, beef, chicken and pumpkin play a big role. These ingredients are exactly what make many winter dishes so filling and down-to-earth. How can I make the dishes a little lighter? Many classic Paraguayan dishes are very filling because corn, manioc, cheese and fat play an important role. If you prefer something lighter, reduce the amount of cheese or fat first, instead of changing the taste completely with low-fat substitutes. Often, a smaller portion with salad, vegetables or boiled manioc as a side dish is enough. Conclusion: Winter Cuisine in Paraguay # Paraguayan winter cuisine is simple, filling and surprisingly varied. When the south wind comes and the evenings get cooler, steaming soups, pan-fried manioc dishes, fresh corn and cheese classics from the oven and sweet feel-good dishes bring good mood to the table.
For me, this has become part of winter in Paraguay: in the morning, when the oven has just been lit, something warm like tortillas or Mbejú, with Mate or Cocido – and Chipa Guasu always works, whether as a side dish or as a meal on its own.
If you want to understand food in Paraguay, you should therefore not only think of Asado, Chipa or Tereré, but also of these warming dishes for cold days.
Want to start with one of these winter classics? Mbejú is an easy place to begin. And if you’re wondering why comfort food like this has a season in Paraguay at all, our overview of winter in Paraguay explains how cold it can get and what the south wind has to do with it.
