🍽️ What is Pasta Frola de Guayaba? # Pasta Frola (also Pasta Frolla or Pastafrola) is a traditional shortcrust pastry tart that can be found in almost every bakery and household in Paraguay. The heart of this tart is a thick layer of fruity guava paste beneath its characteristic pastry lattice. While this specialty is often filled with quince paste (membrillo) in neighboring countries (Argentina and Uruguay), the version with guava (guayaba) is very common here in Paraguay. The pastry is tender and smells wonderfully of vanilla or lemon, which harmonizes perfectly with the intense sweetness of the fruit.
Would you like to try the recipe right away?
Go straight to the recipe 🇵🇾 The cultural tradition behind Pasta Frola de Guayaba # Anyone living in Paraguay comes across this pastry quite quickly. For many people, it is a natural part of merienda and is also often baked when visitors come over or when there is a special occasion.
Historical origin # Pasta Frola goes back to European baking traditions and is closely linked to the Italian pastafrolla and crostata. With immigrants, the basic idea of the lattice tart came to South America, where it was gradually adapted to regionally available ingredients. In Paraguay, the filling with guava paste became established as a particularly popular version.
Importance in the regional cuisine # In Paraguayan cuisine, this tart holds an important place because it is inexpensive to make and at the same time keeps very well. It is often the centerpiece of family celebrations or the classic afternoon merienda. The making of the lattice is often passed down from one generation to the next and is considered a small sign of handmade love for baking.
A closer look at the main ingredients # A good recipe stands or falls with the quality of its ingredients, which in Paraguay are often sourced directly from the local market.
Guayaba - the foundation of the recipe # Guava, called guayaba in Paraguay, is a real vitamin-rich fruit and forms the aromatic center of Pasta Frola. In everyday cooking, it is usually used as a firm paste called “Dulce de Guayaba.”
Nutrients: Guavas contain a lot of vitamin C and provide valuable fiber as well as antioxidants.
Health aspects: The fruit is considered good for digestion and supportive of the immune system, although with the processed paste you should of course keep an eye on the sugar content.
The consistency of the guava paste is crucial for success, because it must not become too runny in the oven. The best option is firm guava paste in a block (“Dulce de Guayaba”). Soft spreads or liquid guava jam are usually too loose for the lattice.
Other special ingredients # Besides the fruit filling, the pastry plays the most important role in the mouthfeel.
A real Paraguayan shortcrust pastry for Pasta Frola is characterized by its softness, which comes from a good amount of fat and egg yolks. It must be stable enough for the lattice, but still melt in your mouth.
Local tip: In Paraguay, lard is often used instead of butter, which gives the pastry an especially tender texture.
Recipe for Pasta Frola de Guayaba - step by step # At a glance Difficulty: Medium Preparation time: about 75 minutes (including baking time) Servings: 12 pieces Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 📝 Main ingredients # 400 g wheat flour (type 405 or Paraguayan “0000”) 200 g cold butter or margarine 150 g sugar 2 eggs plus 1 egg yolk 1 tsp baking powder 1 pinch of salt Zest of one organic lemon or a little vanilla extract 500 g Dulce de Guayaba (guava paste in a block) A little water to smooth out the filling Optional ingredients # A splash of Paraguayan caña (sugarcane spirit) in the dough or wine in the filling for extra aroma. Shredded coconut to sprinkle over the edge after baking. Substitutions # Flexible alternatives depending on availability or dietary needs Pasta Frola is naturally vegetarian and can be adapted quite easily with a few adjustments.
Different filling: If guava paste is not available, quince paste (Dulce de Membrillo) works very well as a substitute. A very thick plum jam also works, although the flavor is a bit different.
Gluten-free: For a gluten-free version, you can use a universal gluten-free flour blend for cakes. A little xanthan and possibly a bit more liquid help keep the dough more pliable.
Vegan version: Butter can be replaced with plant-based margarine or solid coconut fat. Suitable egg substitutes include ready-made egg replacers, applesauce, or a mixture of chia seeds and water.
Important when using substitutes: Gluten-free doughs are often more fragile, so the lattice is easier to place than to weave. With coconut fat, the dough usually browns faster, so keep a close eye on the baking time.
Required kitchen equipment # Large mixing bowl Rolling pin Round baking pan, about 26–28 cm (10–11 inches) in diameter Fork Small saucepan or microwave-safe bowl for warming the paste 👩‍🍳 Step-by-step preparation # Preparation # First, mix the flour with the baking powder and sugar in a bowl.
Cut the cold butter into small cubes and work it into the flour mixture with your fingertips until you get a sandy consistency.
Alternatively, you can use margarine. The dough will usually be a bit softer and less buttery in flavor.
Then add the eggs, the egg yolk, and the lemon zest and quickly knead everything into a smooth dough.
Dough resting time Let the dough rest in the refrigerator for at least 30 minutes so it will be easier to roll out later.
Preparation / baking process # Preheat the oven to 180 °C (350 °F) top and bottom heat.
Cut the guava paste into cubes and warm it in a saucepan with 2 to 3 tablespoons of water until it becomes a spreadable mixture.
Roll out about two thirds of the dough and use it to line the bottom and sides of the greased baking pan.
Spread the guava filling evenly over the pastry base.
Roll out the remaining dough and cut it into strips about 1.5 cm wide.
The lattice pattern (“Enrejado”) requires a bit of patience, but it works more easily if the pastry strips are well chilled.
Lay the strips over the filling in a diamond pattern and press the ends firmly onto the edge. Make sure the guava mixture has cooled down a little and that the strips are thick enough so they do not sink into the filling.
Tip: Whisk egg yolk with a splash of milk and brush the strips with it - this gives the tart its typical golden, glossy look.
Bake the tart for about 30 to 40 minutes, until the lattice is golden brown. 🔄 Variations of the recipe # Regional variations # A popular variation is a thin layer of cream cheese beneath the guava paste - inspired by the classic combination of guava and cheese. The sweet-salty contrast works very well here too.
Did you know? The combination recalls the widespread pairing of cheese and fruit paste in Latin America - especially well known in Brazil as “Romeu e Julieta.”
Dulce de Leche is also often used as a filling or combined with guava.
Modern interpretations # In modern cafes, you can also find Pasta Frola with a touch of dark chocolate in the guava filling or with a shortcrust pastry enriched with ground almonds.
What goes well with Pasta Frola de Guayaba? # To make your meal feel complete, here are a few ideas for side dishes and drinks that pair well with it.
Side dishes Drinks Lightly whipped or unsweetened cream: Softens the sweetness of the guava and makes the pastry feel a little lighter. Mild cream cheese or fresh cheese: Creates a gentle, slightly salty contrast to the sweet filling. Vanilla ice cream: Especially delicious when the tart is still slightly warm. Fresh fruit: A few slices of fresh guava or orange as a decorative side. Café de saquito: A simple filter coffee pairs perfectly with this sweet pastry. Mate: A hot mate tea balances the sweetness of the tart nicely with its herbal notes. Mate Cocido or Cocido con leche: Works especially well if you want something milder with your sweet pastry. Nutritional overview # Per serving (about 80 g):
Calories: 310 kcal Protein: 4 g Carbohydrates: 52 g Fat: 10 g Fiber: 2 g The nutritional values are averages and may vary depending on the guava paste and type of fat used.

Go to the Telegram channel → ❓ Frequently asked questions (FAQ) # Can I prepare the dough the day before? Yes, the dough can easily be prepared the day before and stored in the refrigerator. Before rolling it out, it should sit at room temperature for a few minutes so it does not stay too firm or brittle. Where can I find guava paste in Germany? Guava paste can often be found in Asian markets, Latin American specialty shops, or well-stocked online stores under the name “Dulce de Guayaba” or “Goiabada.” Alternatively, you can use quince paste or a strongly reduced plum jam. Can I use regular jam instead? Regular jam is often too runny and would melt beneath the lattice while baking. If you use jam, you should thicken it with a little starch or cook it down until it is very thick. Guava paste “Dulce de Guayaba” is best. Which pan works best: tart pan, springform pan, or baking tray? A tart pan or a shallow cake pan works best, because Pasta Frola is traditionally baked rather flat. A springform pan also works, and a rectangular pan is practical if you want larger pieces or a tray version. Should I prick the base or blind bake it? Lightly pricking the base with a fork is helpful so it bakes more evenly. Blind baking is usually not necessary as long as the filling is not too runny. Why does the base turn soft or soggy? This usually happens when the filling is too moist or the tart was not baked long enough. A tart that is still warm also often feels softer when cut, even though it becomes firmer once cooled. Can I also bake Pasta Frola in a rectangular pan? Yes, that works without any problem and is very practical for larger quantities. Just make sure not to roll the dough out too thickly and keep an eye on the baking time depending on the pan you use. My lattice sinks into the filling. What did I do wrong? Most likely, the guava filling was still too hot or too runny when you spread it on. Let the mixture cool a little after warming it. Also make sure the dough strips for the lattice are cut thick enough. Why does my dough crack when I roll it out? Shortcrust pastry is sensitive to warmth. If it gets too warm, it tears easily. Chill it again for 15 minutes if it becomes too soft. A splash of cold water while kneading can help improve the binding. What is the best way to store Pasta Frola? The tart keeps for about 3 to 4 days at room temperature in an airtight container. Thanks to the high sugar content of the guava paste, it is quite stable. In the refrigerator, it will even stay fresh for up to a week. Can I freeze Pasta Frola de Guayaba? Yes, the tart freezes very well. It is best to cut it into pieces first and separate them with parchment paper. That way, you can take out individual portions and let them thaw at room temperature. Conclusion # Pasta Frola de Guayaba combines simple shortcrust pastry with a filling that feels very familiar in Paraguay. It is precisely this mix of everyday practicality, sweetness, and tradition that makes the tart so popular to this day. Whether for merienda, for visitors, or simply in between - it can be prepared well in advance and suits many occasions.
Have fun cooking and buen provecho!

🍽️ What is Chupín de Surubí? # Anyone who lives in Paraguay or travels through the country will hardly miss this dish. Chupín de Surubí is a hearty, layered fish stew that is especially served in the regions along the great rivers Río Paraguay and Río Paraná. The name is often associated with the Ligurian-Italian Ciuppin/Cioppino, showing how European influences merged with local ingredients. Unlike a classic soup, Chupín is thicker and becomes especially aromatic through the slow layering of fish, potatoes, and vegetables.
You want to try the recipe right away!
Go directly to the recipe 🇵🇾 The cultural tradition behind Chupín de Surubí # In Paraguayan culture, eating together is a central pillar of social life. A Chupín is often prepared in large pots for the whole family or a group of friends, especially on holidays or after a successful day of fishing by the river.
Historical origin # The origins of this dish lie in shipping and fishing. Immigrants from Genoa brought their fish preparation techniques to South America. In Paraguay, people adapted the recipe to the treasures of their own waters. Although meat is everywhere in Paraguay, the huge rivers offer a welcome and appreciated variety on the menu.
Importance in regional cuisine # Surubí is considered the “king of the rivers.” That is why a Chupín is not just a meal, but often a festive dish. It represents the hospitality of the people here, who proudly like to share their regional products. You can often find this dish on the menus of restaurants located directly by the water.
A closer look at the main ingredients # A good Chupín stands or falls with the quality of its components. There are no shortcuts here if you want to experience the true taste of Paraguay.
Surubí - the foundation of the recipe # Surubí is a large catfish (freshwater fish) native to the subtropical rivers of South America. Its flesh is white, firm, and has a pleasantly mild flavor that does not taste too “fishy.” This also makes it popular with people who do not usually reach for fish very often. From a nutritional perspective, Surubí provides valuable omega-3 fatty acids and is an excellent source of protein. Since it is comparatively low in bones in the flesh, it can be wonderfully cut into thick slices, the so-called “rodajas.”
Other special ingredient(s) # Besides the fish, potatoes and tomatoes play the main role. They form the base for the stew’s creamy consistency. In addition, bell peppers (locotes) and onions add color and aroma and should be fresh and crisp. As they cook slowly, they release their sweetness into the broth, creating the typical character of Chupín.
Tip When buying Surubí, make sure the flesh is firm and smells neutral. At local markets in Paraguay, the fish is often available directly in the morning after it has been caught, which gives the best result.
Recipe for Chupín de Surubí - step by step # At a glance Difficulty level: Medium Preparation time: about 60 minutes Servings: 4 to 6 people Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 📝 Main ingredients # 1.5 kg Surubí (cut into slices about 2-3 cm thick) 1 kg potatoes (waxy, sliced) 3 large onions (cut into rings) 2 red bell peppers (cut into strips) 2 green bell peppers (cut into strips) 4 ripe tomatoes (peeled and diced) 3 garlic cloves (finely chopped) 200 ml dry white wine 200 ml fish stock or water Olive oil or vegetable oil Salt, pepper, bay leaves, and fresh oregano Optional ingredients # 200 ml cream (for a creamier version) fresh or dried chili pepper or hot chili sauce (for heat) Substitutions # Flexible alternatives depending on availability or diet Natural characteristics of the dish
The traditional recipe is naturally completely gluten-free The classic basic version contains no dairy products or lactose at all. Anyone watching their carbohydrates (low carb) can simply reduce the amount of potatoes even more. Fish with limited availability
In Europe, catfish (closest to Surubí) or cod are good substitutes. Monkfish or halibut also keep a firm structure when cooked. Vegan diet
Thick slices of oyster mushrooms provide a very similar texture. Alternatively, use eggplant or zucchini. Firm natural tofu absorbs the flavors of the sauce very well. Dairy products for the creamy version
Coconut milk is an ideal lactose-free and vegan solution. A neutral cashew cream provides an especially velvety note. Low-acid and low-allergen adjustments
For histamine sensitivity, red bell peppers can replace tomatoes. Omit lemon juice. Instead of white wine: use a splash of mild vegetable broth with a drop of apple cider vinegar. Alternatively, use more fish stock or water. Changes in flavor and texture
Saltwater fish are much saltier than the Paraguayan freshwater fish Surubí. Mushrooms and substitute fish often need about ten minutes less cooking time. Plant-based alternatives need additional herbs like oregano for the necessary depth. Required kitchen equipment # A large, deep pot with a fitting lid (ideally a heavy cast-iron pot or a classic cacerola) A sharp chef’s knife A cutting board A ladle for serving 👩‍🍳 Step-by-step preparation # Preparation # First, rinse the fish briefly under cold water and pat it dry with kitchen paper.
Season the fish slices with salt, pepper, and a little lemon juice and let them rest in the refrigerator for about 15 minutes.
Meanwhile, wash all the vegetables and cut them into the appropriate shapes.
If you want to peel the tomatoes more easily, score them crosswise and briefly pour boiling water over them. After that, the skin will come off almost by itself.
If you like, you can also lightly saute the vegetables before layering or lightly sear the fish.
Preparation / cooking process # Generously coat the bottom of the pot with oil and heat it lightly.
Now begin layering: first a layer of onions and peppers, then a layer of potato slices.
Place the marinated fish pieces on top of the vegetable bed.
Spread the diced tomatoes, garlic, and spices over them.
Repeat the process until all ingredients have been used up, ideally finishing with a vegetable layer.
Carefully pour the white wine and fish stock along the edge of the pot.
Cover the pot tightly and let the Chupín simmer gently over medium heat for about 30 to 40 minutes.
Never stir the stew during cooking! Stirring would break the fish pieces and potatoes apart. The Chupín cooks perfectly through the rising steam in the closed pot.
Instead of on the stovetop, you can also prepare the ingredients in a deep baking dish with a lid and cook the dish in the oven.
🔄 Variations of the recipe # With meat or fish # Although the classic Chupín is prepared with Surubí, in Paraguay there are also versions with other river fish such as Dorado or Patí. In rural regions, bacon (panceta) is sometimes added to give the dish a smoky note.
Vegetarian / vegan version # For a fully plant-based version, large pieces of firm tofu, eggplant or zucchini or a mixture of different mushrooms work well. Use a strong vegetable stock instead of fish stock and add a little smoked paprika powder to imitate the depth of flavor.
Modern or creative interpretations # Some chefs in modern cuisine refine their Chupín today with capers or olives, which creates a clear bridge to Mediterranean cuisine. Finishing with a splash of cream shortly before serving is also a popular modern variation that makes the stew smoother.
There are also traditional additions that are used depending on the family recipe. These include Queso Paraguay, which makes the dish creamier, as well as hard-boiled eggs, which are often used as a garnish when serving.
What goes well with Chupín de Surubí? # To make your meal perfectly complete, here are a few ideas for side dishes and drinks that pair well with it.
Side dishes Drinks Cassava: Traditionally cooked cassava (Mandi’o) is the classic and popular side dish in Paraguay.
Rice: Cooked white rice (Arroz blanco) absorbs the wonderful sauce of the Chupín perfectly.
Bread / baguette / galleta: A simple but very fitting side dish for soaking up the aromatic broth.
Tomato and onion salad or green salad as a refreshing component
Cerveza: An ice-cold Paraguayan lager is the best choice on hot days.
Vino Blanco: A dry Chardonnay or a lively Sauvignon Blanc pairs wonderfully with the rich fish.
Tereré: In Paraguay, it is often enjoyed with the meal or afterwards on warm days.
Nutritional overview # For one portion (about 400 g):
Calories: about 450 kcal Protein: 35 g Carbohydrates: 25 g Fat: 22 g Fiber: 4 g The nutritional values are average values and may vary depending on the fat content of the fish and the amount of oil used.

You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → ❓ Frequently asked questions (FAQ) # Which fish is best for Chupín? In Paraguay, Surubí is the first choice. In general, however, any fish with firm flesh that does not immediately fall apart during cooking is suitable. Catfish or cod are good alternatives outside South America. Can I use frozen fish? Yes, but thaw it completely and pat it very dry. How do I prevent the stew from burning on the bottom? Make sure the bottom layer consists of juicy vegetables such as onions and that the heat is not set too high. The liquid should only simmer very gently. Can I reheat the Chupín the next day? Yes, the stew often tastes even better when reheated because the flavors have had time to fully develop. However, reheat it carefully over low heat. Can I freeze the Chupín? That is possible, but the potatoes often suffer in texture. Does the fish need to be scaled? Surubí does not have scales, but smooth skin. Depending on the cut and personal preference, the skin can be cooked with the fish; however, many prefer filleted fish without skin. Is the dish very spicy? No, traditional Paraguayan cuisine is rather mild. The seasoning comes from herbs and vegetables. If you like it spicy, serve a separate chili sauce with it. Conclusion # Chupín de Surubí is more than just a simple fish dish. It is a piece of Paraguayan joy of life and tradition. With its simple ingredients and uncomplicated preparation, it brings the flavor of the great rivers directly into your kitchen. Whether you live in Paraguay or want to discover the country from afar through its cuisine: this stew will delight you with its hearty character.
Give it a try and bring a piece of South America to your plate!
Have fun cooking and buen provecho!
Want to try surubí in a soup? Try Pira Caldo, a Paraguayan fish soup with vegetables, milk, and Queso Paraguay. You’ll find more Paraguayan fish recipes in our fish recipe collection.

summary: If you love fish, you can’t miss out on this classic dish from Paraguayan cuisine. Discover how to easily make this flavorful stew yourself.

🍽️ What is Tropical Ceviche? # Ceviche originally refers to a dish made from raw fish that is denatured by the acidity of citrus fruits. The Tropical Ceviche variation expands this principle with a wonderful component: the sweetness of ripe Paraguayan fruits.
This creates a colorful composition that stands out through its acidity and freshness. The combination of raw fish, exotic fruits such as mango or pineapple, and additions like colorful bell peppers (Locotes) makes the dish a visual highlight on every plate. Because of this aesthetic appeal, the dish is also often served in Paraguay as an elegant starter for special occasions, such as Valentine’s Day . The fish is not heated, but denatured solely by the acidity of limes.
Want to try the recipe right away!
Go directly to the recipe 🇵🇾 The cultural tradition behind Tropical Ceviche # Paraguay may be a landlocked country, but it has enormous river systems such as the Río Paraguay and the Río Paraná. The tradition of eating fish cold or marinated has become established especially in urban centers such as Asunción and Encarnación.
Ceviche in particular has developed into a true symbol in modern fusion cuisine in recent years. It combines the traditional treasures of the region with a light, contemporary way of preparation.
Historical origin # The basic idea of ceviche comes from the coastal regions of South America, especially Peru. Through cultural exchange and migration, this style of preparation reached the heart of the continent. Here, the recipe was adapted to local conditions, with residents using sour limes from their own gardens and fish from local rivers.
Importance in regional cuisine # In a country where the thermometer often rises above 40 degrees, heavy meat dishes at lunchtime can be a challenge for the circulation. Tropical Ceviche offers a welcome change. Today, it is considered a sign of modern, health-conscious eating in Paraguay and is gladly served at social gatherings by the pool or on the terrace.
In Paraguay, the quality of the fish often determines the entire culinary experience, which is why it is best to buy the fish directly at the market in the morning.
A closer look at the main ingredients # For a successful Tropical Ceviche, two components are crucial: the quality of the protein and the perfect ripeness of the fruit.
Fish and seafood - the foundation # In Paraguay, we often use locally farmed tilapia or the highly valued surubí. Tilapia is ideal because its flesh stays firm and absorbs the flavor of the marinade well. Fish provides valuable omega-3 fatty acids and high-quality protein, making it a light alternative to the ever-present beef.
Anyone who prefers a more luxurious version often adds shrimp (camarones), which gives the dish extra texture and color.
Other special ingredients: mango and coriander # Besides the fish, mango plays the leading role in the tropical version. During harvest season, the trees in Paraguay are so full that you can find the fruit on every street corner. Pineapple can also be used as an alternative.
Fresh coriander is also used - known in Paraguay as Kuratũ - and it is essential for the authentic aroma.
Characteristics # For this recipe, the mango should still have a certain firmness. An overripe, overly soft fruit would fall apart in the acidity of the limes and affect the appearance of the dish. The combination of the sharpness of red onions or chili, the authentic aroma of coriander, and the sweetness of the fruit creates the typical flavor profile.
Recipe for Tropical Ceviche - step by step # At a glance Difficulty: Easy Preparation time: approx. 45 minutes Servings: 4 people Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 📝 Main ingredients # 600 g firm fish fillet (for example tilapia or surubí or international white fish) 1 large, firm mango 6 to 8 limes (freshly squeezed juice) 2 red onions 1 bunch of fresh coriander 1 red chili pepper Salt and a pinch of pepper Optional ingredients # 100 g peeled and briefly blanched shrimp 1-2 colorful bell peppers (Locotes) A handful of roasted corn kernels for crunch A splash of olive oil to round off the acidity Some diced avocado for extra creaminess Substitutions # Flexible alternatives depending on availability or diet** This dish is naturally gluten-free and lactose-free.
Instead of tilapia or surubí: Pike-perch, sea bream, sea bass, or cod → What matters is that the fish is absolutely fresh and has firm flesh. If you cannot get fresh fish or do not like it, you can also work exclusively with briefly blanched shrimp.
Instead of mango: Fresh pineapple → contains enzymes that make the fish soften faster.
Instead of coriander: Flat-leaf parsley or a mixture of mint and basil → the authentic character may change slightly.
Required kitchen equipment # A very sharp knife (important for clean fish cubes) A large glass bowl (metal can react with the acidity) A citrus press Cutting board 👩‍🍳 Step-by-step preparation # Preparation # First, rinse the fish thoroughly under cold water and pat it dry with kitchen paper.
Cut the fillet into even cubes of about 1.5 cm.
Peel the red onions and cut them into very thin strips (julienne). Peel the mango and cut the flesh into cubes as well, ideally slightly smaller than the fish pieces. Do the same with the bell pepper - the bell pepper cubes should be about half the size of the fish pieces.
After cutting, place the onion strips in ice-cold water for ten minutes so they lose their aggressive sharpness and stay nice and crisp.
Preparation / curing process # Put the fish cubes into the glass bowl and season them generously with salt.
Squeeze the limes and pour the juice over the fish until it is almost completely covered.
Let the fish rest in the refrigerator for about 15 to 20 minutes until the flesh turns whitish and opaque.
Tip: Add 2-3 ice cubes directly to the liquid to keep the leche de tigre ice-cold.
Add the drained onions, the finely chopped chili, and the mango and bell pepper cubes.
Carefully fold in the freshly chopped coriander.
Taste once more with salt and serve the dish immediately while it is still ice-cold.
Make sure not to leave the fish in the lime juice for too long, otherwise the flesh will become tender and dry. Twenty minutes is often the ideal timing.
🔄 Variations of the recipe # With meat or fish # In Paraguay, people often experiment with different types of fish. The version with surubí strips is especially elegant.
Vegetarian / vegan version # Ceviche de Palmitos is a fantastic local alternative. Here, hearts of palm are sliced and marinated like fish. This version is very popular among residents who prefer a plant-based diet or want to skip fish during intense heat. Alternatively, you can also use oyster mushrooms.
Modern or creative interpretations # Some chefs in Asunción now add a splash of passion fruit juice to the lime marinade. This intensifies the tropical aroma and gives the sauce, known as “leche de tigre”, a bright yellow color and a complex sweetness. Others refine the ceviche with a splash of tomato juice, moving it in the direction of a “ceviche de carretilla”.
What goes well with Tropical Ceviche? # To make your meal perfectly rounded, here are a few ideas for side dishes and drinks that go well with it.
Side dishes Drinks Mandioca: Classic boiled cassava is the neutral companion par excellence. Batata: Sweet potatoes from the grill or oven balance out the acidity. Chipa Guasu: A piece of this savory corn cake goes surprisingly well with it. Tereré: The national drink with lots of mint is the ideal thirst quencher. Clericó: A Paraguayan fruit punch for festive occasions. White wine: A dry Sauvignon Blanc pairs well with the lime. Lemonade: Freshly squeezed with a touch of ginger or with mint and ice. Nutritional overview # The following values refer to one portion of about 250 g of the finished dish.
Calories: 210 kcal Protein: 28 g Carbohydrates: 18 g Fat: 4 g Fiber: 3 g These nutritional values are average figures and may vary depending on the type and amount of fish used as well as the ripeness of the fruit.
More posts like this? 🇵🇾 Did you enjoy this post and want to learn more about Paraguay? Get Paraguay4Life updates by email and stay connected. Get new posts by email Free. You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → ❓ Frequently asked questions (FAQ) # Which fish can I use in Europe / America as an alternative? Outside Paraguay, pike-perch, sea bream, or sea bass are especially suitable. When buying, make sure to choose “sushi-grade” fish, since the fish is only denatured by acid and not sterilized by heat. Alternatively, briefly blanched shrimp can be used if no fresh fish is available. Which fish is best to use in Paraguay? Tilapia is best because it is locally farmed and available very fresh. It has firm flesh that does not fall apart during marination. Surubí is also an excellent choice for a more refined version. Can I still eat the ceviche the next day? It is strongly recommended to eat ceviche immediately. Since the fish is only “cold-cooked”, bacteria are not killed as they are during cooking. An unbroken cold chain is essential. In addition, the acid changes the texture so much overnight that the fish becomes tough and unpleasant in flavor. Is the fish really 'done' after 20 minutes in lime juice, or is it still raw? The acid does change the protein structure (it denatures it), but it does not kill bacteria or parasites as reliably as heat above 70 °C (160 °F). That is why the cold chain and the quality of the fish are the be-all and end-all. If you have doubts about the freshness, choose the blanched version or use high-quality frozen fillets instead. What happens if the fish stays in the acid too long? Fish can actually be “overcooked” in acid. If it marinates for several hours, the texture becomes dry and crumbly because the acid completely breaks down the fibers. For the best flavor experience, you should keep the time frame of 15 to a maximum of 30 minutes exactly. Is frozen fish suitable for ceviche? In fact, high-quality frozen fish is often a very good choice. Industrial shock-freezing kills potential parasites. When thawing, make sure to thaw the fish slowly in the refrigerator and in a sieve so it does not sit in its own juices. Can I briefly fry or boil the fish as well? Traditionally, ceviche is only cured by acid. However, if you prefer to prepare the fish with heat, you can place the cubes in boiling salted water for about 30 to 60 seconds (blanching) and then immediately chill them in ice water. This way, the fish is firm on the outside and safe inside, but it loses some of its typical “ceviche bite”. In technical terms, this moves more in the direction of an ensalada de pescado. What do I do if it is too sour? If the fruit does not yet have the desired sweetness, you can balance the marinade with a small pinch of sugar or a teaspoon of honey. That lifts the entire flavor profile. Can pregnant women or children eat ceviche? Since the fish is not sterilized by heat during preparation, pregnant women, small children, and people with weakened immune systems should avoid eating raw fish. A great alternative for these groups is the vegetarian version with palmitos (hearts of palm). Conclusion # Whether as a romantic starter on Valentine’s Day or as a cool rescue on a hot afternoon in Paraguay - Tropical Ceviche is a feast for the senses. The preparation does not require great culinary talent, only respect for fresh ingredients. Try it next hot weekend and bring a piece of South American joie de vivre to your plate.
Have fun cooking and buen provecho!
Want to try a Paraguayan fish dish warm and hearty instead of fresh and tangy? Then try Chupín de Surubí. You’ll find more Paraguayan fish recipes in our fish recipe collection.
Share & support Did this Tropical Ceviche recipe inspire you and spark your curiosity about Paraguay? Then feel free to give the post a like and share it with other South America enthusiasts - helping make Paraguay’s culinary diversity more visible.
summary: Tropical Ceviche combines fresh fish with the sweetness of ripe mangoes. Learn how to prepare this classic with a Paraguayan touch.
title: Tropical Ceviche: Fish and Mango with a Paraguayan Touch

What can you do with a papaya that is still green and far too firm to eat? In Paraguay, it becomes Dulce de Mamón. Slowly simmered in sugar syrup, the firm fruit turns golden and sweet while still holding its shape.
That contrast is what makes this Paraguayan dessert so distinctive: the papaya, commonly called mamón here in Paraguay, softens and absorbs the syrup without turning into jam. The recipe takes a little patience, but needs only a few ingredients and can easily be prepared in advance.
This recipe uses a straightforward baking-soda method and walks you through the process step by step.
📝 Dulce de Mamón Recipe - Step by Step # At a glance Difficulty: medium Preparation: about 20 to 30 minutes Soaking time: about 1 hour Cooking time: about 2 to 4 hours Servings: about 10 to 15, depending on serving size The exact cooking time depends mainly on how ripe the papaya is and the size of the pieces.
Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 🛒 Ingredients for Dulce de Mamón # For Dulce de Mamón, the most important ingredient is a firm, still-green papaya. You will also need sugar, water and a little baking soda for the soaking step.
Main ingredients # 2 kg firm green papaya (mamón) 1.5 kg white sugar about 2 liters of water 2 tbsp baking soda enough water to cover the papaya for soaking Optional ingredients # 1 to 2 cloves 1 cinnamon stick a little lemon or orange peel a few drops of lemon juice a little vanilla extract a small piece of ginger a small pinch of salt Start sparingly with spices. Cinnamon and especially cloves can quickly overpower the mild flavor of the papaya.
What ingredients can you substitute? # Ingredient alternatives The basic recipe is naturally vegan and gluten-free.
Sugar: You can also use brown cane sugar. It gives the syrup a darker color and a deeper, slightly caramel-like flavor. Baking soda: A traditional alternative is food-grade calcium hydroxide (E526), also known as slaked lime. In Spanish, look for cal apagada apta para alimentos. It is used as a firming agent. Do not confuse it with cal viva or cal virgen, which refer to calcium oxide or quicklime. Kitchen equipment # large bowl or container for soaking large, heavy pot vegetable peeler sharp knife cutting board wooden spoon or long-handled spoon clean jars with tight-fitting lids for storage 👩‍🍳 Step-by-step preparation # Preparation # Wash and thoroughly peel the papayas. Tip: Green papaya can release a sticky, whitish latex when peeled. If you have sensitive skin, wearing gloves can make handling it more comfortable.
Cut the papayas lengthwise and remove the seeds. Cut the firm flesh into roughly 2 to 3 cm cubes, or into strips or slices of a similar thickness. Try to keep the pieces roughly the same size so they cook evenly. Place the papaya pieces in a large bowl and cover them completely with water. Stir in 2 tablespoons of baking soda and let the papaya soak for about 1 hour. Drain, then rinse the pieces several times thoroughly with clean water. Cooking # Prepare the syrup: Put the sugar and about 2 liters of water into a large pot. Heat gently until the sugar has dissolved.
Add the papaya: Carefully place the rinsed papaya pieces into the syrup. If you are using cinnamon, cloves or citrus peel, add them now.
Cook slowly: Let everything simmer gently over low heat. Depending on the ripeness and size of the pieces, the papaya will need about 2 to 4 hours.
Move the pieces as little as possible: Do not stir constantly. Move the papaya only when necessary and do so gently to keep the pieces from breaking apart.
Watch the liquid: If the papaya is still firm but too much liquid has evaporated, add a little hot water and continue cooking.
Check for doneness: The Dulce de Mamón is ready when the pieces have turned increasingly golden and slightly translucent, while the syrup has thickened noticeably but is still pourable.
Adjust the flavor: Add vanilla, a few drops of lemon juice or other delicate flavors near the end of the cooking time.
Let it cool: Remove the pot from the heat. The syrup will thicken a little more as it cools.
Once completely cool, transfer the Dulce de Mamón to clean jars with tight-fitting lids and store it in the refrigerator. It is best eaten soon after making it. In our house, that is rarely a problem because it usually disappears quickly.
💡 Practical tips for Dulce de Mamón # Tips for a good result Choose the right papaya: The fruit should be full-sized, firm and still mostly green. Inside, the flesh should be pale to whitish and noticeably firmer than that of a ripe papaya.
Avoid very ripe fruit: Once the skin starts turning yellow or orange, the fruit becomes fragrant and gives noticeably when pressed. At that stage, the pieces are much more likely to fall apart during the long cooking time.
Adjust the sweetness: This recipe uses 1.5 kg sugar for 2 kg papaya. If Paraguayan sweets are too sweet for your taste, you can reduce the sugar somewhat. The resulting syrup will be lighter and less concentrated.
Cook patiently: Low heat matters more than shortening the cooking time. The papaya should soften while still keeping its shape.
Do not reduce the syrup too far: It continues to thicken as it cools. Take the pot off the heat while the syrup is still easy to pour.
Nutritional overview # The figures below are a very rough estimate per 100 g of Dulce de Mamón, roughly a small dessert serving.
Calories: approx. 280 kcal Protein: approx. 0.5 g Carbohydrates: approx. 68 g Fat: approx. 0.1 g Fiber: approx. 1.5 g These values are only estimates. They can vary considerably depending on the amount of sugar, the ripeness of the papaya, cooking time and the final cooked weight.
🍽️ What goes well with Dulce de Mamón? # A particularly typical pairing in Paraguay combines the sweet syrup with a mild, lightly salted cheese.
Sides Drinks Classic: A slice of Queso Paraguay is probably the most typical accompaniment. The sweet mamón and mild, lightly salted cheese complement each other especially well. If Queso Paraguay is not available, a mild queso fresco or another mild, not overly salty cheese works well.
Lighter: Plain yogurt adds a little acidity and freshness to balance the rich syrup.
Creamy: A small serving of Dulce de Mamón also works well with vanilla ice cream or a little unsweetened cream.
Paraguayan: Cocido, a warm yerba mate drink, pairs well with a small serving of Dulce de Mamón, especially at merienda time.
Strong: Black coffee provides a pleasant contrast to the sweetness.
Simple: With a particularly sweet Dulce, a glass of cold water is often all you need.
🔄 Variations of the recipe # Like many Paraguayan recipes, Dulce de Mamón varies from family to family. Recipes differ in how the fruit is prepared, the amount of sugar used and the flavors added.
Known variations # Dulce de Mamón rallado with Miel de Caña: In this traditional variation, the peeled mamón is coarsely grated and then cooked with Miel de Caña (sugarcane syrup). Rather than large fruit pieces, the result is a softer, darker mixture with the stronger flavor of sugarcane syrup.
With a citrus note: Some recipes add lemon slices or a little citrus peel during cooking. The light acidity creates a fresh contrast to the intense sweetness.
Modern variations # Dulce de Mamón can also be used as part of other desserts. Small pieces work well as a topping for cheesecake.
For guests, I like to serve Dulce de Mamón in small glasses with plain yogurt. It takes the edge off the sweetness and is easy to prepare ahead. Toasted nuts on top add a little extra crunch.

Go to the Telegram channel → 🇵🇾 Background on Dulce de Mamón # Name and spellings # Mamón is the common Spanish name for papaya in Paraguay. In Guaraní, the form mamóne is also used. It was borrowed from the Spanish word mamón.
The name Dulce de Mamón, also often written Dulce de Mamon without the accent, therefore refers to this dessert made from mamón, or papaya.
What makes Dulce de Mamón special? # This version of Dulce de Mamón uses a full-sized papaya that is still firm, green and unripe. That is an important difference from preparations made with fully ripe, soft papaya.
As the fruit cooks slowly, it absorbs the sugar syrup, changes color and becomes increasingly translucent. At the same time, the individual pieces should keep their shape.
The result falls somewhere between cooked fruit and jam: the papaya remains clearly recognizable as pieces of fruit and is served together with its syrup.
What role does Dulce de Mamón play in Paraguay? # Dulce de Mamón is one of Paraguay’s well-known traditional sweets. It is served as a dessert or at merienda time and appears both in family recipes and in traditional Paraguayan cuisine.
As with many traditional recipes, there is no single fixed method. Some families use food-grade calcium hydroxide, others use baking soda, while some use neither. Recipes also vary in the amount of sugar, how ripe the papaya is, the size and shape of the pieces, and the spices used.
One particularly typical pairing is Queso Paraguay. Its mild, lightly salty flavor balances the rich sweetness of the syrup. The same contrast between sweet and salty appears in other Paraguayan desserts as well.
❓ Frequently asked questions # What kind of papaya should I use for Dulce de Mamón? A full-sized papaya that is still firm and green works best for this recipe. The skin should remain mostly green and the fruit should barely give when pressed. Inside, the flesh should still be pale to whitish and firm.
A soft, ripe papaya with yellow or orange skin is much more likely to fall apart during the long cooking time. It is therefore less suitable when you want distinct pieces of papaya in syrup.
Do I need baking soda or food-grade calcium hydroxide? No. There are several traditional methods. Some use food-grade calcium hydroxide, others use baking soda, and some recipes use neither.
This recipe uses baking soda to help the papaya pieces keep their shape during the long cooking time.
If you want to try the traditional calcium-hydroxide method, use only food-grade calcium hydroxide (E526), also known as slaked lime or cal apagada apta para alimentos. Do not use calcium oxide, quicklime, cal viva or cal virgen, and never use a product that is not explicitly suitable for food.
How do I keep the papaya pieces from falling apart? Start with a firm green papaya and cut the pieces as evenly as possible. Rinse them thoroughly after the baking-soda soak, then cook them only over low heat.
Avoid unnecessary stirring. If you need to move the pieces, do so gently so they do not break apart.
How do I know when Dulce de Mamón is done? The papaya pieces gradually become golden and slightly translucent. They should be soft enough to eat while still holding their shape.
The syrup should be noticeably thicker but still pourable. Remember that it thickens further as it cools, so do not reduce it to a very thick consistency while it is still in the pot.
What if the papaya is still firm or the syrup is too thin? If the papaya is still too firm but there is very little liquid left in the pot, add a little hot water and continue cooking gently.
If the papaya is already done but the syrup is still too thin, carefully remove the fruit pieces and let only the syrup reduce a little longer. This helps prevent the finished papaya from falling apart.
How should I store Dulce de Mamón? Let the Dulce de Mamón cool completely, transfer it to clean jars with tight-fitting lids and keep it in the refrigerator. It is best eaten soon after making it.
Discard the entire contents if you notice mold, a fermented smell, bubbling or other unusual changes.
Without a tested canning process, the exact shelf life of a homemade batch cannot be stated reliably. Do not assume that the high sugar content alone makes it safe to store for several months.
Conclusion # Dulce de Mamón is a simple recipe, but it does take a little patience. The slow cooking is part of what makes it special: the firm green papaya gradually turns into golden, sweet pieces of fruit surrounded by syrup.
If you have green papayas to use up or simply want to try a traditional Paraguayan sweet, Dulce de Mamón is a lovely recipe for a quiet afternoon in the kitchen. And I think it is worth trying at least once with a piece of Queso Paraguay on the side.
If you want to see how a similar idea works with a different ingredient, have a look at Dulce de Calabaza. Instead of green papaya, it uses pumpkin. The preparation follows a similar principle, but the finished dessert tastes quite different.
You can find more traditional sweets among our Paraguayan desserts.
Have fun making it and “buen provecho”!

Give the post a like and share it with other South America enthusiasts. That helps make Paraguay’s food and everyday culture more visible.
summary: Dulce de Mamón is a traditional Paraguayan dessert made by slowly cooking firm green papaya in sugar syrup.

Clericó is one of those drinks you see on many tables in Paraguay, especially around Christmas and New Year. That fits December here: while winter dishes and mulled wine are common elsewhere, Paraguay is in the middle of summer. A well-chilled Clericó with fresh fruit feels just right.
Clericó is a chilled Paraguayan drink with chopped fresh fruit and a base of sidra, wine, or juice. In English, it can be described as both a fruit punch and a fruity cocktail.
The recipe itself is simple and leaves plenty of room for variation. For this version, I use sidra, an alcoholic, usually sparkling drink that is especially easy to find here around the end of the year. Four fresh fruits, a little citrus juice, and ice complete the mix.
📝 Clericó Recipe: Step by Step # At a glance Difficulty: Easy Prep time: about 20 minutes Resting time: about 20 to 30 minutes Servings: about 6 large or 8 smaller glasses
Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 🛒 Ingredients for Clericó # For this basic Clericó recipe, four types of fruit are enough. This keeps the mix fruity without letting all the individual flavors disappear into one another.
Main ingredients # 1 bottle well-chilled sidra, about 900 ml ½ small pineapple, about 250 g fruit 1 medium apple about 250 g melon 150 g grapes Juice of ½ lemon or lime 1 to 2 tbsp sugar, only if needed plenty of ice cubes Optional ingredients # You can replace individual fruits from the basic recipe. Good options include:
Banana Peach Orange Pear Banana is quite common in Paraguayan Clericó recipes. It makes the mixture sweeter and softer, but it also turns brown and mushy more quickly. That is why I prefer to list it as an alternative rather than use it in the basic version.
What can you substitute? # Ingredient alternatives and practical adjustments Other alcoholic bases: Instead of sidra, you can use white wine, rosé, red wine, or sparkling wine. The sweeter the base, the less extra sugar you will need.
Alcohol-free: Replace the sidra with the same amount of grape juice. If that is too sweet for you, replace part of the juice with mineral water.
Swap the fruit: Melon can be replaced with peach or banana. Instead of grapes, you can use more apple or peach.
Less sweet: Use more apple and citrus fruit, and leave out the extra sugar at first.
Kitchen equipment # You do not need any special equipment for Clericó:
Cutting board Sharp knife Large bowl or punch bowl Wide-mouth pitcher or jug Spoon for gentle stirring Refrigerator Glasses for serving A bowl or wide-mouth jug is especially practical. It makes it easier to add and stir the fruit and later serve some of the pieces with the Clericó.
👩‍🍳 Step-by-step preparation # Preparation # Peel the pineapple and remove the hard core. Wash the apple and remove the core. Prepare the melon and remove the seeds. Wash the grapes well. You can cut large grapes in half. Cut all the fruit into small, easy-to-eat pieces. Keep the sidra chilled until you are ready to serve. Mixing the Clericó # Place the chopped fruit in a large bowl or wide-mouth jug.
Drizzle with lemon or lime juice. If the fruit is not very sweet, add one tablespoon of sugar to start. Mix gently.
Let the fruit rest in the refrigerator for about 20 to 30 minutes. Some fruit juice will already collect during this time.
Pour in the well-chilled sidra and stir gently.
Add the ice shortly before serving, or put the ice cubes directly into the glasses. This keeps the Clericó from becoming unnecessarily watered down.
Serve some liquid and several pieces of fruit in each glass. A small spoon is useful because the fruit is meant to be eaten as part of the Clericó.
💡 Practical tips for Clericó # How to get the best result Less can be more with fruit: Four well-chosen fruits are enough. Ripe fruit and a good balance of sweet, fresh, and juicy flavors matter more than a long ingredient list.
Chill the sidra well: The colder the fruit and sidra are before serving, the less ice you will need.
Be careful with sugar: Many sidras and ripe fruits are already quite sweet. Start with little or no extra sugar.
Add soft fruit later: Banana and very ripe peach break down more quickly. Add them as late as possible and stir gently.
Keep the fruit-to-liquid ratio balanced: The fruit pieces are an important part of Clericó. If you add too much sidra or wine, the fruit can easily get lost in the drink.
Best served fresh: Clericó is at its best when the fruit still has some bite and everything is well chilled. There is no need to prepare it many hours in advance.
Nutrition information # Based on six generous servings, the basic recipe contains approximately:
Calories: about 160 kcal Protein: about 1 g Carbohydrates: about 25 g Fat: about 0 g Fiber: about 2 g These values are estimates. The type of sidra, the fruit, and any added sugar can change the nutritional values considerably.
🍽️ What Goes Well with Clericó? # In Paraguay, Clericó is not usually paired with one specific dish in the way you might pair wine with a meal. It is more often part of the whole gathering, especially around Christmas and New Year.
A few combinations have a particularly strong connection to Paraguay:
Serve it with Why it works Pan dulce Clericó and pan dulce have a historical connection to year-end hospitality. Both were offered to visitors together. Sopa Paraguaya This savory corn bread is another classic on Paraguayan Christmas and holiday tables. Chipa Guasu The soft corn casserole is common at family gatherings and year-end celebrations and gives a savory contrast to the fruity Clericó. When I serve an alcoholic version, I also put cold water or mineral water on the table. On hot December days, that is a good idea anyway.
🔄 Variations of the Recipe # Like many Paraguayan recipes, Clericó is prepared a little differently from family to family. The fruit and liquid often depend on what is available and what the guests enjoy.
Common variations # With red wine: A fuller version with an interesting historical connection. In the past, kleriko in Paraguay was also prepared with red wine.
With white wine: A fresh option that can be drier than sidra, depending on the wine you use.
With rosé or sparkling wine: A lighter, festive variation that also works well with fresh fruit.
Alcohol-free Clericó: Grape juice replaces the alcoholic base. This version is suitable for children and anyone who does not want alcohol.
Modern variations # For a lighter version, replace part of the liquid with cold mineral water. Fresh mint or a little extra lime can add even more freshness.
Even with modern variations, I would not add too many extras. The fruit should stay at the center of the drink.

You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → 🇵🇾 Background and Tradition # Name and spelling # On menus and in recipes, you will usually see the spelling Clericó. In Paraguay, you may also come across Clerico without the accent and kleriko. All three names refer to the same fruity drink.
What makes Clericó special? # Clericó does not have one fixed recipe. You can see that in the many different versions prepared by Paraguayan families. Whatever is available may end up in the jug. Sometimes it is banana and melon, sometimes apple, grapes, pineapple, or peach. Wine and sidra are both common alcoholic bases.
That flexibility makes Clericó easy to adapt. What matters most is ripe fruit, good chilling, and a balance where neither the fruit nor the liquid takes over completely.
And just like a classic fruit punch, the fruit pieces are an important part of Clericó. They go into the glass and are eaten too. So the little fruit snack comes included. 🙂
What role does Clericó play in Paraguay? # Clericó is especially closely connected with Christmas and the end of the year in Paraguay. That also fits the climate in Paraguay, because Christmas falls right in the middle of summer here. A cold drink with fresh fruit feels much more natural at 30°C (86°F) and above than a winter-style holiday drink.
If you go shopping in Paraguay in December, you will notice the connection quickly. Sidra is stacked in many supermarkets. Nearby you will find pan dulce and the ingredients needed for Sopa Paraguaya, Chipa Guasu, and the big year-end meals.
There is a reason for that. Christmas (Navidad) and the year-end celebrations are, along with Semana Santa, some of the most important times for large family gatherings in Paraguay. Especially on Nochebuena (Christmas Eve) and around Año Nuevo (New Year), extended families often come together. People spend long hours, and sometimes several days, celebrating, eating, drinking, and simply being together. Asado, Sopa Paraguaya, Chipa Guasu, pan dulce, and Clericó are all part of this season for many families.
You can find more about these and other important dates in our guide to holidays in Paraguay.
Kambuchi, kleriko, and a jug by the front door # While researching this article, I came across an old Paraguayan tradition that I especially liked.
The Paraguayan Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare ↗ describes how kleriko used to be prepared with red wine in a kambuchi, a traditional clay jug. When visitors were expected, the jug could even be kept near the entrance of the house. Guests were welcomed with a glass of kleriko, together with pan dulce or other sweets.
The drink was therefore not just a way to cool down. It was also part of year-end hospitality.
Whether a kambuchi is still waiting beside someone’s front door today is probably the exception. Clericó itself, however, has kept its place around Christmas and New Year.
❓ Frequently Asked Questions # Is Clericó a cocktail or a fruit punch? Both descriptions can fit. Clericó is a chilled drink made with chopped fresh fruit and a base such as sidra, wine, or juice. In the way it is prepared and served, it is similar to a classic fruit punch, while alcoholic versions are also often described as a fruity cocktail. What really defines Clericó is the fruit itself: the pieces are served in the glass and eaten along with the drink. Can Clericó be made alcohol-free and served to children? Yes. For children and anyone who does not want alcohol, replace the sidra completely with grape juice. If the mixture is too sweet, replace part of the juice with cold mineral water.
The regular sidra used in this recipe contains alcohol and is therefore not suitable for children.
What fruit is best for Clericó? Pineapple, melon, apple, and grapes work very well together. Banana, orange, and peach are also common choices in Paraguay. Four different fruits are usually enough for a balanced mixture. Do I have to use sidra in Clericó? No. This recipe uses sidra, but red wine, white wine, rosé, and sparkling wine are also possible. Each base changes the sweetness and flavor.
Sidra is an alcoholic, usually sparkling drink that is especially common in Paraguay around Christmas and New Year.
How far in advance can I prepare Clericó? You can cut the fruit about 30 minutes in advance and keep it chilled. I would add the sidra after the fruit has rested. This keeps both the fruit and the drink fresher. Preparing it many hours ahead is less ideal, especially when you use soft fruit. Can I leave out the sugar? Yes. With ripe fruit and a sweet sidra, extra sugar is often not necessary at all. Start without it or use only a small amount and adjust if needed. Can I drink Clericó the next day? Clericó tastes best when it is fresh. Put leftovers back in the refrigerator as soon as possible. By the next day, many fruits will be noticeably softer and the mixture will lose some of its freshness.
If the Clericó has been left out in the heat for a long time, do not keep the leftovers.
Conclusion # Clericó is simple, fruity, and just right for the hot days around the end of the year in Paraguay. At the same time, there is more tradition behind a jug full of fruit than you might expect at first.
The old story of the kambuchi by the front door, a glass of kleriko for visitors, and a piece of pan dulce alongside it shows how closely food, drinks, and hospitality have long been connected here.
If you are looking for another fresh recipe for a hot day, try Tropical Ceviche with mango and lime next. You can find more ideas among our Paraguayan drinks.
Have fun making it, and “buen provecho”!
Share & support Does this make you want to try Clericó yourself? Then give the post a like or share it with someone who might also enjoy this fruity Paraguayan drink. That helps make recipes and stories from Paraguay more visible.
summary: Clericó is a Paraguayan favorite at Christmas and New Year: fruity, chilled, and easy to make.

Quick Facts # Quick facts at a glance Calendar date: March 1; movable public holiday (feriado movible). In 2026, the day off was moved to Monday, March 2. Status: statutory national public holiday in Paraguay Who celebrates: nationwide, especially visible among the state, the military, schools, and families interested in history Why: remembrance of Paraguay’s “heroes” and of the end of the devastating War of the Triple Alliance Peak: often around official ceremonies, depending on the place more likely in the morning and around central squares Bottom line: you will usually notice a quieter atmosphere, less government office activity, and depending on the area more flags and ceremonies 🧭 What is Día de los Héroes? # Heroes’ Day, known locally as “Día de los Héroes", is one of the most important national commemorative days in Paraguay. It is less of a “party holiday” and more of a day when history and national identity become visible. Many people associate it with respect, pride, and also grief, depending on how the past is talked about within the family.
In everyday life, the day often feels like this: fewer “errands”, more “remembrance”. In Asunción, this is especially noticeable around central squares and public buildings. There are more official moments there, sometimes short-notice notices or barriers, and overall the atmosphere is a bit quieter than on normal weekdays.
If you are new to the country: this holiday helps you get a sense of how present history can be in everyday life in Paraguay, even without celebrations happening everywhere.
Historical Background # The day commemorates the end of the War of the Triple Alliance (1864 to 1870), one of the most devastating conflicts in South American history. Paraguay faced an alliance of Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay. The causes were political tensions in the region, questions of power, and military decisions under President Mariscal Francisco Solano López.
What began as a regional conflict developed into a years-long war with enormous consequences for Paraguay. The country lost a large part of its male population, many towns and villages were destroyed, and the economy was left in ruins. Paraguay then had to reorganize itself with great difficulty, also territorially, because the country lost land to Brazil and Argentina. The war ended on March 1, 1870 with the death of López at Cerro Corá in the north of the country. With him, military resistance finally collapsed.
In official remembrance, this moment is considered a historical turning point. Paraguay lost the war, but the narrative in Paraguay often emphasizes perseverance, sacrifice, and national self-assertion. That is exactly why March 1 is not a classic day of victory or triumph, but a day of remembrance.
What often still resonates in daily life is also the view of the time afterward: because so many men were missing, women played a major role in rebuilding many families and communities. Their role is still especially honored today on Día de la Mujer Paraguaya .
What I notice again and again in conversations with locals here: many people do not speak only about “a battle”, but about a period that is still told today as a collective experience. You quickly hear sentences like “that shaped us” or “you don’t forget that”. In family stories especially, the war still appears as a point of reference, even though there are of course no direct eyewitnesses anymore.
🪅 Perception in Society & Traditions # For many Paraguayans, the holiday is emotional because it is associated with sacrifice, perseverance, and the feeling that the country endured despite everything. At the same time, history is not told the same way everywhere. In some families it is spoken about with great reverence, in others more soberly, and that often depends on generation, region, and personal background.
The day is most noticeably felt where the state and schools are visible.
Official ceremonies such as wreath-laying or short remembrance moments often take place at symbolic locations, in Asunción for example around central squares and monuments.
In schools, the day is addressed depending on the institution, sometimes with short presentations, historical context in class, or a small ceremony. This does not always happen exactly on the holiday itself, but often in the period around it.
Symbolism is usually rather restrained: cockades, ribbons, or flowers at remembrance sites, sometimes uniforms at official appearances, and occasionally patriotic music or the national anthem as part of ceremonies.
Typical Food & Drinks on This Day # Día de los Héroes does not have a “must-have dish” like some religious holidays do. More often, it comes down to what Paraguay does really well on days off: time with family, sharing food, Tereré, and depending on the mood maybe also a relaxed barbecue evening.
If you are invited, you will often be offered:
Asado or something hearty from the grill, depending on the family either very simple or on a bigger scale. Chipa, Sopa Paraguaya, Chipa Guasu or Mbejú as a snack or side dish. Tereré almost always, especially on warm days. Tip As a small gift, things you can share almost always work well: ice cream, drinks, or something sweet. If you know their preferences, yerba is also a good idea.
🧩 What Does It Mean Practically in Everyday Life? # Opening Hours & Services # Día de los Héroes is a nationwide statutory public holiday. Differences mainly concern the opening hours of shops and private services. Typically:
Public offices, banks, post offices: generally closed. Supermarkets, shopping centers: often open, but sometimes with reduced staff or different opening hours. Despensas and small shops: may open depending on the location and owner. Pharmacies, gas stations, restaurants: often available, although this varies by city and location. Markets: may operate normally or with reduced activity, depending on the place and market. Planning note: if you depend on a specific errand getting done (bank, public office, parcel), plan as if it were a Sunday. Then you will rarely be completely wrong.
Traffic & Travel # Traffic is often split into two patterns:
In cities, around official places, things can run differently for a while (road closures, detours, more police). On roads out of town, depending on whether it becomes a long weekend, there can be more excursion traffic. For travel, the rule is: buses and taxis do run, but the rhythm and availability can feel different on public holidays. If you are going farther out, it is wise to plan connections and arrival logistics a bit more generously.
Schools, Work, Government Offices # Schools There are generally no regular classes on the statutory public holiday. Private companies handle it differently, depending on the sector and location. Government office operations are generally heavily limited. My everyday tip from Paraguay: if a holiday looks like “just one day” on paper, in practice it is often used as a reason for a family gathering. You notice this in spontaneous meetups, visit rounds, and in the fact that some people simply are not reachable.
Where in Paraguay Is It Especially Relevant? # The holiday is nationwide, but it is often especially noticeable where there are central symbols, more public visibility, or a stronger presence of institutions.
Asunción: more visible symbolism, often around central squares and national buildings. Places with a strong military or government connection: sometimes more ceremonies, more flags, more official presence. City vs. countryside: in the countryside it can be quieter, but family time is even more dominant there. In cities you are more likely to see “the official side”. What kinds of events are typical?
remembrance ceremony, wreath-laying, short parade elements, cultural program points, sometimes folklore. Where do people look for announcements?
official (social) channels of the Municipalidad, local radio stations, churches, sometimes tourism offices or notices. Ask in the neighborhood or in local groups in the community / city. 🤝 Joining in as a Visitor: Do’s & Don’ts # ✅ Do’s # Behave respectfully: at remembrance sites, quiet and restrained behavior feels most appropriate. For many people, Día de los Héroes is less a “holiday” and more a day of respect and remembrance. Clothing: for official places or church, rather covered and neat, especially if you want to take photos. Show interest: a simple “I’m still learning, tell me more” often opens doors. ⛔ Don’ts # No loud jokes or “political hot takes” - for many people, the topic is personal. Better take photos of uniformed people or official proceedings only if it is clearly public and the situation allows it. Alcohol is not “forbidden”, but at remembrance sites it can quickly seem out of place. ⚠ In larger crowds, the standard rules apply: keep your bag close to your body, do not let your phone dangle openly in your hand, bring enough water, and take the sun seriously.
💬 Cheat Sheet: Useful Phrases for Getting Around # Spanish 🇪🇸 # “Feliz Día de los Héroes.” English: “Happy Heroes’ Day."
“Hoy se conmemora el Día de los Héroes en Paraguay.” English: “Today Heroes’ Day is commemorated in Paraguay."
Guaraní 🇵🇾 # “Ko árape ñanemomandu’a ñande héroe kuéra rehe.” English: “Today we remember our heroes." 🗓️ Tips & Planning # Shopping: if you depend on specific products, take care of it beforehand. Fresh items and specialty products in particular are not equally available everywhere on a public holiday. Cash: having a bit of cash in reserve never hurts, in case the bank or certain services are not operating as usual. Fuel: gas stations are usually open, but if many people are on the road, they can feel busier than normal. Appointments: it is best not to schedule public office visits and paperwork for this period, even if individual places might theoretically be open. Invitations: if you are invited, mentally plan for “Paraguay time”. People often do not arrive exactly on the minute, but they stay longer. Excursions: if you want a quiet outing, the early hours are often more pleasant. Later on, there is usually more movement, especially when many people use the day off for family visits. You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → ❓ Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) # Is Día de los Héroes an official public holiday? Yes. Día de los Héroes is a nationwide statutory public holiday and is one of Paraguay’s movable public holidays (feriados movibles). In 2026, the holiday was moved from March 1 to Monday, March 2. Are supermarkets and shopping centers open? Often yes, but usually in holiday mode. Small shops in residential areas can even be especially reliable depending on the place. Should I expect road closures? Sometimes, especially around central squares or remembrance sites. In normal residential neighborhoods, things often stay fairly quiet. Do buses and taxis run normally? Mostly yes, but the schedule can feel different. Plan a bit of buffer time, especially if you need connections. Are schools closed? Often yes, or they operate without regular classes. Some schools hold short program points around the day instead of normal lessons. What is the right way to greet someone? Many people simply say “Feliz Día de los Héroes”. If you are unsure, a respectful comment such as “Que tengan un buen día” is also enough. Are there typical events you can attend? There are often official ceremonies and cultural contributions, but they vary a lot depending on the place. The best way is to check the Municipalidad, local radio stations, or community pages. What happens if March 1 falls on a weekend? The holiday is not moved automatically. Since Día de los Héroes is one of Paraguay’s movable public holidays (feriados movibles), the government may move it by decree to the Monday before or after the original date. Without such a decree, it remains on March 1. In 2026, the holiday was moved to Monday, March 2. Conclusion # Día de los Héroes in Paraguay is not an “event holiday”, but a day when history becomes visible. For expats and newcomers, it is a good moment to understand Paraguay better: what is closed is one side of it. More important is often the atmosphere behind it, meaning respect, remembrance, and the sense that the past remains part of how the country understands itself today.
If you experience it quietly and attentively, you can learn a great deal about culture, communication, and everyday life here in a single day.
