You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → ❓ Frequently asked questions (FAQ) # What’s the difference between Valentine’s Day and “Día de los Enamorados” in Paraguay? In Paraguay, Valentine’s Day is often celebrated as “Día de los Enamorados”-the “Day of the Lovers.” The idea is very similar, but usually more relaxed and sociable: besides couples, friends celebrate too; there are small gestures, shared meals, sometimes school activities, and lots of “love goes through the stomach” vibes. For a menu at home, that means: lighter, summer-friendly, communal-better a relaxed meal than a stiff fine-dining affair. Which dishes work best for a date menu in intense heat? When it’s hot, a menu works best if it’s light, fresh, and not too fatty:
Ceviche (or similar citrus fish dishes): refreshing, quick, perfect as a starter Salads & fruity components (e.g., mango/pineapple, lime, fresh herbs) Grilled dishes instead of heavy braises (short cooking time, less “kitchen heat”) Dessert in glasses (easy to chill, portionable, looks chic) Clericó (also possible alcohol-free): ideal for a summer toast Tip: Plan so you spend max. 20–30 minutes actively at the stove-the rest is prepped or chilling in the fridge. Can I make Clericó alcohol-free? Yes-this works great. For an alcohol-free version you just need a base that’s fruity and not too sweet:
Grape juice + sparkling water (or tonic/ginger ale depending on taste) Alcohol-free white “wine-style” (if available) + sparkling Cold hibiscus/fruit tea (brewed strong, cooled) + sparkling Important: add fruit shortly before serving so it stays fresh. Balance with lime/lemon-that’s what makes it feel “grown-up.” What alternatives work if I can’t get certain ingredients? That’s completely normal in Europe/outside Paraguay-here are some substitutions that work well:
Fish (e.g., surubí) → mild white fillet: catfish, cod, pollock, pangasius (if you like it), pike-perch Queso Paraguay → a young, mild cheese that melts well: mozzarella (firmer), young gouda, mild fresh cheese; for a “squeaky” texture: halloumi (sparingly) Dulce de Mamón (sweet papaya) → papaya jam, mild mango chutney, or apricot/peach jam; then perhaps serve a small cheese plate alongside Cassava starch / almidón de mandioca → tapioca starch (very close), or potato starch (texture slightly different) Dulce de leche / milk caramel → caramel cream / toffee spread Locote / mild pepper-chiles → pointed sweet pepper + optionally a hint of chili Can I prep anything the night before? A lot-and that’s exactly what makes a menu relaxed. Here are the best “prep-ahead” building blocks:
Starters / fresh dishes
Ceviche & co.: prep the marinade (lime/lemon, onion, spices). Marinate and finish the fish shortly before serving-otherwise it becomes too “cooked.” Doughs / mixtures
For mbejú/sopa paraguaya/chipa guasu: weigh dry ingredients, grate cheese, pre-chop onions. For many batters it even works to prep the full mixture, cover, chill, and bake/fry the next day. Desserts
Dessert in glasses: make completely the day before and keep in the fridge (often looks even better the next day). Fruity components: chop, chill, and if needed, use lime to prevent browning. Drinks
Clericó: wash/chop fruit and chill; chill the base (juice/wine/alcohol-free). Mix and add sparkling right before serving. General
Set the table/décor the day before, get serving plates ready, and make the fridge “service-ready.” Then on Valentine’s night you only need to: finish + plate + enjoy. Which dishes are naturally vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free or lactose-free-and how can I adapt them? Here’s a quick guide to the dishes in this menu-without claiming medical guarantees, but practical for the kitchen. For details (e.g., ingredient lists, suitable alternatives), it’s best to check the individual recipes.
Often naturally gluten-free (with classic ingredients) # Many Paraguayan dishes are based on corn and cassava rather than wheat. In this menu, the following are therefore often gluten-free (or easy to keep gluten-free):
Mbejú / Mbejú Relleno (cassava starch) Chipa Guasu (corn) Sopa Paraguaya (corn) Alfajores de Maicena (cornstarch) Watch-outs (gluten traps): mixed flours, breadcrumbs, ready-made spice mixes, baking powder/binders, and some cheese products can contain additives. When in doubt, quickly check the ingredient list.
Vegetarian: what works “as is,” and what’s easy to adapt? # Naturally vegetarian (classic versions):
Chipa Guasu Sopa Paraguaya Pasta Frola de Guayaba (classically vegetarian) Alfajores de Maicena Mousse de Maracuyá (usually vegetarian) Vegetarian, easy to do:
Mbejú Relleno: choose a vegetarian filling (e.g., cheese, vegetables) Crepes de Verdura: already the vegetarian option in the menu Vegan: rarely “as is,” but doable # For many classics, eggs, milk, or cheese are part of the standard recipe. If you want to cook vegan:
Milk/cream → plant milk / plant cream Butter/lard → vegetable oil Cheese → vegan shredded cheese (texture differs) or build flavor with nutritional yeast + salt + a bit of acidity Result: not 1:1 traditional, but often very tasty. Easiest vegan option in this menu: a salad or a vegan vegetable version (e.g., “chupín-style” without fish, with potatoes/tomatoes/vegetables).
Lactose-free: usually quite doable # Many components can be made lactose-free quite well:
Cream/milk → lactose-free versions Cheese → lactose-free cheese or (with aged cheeses) often naturally very low in lactose-though not always guaranteed Note: Dishes like Surubí a la Crema, chupín (with cheese), and Dulce de Mamón with Queso Paraguay are clearly dairy-heavy in the standard version, but can be adapted easily with lactose-free products.
What is a “Desayuno Sorpresa”-and how do I put one together quickly? A “Desayuno Sorpresa” is a surprise breakfast (often as a basket/box)-perfect if you can’t manage a big dinner, or as an add-on the next morning. Quick setup:
1–2 sweet components (fruit, pastries, jam/honey) 1 savory component (sandwich, cheese, savory pastry) drink (coffee/tea/juice-or a mini alcohol-free clericó) a small card/note + possibly a flower / cuddly toy or picture frame Tip: With a Paraguayan touch (e.g., tereré vibes, local fruit, ñandutí décor) it feels extra special. What décor feels Paraguayan without being kitschy? Subtle is best here:
Ñandutí as a small accent (coaster, ribbon, detail in the napkin fold) natural materials: wooden board, ceramics, linen napkins one or two colors, e.g., warm white + an accent (red/coral/green) local flowers or a “garden bouquet” look instead of rose overload That way it feels authentic and still romantic. Summary # Valentine’s Day in Paraguay is a celebration of the senses. Whether it’s traditional Mbejú, a refined surubí dish, Sopa Paraguaya, or the sweet temptation of a pasta frola: food here is a universal language of love. The blend of indigenous heritage, colonial influences, and modern fusion cuisine makes “Día de los Enamorados” a culinary experience that radiates warmth and joie de vivre.
¡Feliz Día de los Enamorados y “buen provecho”!
Want to give your Valentine’s evening a Paraguayan touch without cooking a whole menu? Start with a well-chilled Clericó. For more on how the Día de los Enamorados in Paraguay is celebrated, see our Valentine’s Day overview.
Share & support Did this traditional Valentine’s menu 🇵🇾❤️ inspire you and spark your curiosity about Paraguay? Then feel free to give the post a like and share it with other South America enthusiasts-helping make Paraguay’s culinary diversity more visible.

title: Valentine's Day in Paraguay: Romantic Recipe Ideas for Two

content:
Mazamorra, known in Guaraní as Kaguyjy, is a traditional Paraguayan dessert made with locro, a dried white corn. As it cooks slowly, the kernels soften and the dessert develops its creamy texture.
When I first tried Mazamorra, my first thought was: “A little like rice pudding – just with corn.” The comparison only goes so far, though. The soft corn kernels remain clearly noticeable and give the dessert its own distinctive texture.
In conversations with Paraguayans, you also notice that for many people Mazamorra is closely connected with childhood, family, and familiar everyday cooking.
This Mazamorra recipe follows a modern Paraguayan preparation with baking soda, milk, and sugar. The base is only mildly sweet, so you can adjust the sweetness later to your taste.
📝 Mazamorra Recipe: Step by Step # At a glance Difficulty: Easy Total time: about 2 hours plus soaking time Soaking time: 8–12 hours Servings: about 8 dessert servings Suitable for: vegetarian, naturally gluten-free Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 🛒 Ingredients for Mazamorra # Main ingredients # 500 g locro (dried white corn) about 3 liters water, plus more if needed ½ tsp baking soda (bicarbonato de sodio) 1 liter whole milk 150 g sugar Optional ingredients # 1 cinnamon stick a little peel from an unwaxed orange or lemon a small splash of vanilla extract after cooking What can you substitute? # Ingredient substitutions Locro: Outside Paraguay, you can usually find dried white corn at Latin American grocery stores or online, often labeled maíz blanco para locro. Popcorn kernels are not suitable.
Hominy: Canned hominy is a quick alternative. It needs much less cooking time, although the final texture will be somewhat different.
Milk: For a vegan version, use unsweetened oat, almond, or coconut milk.
Sweetener: Miel de caña works especially well for adding extra sweetness at the table. You can also use honey, although it has a noticeably different flavor.
Dietary notes: Mazamorra is vegetarian and naturally gluten-free. With plant-based milk and without honey, it can also be made vegan.
Kitchen equipment # large pot, preferably heavy-bottomed large bowl for soaking colander wooden spoon 👩‍🍳 Step-by-step preparation # Preparation # Rinse the locro thoroughly and soak it in plenty of water for 8 to 12 hours, preferably overnight. In warm weather, keep the corn in the refrigerator while it soaks.
The next day, drain the soaking water and rinse the corn again.
Cooking # Start the locro: Put the soaked corn in a large pot with about 3 liters of fresh water. If you are using a cinnamon stick or citrus peel, add it now.
Cook slowly: Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to medium-low and let it simmer. Stir regularly so nothing sticks to the bottom.
Add the baking soda: About halfway through the cooking time, stir in the baking soda. In modern recipes, it takes the place of the filtered wood-ash lye used in older preparations and contributes to the typical color and texture.
Watch the liquid: The locro should always have enough liquid while cooking. If it starts to dry out, add hot water little by little.
Cook until almost tender: Continue cooking until the corn kernels are almost completely soft. Cooking time can vary depending on the locro, so the texture matters more than the clock.
Add milk and sugar: Once the corn is nearly soft, add 1 liter of milk and 150 g of sugar. Stir well and simmer for another 10 minutes over low heat.
Finish the flavoring: Remove the cinnamon stick and citrus peel. If you like, stir in a little vanilla extract now.
Serve or cool: Mazamorra can be eaten warm, lukewarm, or fully chilled. It will thicken a little more as it cools.
💡 Practical tips for Mazamorra # Getting the texture right Add hot water as needed: Locro absorbs a lot of liquid during the long cooking time. If the water cooks down too much, add more hot water.
Watch it closely after adding the milk: Once the milk and sugar are in the pot, stir more often and keep the heat low.
Do not let it get too thick in the pot: Mazamorra thickens as it cools, so it can still look a little looser when you take it off the heat.
Nutrition overview # The values below are based on one of eight servings of the basic recipe.
Calories: about 340 kcal Protein: about 9–10 g Carbohydrates: about 65 g Fat: about 4 g Sugar: about 25 g Note: These values are estimates. Miel de caña, honey, condensed milk, fruit, or any additional sweetener are not included.
🍽️ How is Mazamorra served? # Mazamorra can be eaten warm or chilled. Since the basic recipe is only mildly sweet, everyone at the table can adjust the sweetness to their own taste.
With miel de caña or sugar: Sugarcane syrup is one of the classic additions to Kaguyjy. Even a small amount adds a strong, caramel-like sweetness. Alternatively, you can sweeten it with a little extra sugar.
With a little milk: Chilled Mazamorra can be served with a small splash of milk.
With cinnamon: A little ground cinnamon works especially well with the milk version and complements its mild sweetness.
🔄 Recipe variations # Alongside the traditional serving styles, Mazamorra can also be adapted in more modern ways.
With fruit or fruit compote # Well-chilled Mazamorra pairs nicely with fresh fruit or a fruit compote that is not too sweet.
Good options include:
mango guava papaya banana Mango, papaya, and banana mainly add natural sweetness, while guava brings a stronger fruit flavor.
With sweetened condensed milk # For a creamier and much sweeter dessert version, drizzle a little sweetened condensed milk over the Mazamorra when serving. Since condensed milk already contains plenty of sugar, the Mazamorra usually does not need any extra sweetening.
Did you know? Mazamorra can mean very different things depending on where you are.
In Peru, the purple mazamorra morada is well known. In Colombia, mazamorra paisa is made from soft-cooked white corn and served with milk and panela, an unrefined cane sugar – and in Córdoba, Andalusia, the same name suddenly gets you a cold, savory cream made with almonds, bread, and garlic.

You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → 🇵🇾 Background: Mazamorra and Kaguyjy # Two names for one dish: Mazamorra and Kaguyjy # Kaguyjy is the Guaraní name for Mazamorra in Paraguay. Today, both names are used for this traditional sweet dish made with locro.
Traditional Guaraní names even distinguish between the different ways Kaguyjy is served:
kaguyjy eírare → with miel de caña kaguyjy kambýre → with milk kaguyjy asukáre → with sugar Indigenous roots and traditional preparation # The roots of Kaguyjy go back to Indigenous Guaraní corn cuisine. Its name is also connected with older Guaraní preparations: kagui referred to ceremonial drinks, some of them made from corn, while jy refers to cooking or a thick preparation. The name reflects this older culinary context, although Kaguyjy itself has been passed down as a cooked, thickened corn preparation.
The base is locro, a hard white corn. Traditionally, it was soaked and then simmered in water until the kernels were soft and the liquid had thickened.
Toward the end of cooking, filtered wood-ash lye (lejía) was added. It helped give the corn its slightly yellowish color and also affected the flavor. Not just any wood ash was used, because the type of wood could influence the result.
Today, this method is much less common. Modern Paraguayan recipes often use a small amount of baking soda, or bicarbonato de sodio, instead. That is also the practical method used in our recipe.
Corn appears in many other forms in Paraguayan cooking as well – from Sopa Paraguaya and Vori Vori to other recipes with corn.
Mazamorra in everyday Paraguayan food culture # Mazamorra is not an elaborate celebration dessert. Made with just a few simple ingredients, Kaguyjy was long part of straightforward everyday cooking and, for many Paraguayans, is still closely connected with memories of childhood and family.
Accounts of earlier times also mention women who sold Mazamorra. In the afternoons, they walked through neighborhoods with their pots and sold the freshly cooked dessert from door to door. These vendors were once a familiar part of the street scene, much like chipa sellers and other traveling food vendors.
Mazamorra is still part of Paraguay’s culinary tradition today. This is reflected not only in family recipes and memories, but also in its official recognition: In Resolution No. 05/2018 ↗, DINAPI includes Mazamorra on a list of Paraguay’s gastronomic and culinary heritage that was declared to be of national interest.
Mazamorra is not the only way locro is connected with Paraguayan food culture. Locro also plays a role in a tradition that is still very much alive. On October 1, Jopara and Karai Octubre are closely linked in Paraguay: people traditionally eat Jopara – a hearty stew made with locro, beans, and other ingredients depending on the recipe. According to folk belief, it is meant to keep scarcity and hardship away.
❓ Frequently Asked Questions # What kind of corn do I need for Mazamorra? For Paraguayan Mazamorra, use locro, a dried white corn. Fresh sweet corn, popcorn kernels, and cornmeal do not produce the typical texture. Do I need to soak locro before cooking? Yes. It is best to soak the locro in plenty of water for 8 to 12 hours or overnight. This helps the hard dried corn cook more evenly and more quickly afterward. Why is my corn still hard? Sometimes locro simply needs more time. The variety, age, and storage conditions can all affect cooking time. Make sure it has soaked long enough, has plenty of liquid, and is simmering steadily. If the water gets low, add more hot water and keep cooking until the kernels are truly soft. Is Mazamorra served warm or cold? Both are possible. Mazamorra can be eaten warm or lukewarm right after cooking, but in Paraguay it is also served completely cooled and chilled. It becomes a little firmer as it cools. How long does Mazamorra keep, and can I freeze it? Transfer leftovers to smaller containers as soon as possible, cover them well, and store them in the refrigerator. Mazamorra will keep for about 3 to 4 days.
You can freeze it, although the texture may change after thawing. When reheating, add a little milk if the Mazamorra has become too thick.
Is Mazamorra gluten-free? The basic ingredients – corn, milk, and sugar – are naturally gluten-free. If you have celiac disease, make sure the locro and any other ingredients are labeled appropriately and have not been cross-contaminated with gluten-containing products. Can I make Mazamorra vegan? Yes. Replace the cow’s milk with an unsweetened plant-based milk such as oat or almond milk. Miel de caña also works well for adding sweetness. Honey, however, is not a vegan alternative. Conclusion # Mazamorra shows how a few simple ingredients can become a dish with deep roots in Paraguayan culinary tradition. The recipe itself stays simple, and you can adjust the sweetness when serving with a little miel de caña.
The difference from rice pudding becomes obvious with the first spoonful: the soft corn kernels give Mazamorra its own distinctive texture and turn a short ingredient list into a dessert that is hard to confuse with anything else.
Enjoy making it, and buen provecho!
If the comparison with rice pudding made you curious, try Arroz con Leche next. You can find more sweet classics among our Paraguayan desserts and sweets.
Share & support Know someone who enjoys trying Paraguayan recipes? Share this recipe with them, or leave a like if you enjoyed the article.
summary: Mazamorra, or Kaguyjy, is part of Paraguay’s corn-based cuisine. This recipe combines traditional locro with a practical modern preparation.
title: Mazamorra Recipe: Paraguayan White Corn Dessert

When the smell of Asado is in the air in Paraguay, there is often more than just meat on the table. Next to it, you often find Chipa Guasu: a juicy corn casserole that combines slightly sweet fresh corn, tasty onions and the typical Paraguayan cheese (Queso Paraguay).
Chipa Guasu is a traditional Paraguayan recipe that is deeply rooted in everyday cooking in the country. If you live in Paraguay or stay here for a while, you will sooner or later come across it almost automatically: at family meals, at relaxed Sunday Asado gatherings or at events around holidays.
This mix of simple ingredients, little effort, juicy flavor and shared meals makes this dish a firm part of Paraguayan cuisine.
In this article, I show you step by step how to make Chipa Guasu yourself, which ingredients you can replace and what you should keep in mind so that the corn casserole stays nice and juicy.
📝 Chipa Guasu recipe - step by step # At a glance Difficulty: Easy Preparation time: approx. 15 minutes preparation + 45 to 60 minutes baking time Servings: 6 to 8, depending on whether you serve it as a main dish or side dish Cooking with US measurements? Temperatures are also provided in Fahrenheit. Our cooking measurement guide offers practical conversion tables for cups, ounces, and other units. 🛒 Ingredients you need # You probably already have most of the ingredients at home. The following overview shows you what you really need for the basic recipe and what you can add if you want to refine it.
Main ingredients # 1 kg corn (fresh or frozen corn) 3 eggs 400 g Queso Paraguay 400 to 500 ml milk 2 onions 100 g butter, lard or oil salt to taste Optional ingredients # A little cream for extra creaminess Fresh bell pepper or Locote for color and freshness Pepper, garlic or chili for more spice Fresh herbs such as chives Which ingredients can you replace? # Flexible alternatives for availability or diet Chipa Guasu is naturally gluten-free and, in its classic basic version, vegetarian.
Corn: Fresh corn is ideal. As an alternative, you can use frozen corn or canned corn, although frozen corn is usually less watery.
Cheese: Instead of Queso Paraguay, you can use mild cheese such as young Gouda, Edam, butter cheese or mozzarella. A mix of feta and mozzarella adds a little more flavor.
Milk: Lactose-free milk works 1:1. Plant-based milk such as oat or soy milk is also possible, but it changes the flavor slightly.
Fat: Instead of butter or lard, you can use neutral vegetable oil. For more flavor, you can also mix butter and oil.
Kitchen tools you need # Cutting board, knife and a pan for softening the onions Stand blender or food processor, alternatively a hand blender A large bowl A rectangular baking dish 👩‍🍳 Step-by-step preparation # Preparation # Prepare the corn and cheese: Cut the corn kernels from the cob or use prepared corn. Cut the cheese into small cubes or grate it coarsely. Soften the onions: Cut the onions into small cubes and cook them in the oil until translucent. Let them cool briefly afterwards. Blend: Put the corn together with the milk into the blender. Blend the mixture only roughly. A few whole corn kernels give it a great texture! Mix: Beat the eggs in a large bowl until foamy. Stir in the onion-oil mixture, the corn mixture and the crumbled cheese. Season with salt. Baking # Preheat the oven to 180 to 200 °C (350 to 400 °F) top/bottom heat.
Grease the baking dish and pour in the mixture.
Then place the corn casserole in the oven for approx. 45 to 60 minutes, until the top is golden brown and the mixture has set.
Let it rest briefly. Chipa Guasu tastes especially good lukewarm and is easier to cut.
💡 Practical tips for Chipa Guasu # So your corn casserole stays nice and juicy Do not blend the corn too finely: A few whole or roughly chopped corn kernels give the typical texture. Keep an eye on moisture: Canned corn and fresh mozzarella should drain well, otherwise the mixture can become too soft. If the ingredients are very moist, use a little less milk. Frozen corn is often the better alternative to canned corn. Choose a mild cheese: Mild cheese works best. Very strong cheese, for example mountain cheese, can quickly overpower the natural sweetness of the corn. Do not use a dish that is too large: In a very large dish, the casserole becomes flatter and dries out faster. Do not bake it too long: The top may be golden brown, but inside it should still stay juicy. Nutrition overview # The values refer to one portion when the basic recipe is divided into about 8 servings.
Calories: approx. 400 to 450 kcal Protein: approx. 16 to 20 g Carbohydrates: approx. 28 to 35 g Fat: approx. 25 to 32 g Fiber: approx. 3 to 5 g Sugar: approx. 8 to 12 g, mainly naturally from corn and milk Note: These values are estimates and vary depending on the exact ingredients, type of fat and portion size. With 6 larger portions, the values are higher.
🍽️ What goes well with Chipa Guasu? # As a gluten-free and vegetarian dish, this juicy corn casserole can be served in many different ways depending on the occasion. Here are a few ideas that go well with it.
Side dishes Drinks Classic: with Asado, grilled meat and manioc (Yuca) Fresh & light: with green salad, tomato salad or simple coleslaw Paraguayan combination: with empanadas, Tortillas Paraguayas or Pajagua Mascada For many people: as a side dish on a larger family table with meat, salad and other small dishes Typically Paraguayan: Tereré on hot days Classic & simple: water, also nice with lemon Fruity: fresh juices or lemonade For family celebrations: Clericó with fresh fruit, especially around Christmas and New Year For cooler days: Mate cocido or coffee 🔄 Recipe variations # Chipa Guasu already tastes very good in its classic version, but it can also be changed into hearty or modern versions.
Well-known variations # 🥩 Chipa Guasu So’o with minced meat filling # A well-known hearty variation is Chipa Guasu So’o, meaning the corn casserole is combined with a meat filling. Usually, minced beef is cooked first and then baked between two layers of corn mixture. This makes the dish much more filling and works well as a main dish.
Ingredients for the meat filling:
approx. 400 to 500 g minced beef 1 onion 1 small bell pepper or Locote 1 to 2 garlic cloves salt, pepper and cumin to taste a little oil for frying optional: a little tomato or tomato paste Quick preparation:
Finely chop the onion, Locote and garlic and cook them in a little oil. Add the minced beef and fry until crumbly. Season with salt, pepper and a little cumin. Optionally add a little tomato or tomato paste and let it cook down briefly. Then place half of the Chipa Guasu mixture into the dish, spread the meat filling on top and cover it with the rest of the corn mixture. Bake as in the basic recipe until the top is golden brown and the mixture has set.
Modern variations # For a creamier variation, you can replace part of the fresh corn with pumpkin and mix it into the batter along with the other ingredients. This makes the whole dish slightly sweet and keeps it nice and moist. As an alternative, you can use sweet potato instead of pumpkin.
Small muffins are also possible. They are good for buffets, picnics or as finger food.

You can unsubscribe at any time. Sign-up with email confirmation. You can find privacy information in the Privacy Policy. On Telegram and interested in Paraguay4Life? Go to the Telegram channel → 🇵🇾 Background information about the recipe # What makes Chipa Guasu special? # Chipa Guasu is a traditional Paraguayan corn dish that shows how much flavor can come from a few simple ingredients. Fresh corn, onions, eggs, milk and cheese together do not make a dry cake, but rather a soft corn casserole with a slightly sweet taste.
The name itself also tells you something:
Chipa in Paraguay stands for a traditional baked food. Guasu means “big” in Guaraní. So Chipa Guasu means something like “big Chipa”. Unlike the small Chipas made from manioc starch, it is not shaped as individual baked goods. Instead, it is baked in one large dish and then cut into pieces.
Chipa Guasu or Sopa Paraguaya? Chipa Guasu and Sopa Paraguaya are often compared because both dishes are classics of Paraguayan cuisine and contain ingredients such as corn, cheese, onions, eggs and milk.
Chipa Guasu is made with fresh corn or corn kernels. This keeps it softer, juicier and more like a casserole.
Sopa Paraguaya is made with cornmeal. It is firmer, more bread-like and usually easier to cut into clear pieces.
If you are looking for a soft, juicy corn dish, Chipa Guasu is the better choice. If you want a firmer side dish, Sopa Paraguaya is often more suitable.
What role does Chipa Guasu play in Paraguay? # This traditional corn casserole is closely connected in Paraguay with family, simple ingredients and shared meals. If you live in Paraguay or stay here for a while, you will sooner or later come across it almost automatically: at family meals, on holidays or at Asado, the relaxed Paraguayan Sunday barbecue.
Chipa Guasu is more than just a side dish. Often, this oven dish comes straight to the table in one large baking dish and is shared. That fits well with Paraguayan food culture: it is not served in a complicated way, but eaten together.
Especially in the countryside (campo), fresh corn plays an important role. Around the corn harvest, when a lot of Choclo is available, Chipa Guasu is prepared especially often. Modern ovens are also used, but the traditional Tataqua, the Paraguayan clay or stone oven, is often preferred for this.
Served warm from the oven, this classic is especially good on cooler days and fits wonderfully with typical winter dishes in Paraguay. At the same time, it is not only a winter dish. On warm days, Chipa Guasu goes well with a fresh salad and belongs to the simple summer dishes that fill you up without much effort.
That is what makes Chipa Guasu so typically Paraguayan: it is uncomplicated, filling, affordable and still something special. It connects local ingredients, family and shared meals in a dish that works just as well in everyday life as on holidays.
Its cultural roots are also reflected in the fact that Chipa Guasu is one of the traditional foods that DINAPI included in an official list of Paraguay’s gastronomic and culinary heritage ↗ in 2018.
Which ingredients shape Chipa Guasu? # The nice thing about this recipe is that many ingredients are often already found in Paraguayan households. Corn, eggs, milk, cheese, oil and salt are part of the typical basic food staples in many families.
The fresh corn and typical Queso Paraguay are especially important. They shape the flavor, texture and character of the dish.
Corn - the heart of Chipa Guasu # Without corn, Chipa Guasu would not be possible. In Paraguay, fresh corn, often called Choclo here, is a firm part of everyday cooking and plays an important role in many traditional dishes.
Corn is much more than an ingredient in Paraguay. It is:
a basic food a cultural symbol the base of many recipes like this one, Sopa Paraguaya, Vorí Vorí or Paraguayan corn tortillas For this Paraguayan corn casserole, fresh corn is especially important because it shapes the flavor, sweetness and consistency. It makes the casserole juicy, slightly sweet and gives it the typical yellow color.
Corn also provides carbohydrates, fiber and different vitamins and minerals. Together with the other ingredients, it becomes a dish that keeps you full for a long time.
Queso Paraguay - the typical cheese # Classic Queso Paraguay is a fresh, mild cow’s milk cheese. It is not aged for long, tastes slightly tangy to milky and has a soft but sliceable texture. When baked, it does not melt away completely. It keeps a little bite and still combines well with the other ingredients.
In the countryside, you often get Queso Paraguay directly from neighbors, small producers or local markets. In cities, you usually find it in the supermarket, in the refrigerated section or at the cheese counter.
❓ Frequently asked questions # Can I prepare Chipa Guasu ahead of time? Yes, you can prepare the mixture a few hours ahead and keep it covered in the fridge. Before baking, it should stand at room temperature for a short time so it does not go into the oven ice-cold. If the mixture feels very firm after chilling, stir it briefly again. Can you freeze Chipa Guasu? Yes, Chipa Guasu freezes well. It is best to let it cool completely, cut it into portions and pack it airtight. For reheating, the oven works better than the microwave because the surface becomes a little firmer again. How long does Chipa Guasu keep in the fridge? Chipa Guasu keeps for about 3 to 4 days in the fridge if it is well covered or packed airtight. You can serve it cold or warm it briefly in the oven. Is Chipa Guasu gluten-free? Yes, Chipa Guasu is gluten-free in its classic basic version because it is made with corn instead of wheat flour. But if you need to cook strictly gluten-free, make sure that the cheese, spices or ready-made replacement products do not contain additives with gluten. Can I make Chipa Guasu without a blender? Yes, you can. You can roughly chop the corn with a hand blender or mash part of the kernels with a fork. The texture will be a little more rustic, but that fits Chipa Guasu well. However, the corn should not stay completely whole because the mixture will bind less well. Why does my Chipa Guasu become too dry? This often happens when the baking time is too long, the baking dish is too large or the mixture does not contain enough liquid. Chipa Guasu should stay juicy inside and not feel like a dry cake. A slightly smaller dish, well-drained corn and, if needed, a small splash of milk or cream can help. Is Chipa Guasu a main dish or a side dish? Both are possible. In Paraguay, Chipa Guasu is often served with grilled food or larger meals, but it can also work on its own or with something fresh as a simple vegetarian dish. What is the difference between Chipa Guasu and Sopa Paraguaya? The main difference is the base. Chipa Guasu is made with fresh corn or corn kernels, so it stays juicy, soft and more like a casserole. Sopa Paraguaya is made with cornmeal and is firmer, more like a savory corn bread. Conclusion # Chipa Guasu shows how much flavor can come from simple ingredients. With fresh corn, cheese and onions, you get a juicy corn casserole that belongs to traditional Paraguayan cuisine and still fits easily into everyday life.
Have fun cooking and buen provecho!
Love the combination of corn and cheese? Try Vori Vori too, where the same duo becomes small dumplings in a hearty chicken soup. You’ll find more Paraguayan recipes with corn in our corn recipe collection.
Share & support Did this traditional Chipa Guasu recipe inspire you and make you curious about Paraguay? Then feel free to give the post a like and share it with other South America fans - and help make Paraguay’s culinary variety more visible.
summary: Chipa Guasu is more than just a side dish: it is a piece of Paraguayan life. Here is how to make this juicy corn casserole at home.
title: Chipa Guasu Recipe: Juicy Corn Casserole from Paraguay
